parts.title: The imbalances, and how to plan with them
parts.blurb: Ten differences that decide what a position is about, one lesson each, then the routine that turns them into moves. Finishes with a position where naming the imbalances is the only way to find the move.

parts.title: Knights
parts.blurb: What a knight is actually good at, rank by rank, and the two ways it dies. Bad squares can be fixed. Being dominated cannot.

parts.title: Bishops
parts.blurb: Forget good bishops and bad bishops. A bishop is active, useful, or a tall pawn, and telling which is which decides what you should be trading and what you should be burying.

parts.title: Bishops against knights
parts.blurb: The fight the two previous parts were preparing you for. Break up the pair, deny the knight its squares, and shape the board so your own minor piece is the one that matters.

parts.title: Rooks
parts.blurb: A rook is worth what its file is worth. How to make a file, how to take one that is contested, when to open it, and why a rook on the seventh with no targets is worth almost nothing.

parts.title: Playing the player, and yourself
parts.blurb: The half of the book that is not about the board. Greed, fear of material imbalance, reacting to threats that were never made, and the habit of asking what your position wants instead of what the opponent is asking of you.

parts.title: Target consciousness
parts.blurb: Before you can attack anything you have to know what there is to attack. Building the inventory, and the one case where the imbalances demand that you drop everything and go for the king.

parts.title: Statics against dynamics
parts.blurb: Some advantages keep and some expire, and the two demand opposite speeds. How to tell which you are holding, how to convert one into the other, and why the roles in a position are not fixed.

parts.title: Space
parts.blurb: The imbalance amateurs respect least and grandmasters prize most. Why room to move wins games on its own, how to keep an advantage in it, and the four ways out when you are the one being squeezed.

parts.title: Passed pawns
parts.blurb: The pawn everyone overvalues. When a passer is a game winner, when it is a piece of furniture, and why handing one to the opponent is sometimes the strongest move on the board.

parts.title: Imbalances in the opening
parts.blurb: Where the imbalances you have spent the whole course learning about actually come from. Knowing what a line gives both sides, choosing openings that fit you, and treating a theoretical position as an argument rather than a memory test.

lessons.title: What an imbalance is
text: An imbalance is any significant difference between the two sides. Notice what that definition leaves out. It says nothing about who is better. A difference belongs to whoever can use it, and in almost every position both players own several.

The starting position is the only position in chess with no imbalances at all. It is perfectly symmetrical. White moves, the symmetry breaks, and from that moment on the board has something to tell you.

That is the whole point of naming them. A plan is not something you invent out of taste or mood. It is something you read off the board. Find the differences, then look for moves that use them, and the plan tends to appear on its own.

The list runs through the rest of the course. Superior minor piece, pawn structure, space, material, control of a key file, control of a hole or weak square, lead in development, initiative, king safety, and statics against dynamics.

ex.prompt: Which of these is the working definition of an imbalance?
ex.why: An imbalance is a difference, not an advantage. Deciding who benefits from it is the next step, and often both sides benefit from different ones.
options: An advantage held by one side
Any significant difference between the two positions
A difference in material
A threat that has to be answered

ex.prompt: You have listed the imbalances in a position. What do you do next?
ex.why: Chase moves, not plans. When your moves cater to the imbalances, the plan turns out to have been there all along.
options: Choose the plan you enjoy playing most
Look for moves that take advantage of them
Count material and start trading
Wait and see what the opponent commits to

ex.prompt: No imbalances exist yet. Play a first move that takes central space and frees two pieces at once.
ex.why: Both central pawn moves claim space and open lines for a bishop and the queen. The first imbalance of the game is created by White in one move.

lessons.title: Superior minor piece, bishop over knight
text: Bishops and knights are both worth about three points, which is exactly the kind of accounting that hides the truth. What matters is what each one does in the position actually on the board.

White has a bishop raking two long diagonals that cut into the black position. Black has a knight with nowhere useful to go and no square it can reach that changes anything. The point count says the game is level. The board says otherwise.

The bishop is not the only difference here. White also owns more central and queenside space, a target on a7 that a rook can reach through b1 and b7, and a mating idea after the bishop steps to c3 and the queen follows to d4. Imbalances stack up, and the winning plan usually uses several at once.

ex.prompt: Two minor pieces are left on the board. Click the one that is winning the fight.
ex.why: The bishop hits two open diagonals and can switch between them in one move. The knight defends and does nothing else.

ex.prompt: Everything is working except one white piece. Bring it into the game.
ex.why: Both rook moves are good. The rook was the only white piece with no job, and finding the idle piece is the most reliable question in a position you do not understand.

ex.prompt: White switches to a mating plan. Play the move that starts it.
ex.why: The bishop steps aside so the queen can take the long diagonal behind it. With the knight tied down and the king short of cover, Black has nothing to meet the battery with.

lessons.title: Superior minor piece, knight over bishop
text: Reverse the previous lesson and nothing about the principle changes. Here the bishop is the bad piece, hemmed in by pawns on squares it can never attack, and the knight is the best piece on the board.

The knight sits on e6 and cannot be removed. That is the difference between a good square and a home. A piece that can be chased away is a visitor. A piece that no pawn can ever attack has moved in permanently.
White adds space on all three sectors and a rook route to b7 hitting a7 and c7. Again the win comes from stacking imbalances rather than from any single clever move.

ex.prompt: Click the minor piece that rules this position.
ex.why: The knight attacks squares deep in the black camp. The bishop is boxed in by its own pawn structure and has no future.

ex.prompt: Why can Black never drive the knight off e6?
ex.why: Only a pawn on d7 or f7 could hit e6, and neither pawn exists any more. A square no enemy pawn can reach is a permanent home.
options: The knight is defended too many times
No black pawn can ever attack that square
Every black piece is pinned
Taking it would lose the queen

ex.prompt: Open a second front. Start the rook manoeuvre aimed at a7 and c7.
ex.why: The rook lands on the seventh rank with tempo. Black cannot both hold the b file and watch the knight.

lessons.title: Pawn structure, the further advanced passer
text: Black is a pawn up and has two passed pawns against one. Counting says Black is winning comfortably. Black is in fact lost.

A passed pawn is not a number to be totted up. What decides its worth is how far it has travelled and how much of the army is helping it. White has one passer on b6, one square from the end, with the queen, both rooks and the bishop all pointing at b8.
Black has two passers that are barely off the start line and nothing organised behind them. One pawn with a team behind it beats two pawns on their own.

ex.prompt: Black has an extra pawn and two passers to White's one. Who is better?
ex.why: Advancement and support beat raw count. White queens by force and Black never gets going.
options: White
Roughly equal
Black

ex.prompt: Click the square White's whole position is aimed at.
ex.why: Every white piece is working on b8. Once you see the target square, the moves that get you there are easy to find.

ex.prompt: White to move. Push the point home.
ex.why: The pawn cannot be stopped without giving up a rook, and after the dust settles White simply invades on c8.

lessons.title: Pawn structure, hunting the weak pawn
text: Black has an isolated pawn on e6. No pawn can ever defend it, so pieces have to do the job, and pieces that are busy defending are not doing anything else.
White has three attackers on it already and is still not finished. Chess is a team game, and the way to win a target is to keep adding attackers until the defenders run out.

The bishop swings to h3 as a fourth attacker and the knight comes to g5 as a fifth. At that point the pawn is beyond saving, and the defensive contortions Black needs create fresh weaknesses somewhere else.

ex.prompt: Click Black's weakest pawn.
ex.why: It is isolated, so no pawn will ever defend it. Every attack on it has to be met by a piece.

ex.prompt: Three white pieces already hit e6. Bring a fourth.
ex.why: The bishop had no other purpose, and from h3 it joins the pile. The knight follows to g5 as the fifth attacker.

ex.prompt: What is the method being used against the weak pawn?
ex.why: Count attackers against defenders. If you can add one more attacker than the opponent can add a defender, the target falls.
options: Trade pieces until the endgame
Add attackers until they outnumber the defenders
Push pawns at it
Win a different pawn first

lessons.title: Space
text: Black is so cramped that the pieces are treading on each other. White has claimed territory in every sector and the white pieces have somewhere to go on every move.

Space on its own does not win anything. It wins when you use it to break into enemy territory, which is why a space advantage almost always ends in a pawn break. Here White can open the queenside with c5 or the kingside with g5, and both advances take even more ground on the way.

The other half of the rule belongs to the cramped side. Trades help the player with less room, because the fewer pieces are left, the less the shortage of squares hurts. So the player with space avoids trades and the player without them seeks them out.

ex.prompt: Extra space converts into something real only when you...
ex.why: Territory is a means. Without a break the extra room is just a nicer looking position that never gets anywhere.
options: Trade pieces off
Break into enemy territory
Win material with it first
Castle on the opposite wing

ex.prompt: White has room on both wings. Open a road into the black position.
ex.why: Both breaks are logical, and both grab more space as they go. Rcg1 and Rh1, preparing g5 first, are reasonable too.

ex.prompt: Which side wants to trade pieces here?
ex.why: The cramped side trades. Each pair that comes off gives the remaining black pieces more of the little room there is.
options: White, to reach a winning endgame
Black, to make the shortage of squares hurt less
Neither side

lessons.title: Material
text: White is solid and Black looks active, which is the moment most players stop looking. The c7 pawn is still at home, and that detail hands White the chance to take on b7.

One pawn does not end the game. What it does is change the terms. Every trade from here brings White closer to an endgame a pawn up, so Black has to avoid the simplification that would normally be the way to neutralise a solid position.

The capture also leaves a hole on c6 and gives White the long light squared diagonal. And it puts Black under a kind of pressure that does not appear in any evaluation, which is the obligation to prove the pawn was worth something.

ex.prompt: White to move. Take what is on offer.
ex.why: The bishop grabs the pawn and comes home. Black has no way to trap it, and 1...c6 2.Qc4+ or 1...Bg4 2.Qc4+ both lose more material.

ex.prompt: Why is one pawn worth spending two moves on here?
ex.why: This is what endgame odds means. Being a pawn up turns the normal defensive resource of trading into something Black cannot afford.
options: It wins the game on the spot
Every trade from now on brings White nearer a won endgame
It opens a file for the rooks
It creates a passed pawn immediately

ex.prompt: Taking on b7 leaves a permanent hole in Black's camp. Click it.
ex.why: With the b pawn gone, c6 can never be defended by a pawn again, and the white bishop owns the diagonal running through it.

lessons.title: Control of a key file
text: The e file is the only open file on the board and White has both rooks on it. Add more space and a bishop that owns the long light squared diagonal and White is clearly better.

The catch is that plenty has already been traded and the bishops are of opposite colours, which is the classic recipe for a draw. Black also intends to put a rook on e8 and swap the heavy pieces off the file, and a file with no rooks on it is worth nothing.

So White plays Bc6 and takes the e8 square away for good. What follows is worth naming, because it is a state rather than a move. Black now has no active plan at all and can only wait. White plays for a win or a draw. Black plays for a loss or a draw. Nobody wants that side of the bargain.

ex.prompt: Black wants to neutralise the file. Click the square Black is heading for.
ex.why: A rook to e8 forces trades along the file, and once the rooks come off, opposite coloured bishops make the draw very likely.

ex.prompt: Stop that idea and take the file for good.
ex.why: The bishop covers e8 from a distance. Black cannot contest the file any more and is reduced to waiting.

ex.prompt: Play has continued Bc6 Qg4 Re4. Click the white piece that must now stay exactly where it is.
ex.why: The rook on e4 also sees e8, but a rook there only offers a trade, which is precisely what Black wants. The bishop covers e8 without offering anything back, so the moment it steps off that diagonal, Rde8 arrives and the file is neutralised.

ex.prompt: After Bc6, what results is Black playing for?
ex.why: With no active plan available, the best Black can hope for is that White fails to break through. That asymmetry is worth more than most material advantages.
options: A win or a draw
A loss or a draw
All three are still open

lessons.title: Control of a hole
text: Both minor pieces have fallen on hard times. The black bishop is buried behind its own pawns with no way to improve. The white knight sits on c1, which is no better.

The difference is that the knight has somewhere to go and the bishop does not. Two squares in the black position can never be attacked by a pawn again, d5 and e6, and a knight that reaches one of them cannot be evicted.

Once you know the destination, the route takes care of itself. Nd3 followed by Nf4 and Ne6 takes three moves, and spending three moves to install a piece for the rest of the game is a bargain. Short range pieces need to be walked to where they are going, and there is usually time to do it.

ex.prompt: The knight has two dream squares available. Click the better one.
ex.why: Both are holes, but e6 is deeper, hits more of the black camp and stares at the black king's cover. Aim for the best square, not the nearest one.

ex.prompt: Start the journey. Play the first move of the route to e6.
ex.why: Either square works as a staging post. Nd3 and Ne2 both head for f4 and then e6.

ex.prompt: What makes e6 a home rather than just a good square?
ex.why: The d and f pawns that would have covered e6 are gone or fixed. Nothing can ever ask the knight to leave.
options: It is defended by two white pieces
No black pawn can ever attack it
It cannot be reached by the black king
It is on an open file

lessons.title: Lead in development
text: White has given up a pawn in the opening and has two pieces out to Black's one. More to the point, every remaining white piece has a natural square waiting for it, and the black pieces do not.

A lead in development is a wasting asset. It has to be used before the other side catches up, and the way to use it is to open lines while the enemy king is still in the middle. That is what every gambit is buying with its pawn.

The defender's job is the mirror image. Keep the position closed, get castled, and let the extra material do the talking once the pieces are all out. Black went wrong here by developing to a square that invited e5, and the game did not last much longer.

ex.prompt: You are the side behind in development. What is the right policy?
ex.why: Opening the position plays into the hands of whoever has more pieces ready. Close it, castle, and the extra pawn starts to matter.
options: Open lines and fight for the initiative
Keep things closed until the king is safe and the pieces are out
Trade queens immediately
Push pawns on the wing

ex.prompt: Black replies 6...Nf6, which does nothing about the centre. Rip the position open.
ex.why: A second pawn buys the lines. Black had to try 7...Ng4, since after the game continuation the king never escapes the centre and the knight mates on c7.

lessons.title: Initiative
text: The initiative is best understood as whose agenda the game is following. Whoever is being asked questions has lost it, and whoever is asking them has it.

White has just played Nh4 with the idea of Ng6, and would like to bring the other knight to e3 and then d5. Black can stop the threat with Kh7, and that is exactly the trap. A purely defensive move answers the question but leaves White free to keep asking new ones.

Qf7 stops Ng6 and attacks the knight on c4 in the same breath. Now the e3 square is unavailable and any knight retreat drops the a2 pawn. Nothing about the material has changed, but the roles have swapped, and White is the one scrambling.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Meet the threat with a move that makes one of its own.
ex.why: It covers g6 and hits c4 at the same time. Defending and pushing your own agenda in one move is how the initiative changes hands.

ex.prompt: Kh7 also stops Ng6. Why is it worse?
ex.why: After Kh7 White continues Bxc5 and Ne3 heading for d5, and Black never gets a word in. A move that only defends hands over the whole conversation.
options: It loses a pawn
It is purely defensive, so White keeps a free hand
It walks into a discovered check
It blocks the rook

ex.prompt: After Qf7, click the white piece that has become a problem for White.
ex.why: The knight is attacked and has no comfortable square. Most retreats drop the a2 pawn, and moving it at all gives up the d5 plan.

lessons.title: King safety
text: White is a pawn down. In exchange White is fully developed, castled, and looking at a black king that is still sitting in the centre with the e file about to open.

A king in the middle is not a small inconvenience to be tidied up later. It is the imbalance that decides more short games than any other, and the side that owns it usually has one move to fix it and never gets that move.

The finish is worth playing through, because the pattern of dragging a king out into the open recurs constantly. What matters for the rest of the course is not the combination itself. It is recognising the moment when the enemy king has run out of time.

ex.prompt: White is a pawn down. What justifies playing for an attack?
ex.why: Development and king safety are the two imbalances in White's favour, and both fade the moment Black castles. That is why the attack has to start now.
options: The bishop pair
A lead in development and a black king still in the centre
A passed pawn
Control of the only open file

ex.prompt: White to move. Open the king up.
ex.why: The king is pulled out and never gets home. Black should decline with Qc7, but after Nxh8 there was not much left to play for either.

lessons.title: Statics against dynamics
text: White has an isolated pawn on d4. Two world class players can look at this position and want opposite sides of it, and both of them are right.

Black sees a static weakness. The pawn cannot be defended by another pawn, it will still be there in the endgame, and the square in front of it is a permanent home for a black piece. Static advantages are patient. They keep.

White sees a dynamic strength. The pawn takes central space, it denies c5 and e5 to the black pieces, and the extra room fuels a kingside attack. Dynamic advantages are not patient. They have to be turned into something before they fade, either a knockout or a static plus of your own.

ex.prompt: Click the black piece that is already doing the main job against the isolated pawn.
ex.why: The knight sits on the square directly in front of the pawn, which no white pawn can ever attack. It blockades the pawn and cannot be moved on, and that is the whole static case for Black.

ex.prompt: A dynamic advantage has to be...
ex.why: Dynamic factors are on a clock. Convert them into a knockout or into a lasting static advantage, or watch them evaporate.
options: Defended carefully and kept for the endgame
Used quickly, before it disappears
Traded off for material
Ignored until the position stabilises

ex.prompt: Which side is happier when many pieces come off?
ex.why: Trades kill the dynamic half of the argument and leave the static half standing. The isolated pawn is a middlegame asset and an endgame liability.
options: White, because the attack simplifies
Black, because only the weak pawn is left
Neither, the position is symmetrical

lessons.title: Planning is reading, not inventing
text: Once the imbalances are second nature, a position like this is read rather than solved. White has queenside space. The black c7 pawn is potentially weak, and pushing it to c6 or c5 walks into bxc6, leaving a weak b6 pawn and a hole on b5. The d5 pawn can never be defended by another pawn. Black's only counterplay is on the kingside, where four black pieces are already pointing.

Two more entries matter more than the rest. The black bishop on d6 supports c7 and would lead any kingside attack, so it is Black's most useful piece. The white bishop on b2 stares into its own pawn chain, so it is White's least useful piece.
Put those two facts side by side and the move suggests itself. Trade the worst piece you own for the best piece the opponent owns. That is not a plan anyone invented. It is what the list says to do.

ex.prompt: Click White's least useful piece.
ex.why: The bishop on b2 looks down a diagonal blocked by its own d4 pawn. Find your worst piece and you have usually found your move.

ex.prompt: Trade it for Black's most useful piece. Play the move.
ex.why: White's worst piece comes off for the bishop that both guarded c7 and would have led the kingside attack. That is the best trade available on the board.

ex.prompt: Black recaptured with the c pawn rather than the rook. What did that buy, and what did it cost?
ex.why: Recapturing with the rook would have left c7 as a permanent worry. The pawn recapture cures that and takes e5 away from the white knight, and the price is a d5 pawn that needs babysitting for the rest of the game.
options: It wins a pawn but loses the exchange
It removes the weak c7 pawn and covers e5, at the cost of a permanently weak d5
It opens the c file for Black
It defends the b6 pawn but weakens the king

ex.prompt: Play has continued Rc1 Ndf6 h3. Click the pawn White will spend the rest of the game working against.
ex.why: Topalov said it plainly. It did not matter how long it took, because in the end the rooks would come off and the structural problems would be all that was left.

lessons.title: Following the board against your own taste
text: White is in complete control. The d file belongs to White, which turns both black rooks into spectators, and the white queen sits on one of the weakened kingside dark squares. Black can barely move, so there is no incoming fire to worry about.
Agonising over a plan here gets you nowhere. Asking one question gets you everything. White owns the kingside dark squares, so which piece can still penetrate on them?

The candidates run out fast. Ng5 leaps to a dark square and threatens f7, but Qxg2 is check. Rf4 heads for f7, but Qxd7 takes the rook. That leaves exactly one white piece that can travel the dark square highway, and beginner conditioning says it is the one piece you never use before the endgame.

ex.prompt: Why do the natural Ng5 and Rf4 both fail?
ex.why: Both moves are the right idea and the wrong piece. Ruling them out is what leaves only one candidate standing.
options: Both hang a rook to a knight fork
Qxg2 is check after one, and Qxd7 wins a rook after the other
Both allow a perpetual check
Black simply castles out of trouble

ex.prompt: One white piece can still reach the dark squares. Send it.
ex.why: If you had a bishop on d2 you would play Bh6 and force mate without a second thought. The king does the same job here. Kh6 followed by mate on g7 cannot be met.

ex.prompt: What made this move findable?
ex.why: The imbalance was ownership of the kingside dark squares. Once that was named, the search was reduced to a list of pieces, and the list had one entry left.
options: Deep calculation of every line
Naming the imbalance first, then asking which piece could use it
Recognising a known mating pattern
Playing the most aggressive move available

lessons.title: Three ways of thinking
text: Silman runs one game past three imaginary players. Mr Metallic quotes an engine number after every move and understands none of it. Mr Pink knows only material and threats, so he counts the pawn and looks for the next check. Mr Orange thinks in imbalances.
White has just grabbed a second pawn on c6. Mr Metallic reports a healthy plus. Mr Pink is delighted, because a pawn is a pawn and the endgame will take care of itself.

Mr Orange sees what the pawn actually cost. Recapturing gives Black a lead in development, which is a dynamic plus that has to be used quickly, control of the hole on d4, which is permanent, and pressure against a backward white d pawn, which is also permanent. He is a pawn down and he is better, and he can say exactly why.

ex.prompt: Black to move, a pawn down. Play the recapture.
ex.why: The knight recapture develops, adds a second attacker to d4 and keeps the pressure on the backward d pawn. Every point of Black's compensation comes from this one move.

ex.prompt: What did Black get for the pawn?
ex.why: One dynamic asset that has to be spent soon, and two static ones that keep. Being able to list them is the whole difference between Mr Orange and the other two.
options: A direct attack on the king
A lead in development, the d4 hole, and a backward white d pawn
The bishop pair and an open file
Nothing concrete, it is a bluff

ex.prompt: Mr Metallic quotes accurate engine numbers throughout. Why is he not the player to imitate?
ex.why: An engine is useful and can also become a crutch that prevents you from improving. Borrowing a number is not the same as understanding a position, and the difference shows the moment you sit down at a board.
options: The numbers are usually wrong
He repeats an evaluation without understanding what produces it
He calculates too slowly to use in a real game
He ignores the clock

lessons.title: Talk to the board
text: Here is the routine itself, in the order it has to happen. First the Armageddon Discourse, which means checking for crude threats and obvious tactics. Players above about 1800 do this without noticing. Anyone prone to blunders should do it deliberately.
Then, and only then, the real work. Name the imbalances for both sides. Then ask the board what move, or short series of moves, takes advantage of them.

Notice what is missing. You are not hunting for a plan. Chasing the word plan is what makes people freeze. Chase moves that cater to the imbalances and the plan turns out to have been there all along.

White reasons through it out loud. Black will play Bg7 and tie White to the e5 pawn. White's assets are the hole on f6 that g6 created, a lead in development, and a black king still in the centre, and all three fade the moment Black castles. So something has to happen now.

ex.prompt: What comes first when it is your move?
ex.why: Make sure the hammer is not about to land, then move on to the loftier considerations. Positional understanding does not survive hanging a piece.
options: Name the imbalances
Check for crude threats and basic tactics
Decide on a plan
Calculate the most forcing line

ex.prompt: Bg5 heads for the f6 hole. Why does White reject it?
ex.why: Aiming at the right square with the wrong move order achieves nothing. The idea survives, the move does not.
options: It loses a piece to a knight fork
Bg7 comes, and then Bf6 Bxf6 exf6 Ng8 just wins the e pawn
It blocks the g file
It allows Black to castle with check

ex.prompt: Black is about to castle and solve everything. Play the move that stops that being comfortable.
ex.why: Ripping the position open is the only way to use a lead in development and a central king before both disappear. Qd2 and Bh6 was the quieter option and White judged it as not enough.

ex.prompt: Silman warns against chasing one thing in particular. What?
ex.why: Look for moves that cater to the imbalances rather than for a grand plan. Do that and plans materialise on their own, which is the opposite of how most players are taught.
options: Material
The word plan
Checks
Symmetry

lessons.title: Reading a position, Nisipeanu against Milov
text: This is the whole method in one move. The position is sharp, so counting weak pawns on a6, c5, e4, f2 and h2 is not the right conversation to be having.

Look at what the position is offering instead. The knight on g7 is pinned. If the bishop were not on h6, Qh8 would be check and mate would follow. If Qf6 were available it would win the knight. Every one of those observations points at the same move, which is Bf4.

Bf4 loses on the spot to Qxf4. Most players stop there and settle for something quieter. White asked a better question, which was how to make Bf4 possible, and the answer was Rg4. The move is not clever in itself. It is what happens when you refuse to let go of the right idea.

ex.prompt: Why does the natural 1.Bf4 fail right now?
ex.why: 1.Bf4 Qxf4 2.Qh8+ Ke7 3.Qxg7 Qxf2+ and it is Black who is checking. The idea is right and the move order is wrong.
options: It hangs the g1 rook
Black simply takes it with the queen
It allows perpetual check
The bishop gets trapped

ex.prompt: Bf4 would win if it were possible. Play the move that makes it possible.
ex.why: The rook defends f4 in advance and now Bf4 cannot be met. Black has no answer, and the game ended a move later.

lessons.title: Knights are short range
text: Start with the weakness, because everything else about knights follows from it. A knight crawls. A bishop teleports.

The pawn on a6 is the only target on the board. The bishop attacks it in one move, from e2 or from b7. The knight needs four, something like Ng4, Ne5, Nd3, Nc5, and by then the position it was aiming at has usually changed.

This is why knight play has to be planned backwards. Decide the square you want first, count the moves it takes to get there, and only then decide whether you can afford the trip. A bishop can improvise. A knight cannot.

ex.prompt: Play the bishop move that attacks the a6 pawn immediately.
ex.why: Either one does it in a single move. Long range pieces switch targets almost for free, which is the whole difference in this position.

ex.prompt: How many moves does the knight need before it attacks a6?
ex.why: Ng4, Ne5, Nd3, Nc5 is one route and there is nothing quicker. Four moves is a long time to be doing nothing else.
options: One
Two
Three
Four

ex.prompt: What does this force you to do differently with a knight?
ex.why: A bishop can be redirected as the position changes. A knight commits several moves in advance, so the destination has to be chosen before the journey starts.
options: Keep it near your own king
Pick its destination first, then count the route
Trade it off as soon as possible
Only move it when it captures something

lessons.title: Knight as blockader
text: Something has to stand in front of an enemy passed pawn, and the piece you choose for the job matters more than it looks.

A bishop doing this work is purely defensive. It sits there and it blocks, and that is the whole of its contribution. The knight on f4 blocks the f pawn just as well, and because it jumps rather than slides, it is attacking e6 and g6 at the same time. The blockade costs it nothing.

Add the second difference and the game is over. The white king is free to walk wherever it likes while the black king is tied to the pawns, so White simply marches the king to b7 and pushes the c pawn.

ex.prompt: Click the piece that is blockading a passed pawn and attacking at the same time.
ex.why: The knight holds f5 and hits e6 and g6 from the same square. The bishop on c6 blocks nothing and attacks nothing useful.

ex.prompt: The pieces are settled, so the king decides it. Start the march.
ex.why: White walks to b7 and follows with c6. Black cannot copy the plan, because the black king has to stay near the pawns while the white king has nothing to defend.

ex.prompt: Why is a knight often the better blockader?
ex.why: A blockading bishop or rook is doing one job. A blockading knight is doing two, because the squares it attacks are not on the line it is blocking.
options: It cannot be attacked by pawns
It keeps attacking while it blocks
It is worth less, so it risks less
It can retreat more easily

lessons.title: Knights are masters of closed positions
text: The pawns are locked and nothing can be opened. That single fact decides which minor piece is better before anyone works out a plan.

A bishop needs open diagonals, and there are none. The black bishop on c8 cannot influence anything and cannot do a thing about White's idea of Nd3 followed by a capture on c5. The knight does not care that the position is closed, because it jumps over the blockage rather than looking through it.

There is a second knight advantage hiding in the finish. A bishop touches one colour of square forever. When the knight lands on c5 it takes a pawn on a dark square, attacks the bishop on a light square, and defends its own pawn on a light square, all in one move.

ex.prompt: The pawn structure is locked. Which minor piece do you want?
ex.why: Closed means the diagonals stay shut. A knight reaches squares no bishop can reach here, so the position type decides the piece.
options: The bishop, because the position may open later
The knight, because it jumps over the blockage
It makes no difference in a closed position

ex.prompt: Black has tried a5 in desperation. Send the knight on its way to c5.
ex.why: Nothing Black does prevents the knight from reaching c5, because the bishop cannot cover a dark square and the pawns cannot move.

ex.prompt: Nxc5 does three things at once. What is the underlying reason a bishop could never do that?
ex.why: The capture is on a dark square while the bishop it attacks and the pawn it defends are both on light squares. Only a knight works on both colours.
options: A bishop cannot capture pawns
A bishop only ever touches one colour of square
A bishop cannot defend its own pawns
A bishop moves too far in one go

lessons.title: Knights on the first and third ranks
text: A knight on the back rank looks like a wasted piece, and usually it is. Not always.

The knight on f1 is not going to win anything from there, but it is holding h2, and with a black queen on h4 that is not a small job. Judging a piece by the rank it stands on rather than by the work it does is how good defensive pieces get thrown away.

The knight on c3 shows the other side of the third rank. It presses on d5 and it supports the e4 advance, which takes more space and adds another attacker to d5. A third rank knight is usually a piece with a future rather than a piece with a post.

ex.prompt: Click the knight whose job is defensive rather than aggressive.
ex.why: It guards h2 against the queen on h4. The square is poor, the function is not, and those are different questions.

ex.prompt: The other knight is supporting a pawn break. Play it.
ex.why: The knight on c3 backs this up. The break gains central space and adds a second attacker to d5, which is where the game is being decided.

ex.prompt: How should you judge a knight sitting on the first rank?
ex.why: Rank is a rule of thumb, not a verdict. Ask what happens to your position if the piece disappears, and you have your answer.
options: Always bad, move it at once
By whether it is doing a job worth doing
Always fine, knights belong at home early
By how many squares it attacks

lessons.title: Knight on the fourth rank
text: The fourth rank is where a knight starts to be a real piece. It is far enough forward to threaten things and still close enough to come home.

This one is doing three separate jobs. It covers squares behind it on the second and third ranks, it blockades the isolated black pawn on d5, and it can jump to b5, c6, e6 or f5 whenever one of those becomes useful. Black has to keep watching all four.

It can also change its mind, which is the part players tend to miss. The knight can step back to e2 and rejoin the attack on d5 from f4, with the rook and queen piling in behind. Reaching a good square is not a commitment to stay on it.

ex.prompt: Click any square in Black's half that the knight can leap to.
ex.why: All four are available, and Black has to watch every one of them. A piece that threatens four entry squares does not have to use any of them to be worth its place.

ex.prompt: What is the knight doing besides threatening to jump?
ex.why: It sits directly in front of the isolated pawn, which no white pawn could ever do. Blockading and attacking at the same time is the knight speciality.
options: Defending the white king
Blockading the isolated d5 pawn
Attacking the black queen
Holding the only open file

lessons.title: Knight on the fifth rank
text: On the fifth rank a knight stops being a useful piece and starts being a problem the opponent has to solve.

White's knight on e5 has a permanent support point, so it cannot be chased, and from there it eyes c6, d7, f7 and g6. Every one of those is deep in the black position. Black cannot trade it off and cannot attack it, which leaves living with it as the only option.

Compare the black knight on c7, which is doing nothing but defending. It would love the mirror square on d5, and it cannot have it, because White answers with c4 and the knight has to go back where it came from. A square you can be evicted from is not an outpost.

ex.prompt: Two knights are on the board. Click the one that is dictating the game.
ex.why: It cannot be attacked by a pawn and it watches four squares in Black's camp. The c7 knight is a defender with no prospects.

ex.prompt: Click a square in Black's half that the e5 knight is watching.
ex.why: All four, and each of them is a square Black would rather keep private. This is what a supported knight on the fifth rank costs the defender.

ex.prompt: Why can the black knight never settle on d5?
ex.why: A pawn can always evict it, so d5 is a visit rather than a home. That single difference is why one knight is winning the game and the other is not.
options: It would be pinned against the queen
White plays c4 and chases it away
It is covered by the white rooks
The knight cannot reach d5 at all

lessons.title: Knight on the sixth rank
text: A knight on the sixth rank is usually decisive, and this position is past the point of defending.

The knight on d6 batters away at squares all through the black camp while the black bishop on d7 has nothing to do at all. Going further would actually reduce the number of squares it controls, so the seventh and eighth ranks are only worth visiting if there is material or a concrete threat waiting there.

White has two winning plans and the choice hardly matters. Ra3 followed by Rda1, Qa2 and axb5 breaks through on the a file. Ne4 heading for f6 sets up a fresh sixth rank post and brings the rook to d6. Both take several quiet moves, and that is fine. In a position with no tactical emergency there is time to walk a knight where it needs to go.

ex.prompt: Click the black piece that has no future in this position.
ex.why: Its own pawns take the squares it would want and it defends nothing that matters. This is the bishop the white knight is being compared against.

ex.prompt: Start one of White's two winning plans.
ex.why: Ra3 prepares Rda1, Qa2 and axb5 to break down the a file. Ne4 heads for f6 and frees d6 for a rook. Neither is forced and both win.

ex.prompt: Why does White not hurry the knight to the seventh or eighth rank?
ex.why: Deeper is not automatically better for a knight. Go further only when material or a concrete threat is waiting, not on principle.
options: It would be trapped there
It would control fewer squares for no gain
The knight is needed on defence
Black could take it

lessons.title: Improve your worst piece
text: White has a fine attacking position and Black has no counterplay worth the name. In the game White reached for something immediate with Bc1, threatening f5, and after Rh8 and Rg4 the reply Ng7 held everything together.
The better question was not what to threaten but which piece was letting the team down. The knight on e2 is contributing nothing while every other white piece is aimed at the black king.

Where does it want to be? e4 is a support point, and from there it hits d6, f6 and g5, at which point any move by the black knight on e8 runs into Nf6 with check. Once the destination is chosen the route needs no calculation whatsoever. Nc3 and then Ne4.

ex.prompt: Every white piece but one is aimed at the black king. Click the piece that is not helping.
ex.why: The knight on e2 has no target and no future on that square. When you cannot find a move, finding your worst piece is the reliable substitute.

ex.prompt: Its best square is e4. Play the first move of the route.
ex.why: No calculation is required once the destination is known. Even trading it off suits White, because dxe4 opens the way for f5 with the black king still short of defenders.

ex.prompt: What is the general habit this position teaches?
ex.why: Chess is a team game. If a piece is not in the battle, dragging it there is almost always worth more than a threat the opponent can answer.
options: Always attack the king with every piece
With no clear move, improve your worst placed piece
Trade pieces when you are attacking
Push a pawn whenever you are unsure

lessons.title: Hole you cannot reach
text: Both sides have a hole here. White would love a knight on f5 and Black would love one on f4, so on a first glance the position looks balanced in that respect.

It is not, and the reason is the rule worth taking away from this lesson. A hole is not a problem if the enemy pieces cannot reach it. White gets to f5 from e3 or from g3 whenever it suits. Black would need to come through e6 or g6, and both of those squares are poisoned, so the hole on f4 might as well not exist.

White is in no hurry either. Going to f5 early only lets Black trade the knight off. The knight goes there when it can stay there, which in practice means after enough pieces have come off that landing on f5 wins a pawn on d6 or h6, or at least ties a defender to each.

ex.prompt: Both sides have a hole. Click the one that is actually worth something.
ex.why: White can reach f5 from e3 or g3 at will. Black cannot get a knight to f4 because both jumping off squares, e6 and g6, are unavailable.

ex.prompt: Why does White avoid playing a knight to f5 immediately?
ex.why: Occupy an outpost when the piece can stay on it. Arriving early just invites the exchange that removes the whole advantage.
options: It would be captured by a pawn
Black could simply trade it off
It blocks the f pawn
The knight is needed on the queenside

ex.prompt: The real play is on the queenside. Build up before opening it.
ex.why: White keeps the tension and triples on the b file first. Rushing to open it before the heavy pieces are ready would throw away the one sector where White has all the play.

lessons.title: Domination by a bishop
text: Everything has a downside, and the knight has one beyond being slow. It can be dominated, which means having every square taken away from it at once, and the piece that does this best is the bishop.
The direct try fails. After a5 Nc6 a6 Kf6 Bd5 Na7 the knight gets in front of the pawn and holds it. So instead of pushing, White takes the knight's squares away first.

Bd5 does it. The knight is not attacked and not trapped in the usual sense, and yet b7, c6 and e6 are all covered, while Nf7 loses to Bxf7. The knight is a spectator, and now the pawn walks in. Even the king coming to the rescue does not help, because a6 followed by Kxd5 a7 promotes with a tempo to spare.

ex.prompt: Why does the immediate a5 fail?
ex.why: A knight in front of a passed pawn stops it dead. The pawn has to be pushed after the knight has been dealt with, not before.
options: The knight forks the king and pawn
Nc6 and Na7 gets the knight in front of the pawn
The black king arrives in time
The bishop gets trapped on a2

ex.prompt: Take the knight's squares away instead. Play it.
ex.why: b7, c6 and e6 are all covered and Nf7 drops to Bxf7. The knight never moves again, and the pawn queens even after Black wins the bishop.

lessons.title: Entombed by enemy pawns
text: Domination by a bishop needs a bishop. Pawns can do the same job, and when they do it the result is permanent.

The advance g4 looks like an ordinary attack on the knight, and dealing with it should be routine. It is not. e5 and g5 are unavailable, and Nh4 loses a pawn to Bxh4 followed by gxh4 and Qxh4 with a strong attack, so the knight has to crawl back to g1.

Then comes the move that makes it a lesson rather than a trick. f3 seals the tomb. The knight can never move again, and the white king is shut in the same cell, so Black is effectively playing with two extra pieces.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Start by asking the knight a question.
ex.why: Nh4 would drop a pawn to Bxh4, and e5 and g5 are covered, so g1 is the only square left.

ex.prompt: The knight has crawled back to g1. Now shut the door.
ex.why: The knight has no move for the rest of the game and the white king is locked in with it. Black is a piece up in every way that counts, without having won anything.

lessons.title: Entombed by its own pawns
text: This one is almost comic. White is a piece for a pawn ahead and should resign.

The pawns on f2 and g3 belong to White, and they have taken away every square the knight on h1 could ever use. A piece that cannot move is not worth a piece. It is worth nothing at all, and White is effectively playing a king and two pawns against a king and three.

So Black simply walks the king in. The c pawn is given up to open the door, the king collects h1 and f2 on the way through, and the g pawn decides it. Nothing here is a tactic. It is the arithmetic of a piece that does not exist.

ex.prompt: White is a piece for a pawn up. Who is winning?
ex.why: The knight has no legal square that is not covered by White's own pawns, so White is playing a piece down in practice while being a piece up on paper.
options: White
Roughly equal
Black

ex.prompt: What has actually gone wrong for White?
ex.why: Your own pawns can bury your pieces just as effectively as the opponent's. Corner knights are especially easy to bury, because they have so few squares to start with.
options: The knight is trapped on the edge by enemy pawns
White's own pawns on f2 and g3 take every square the knight needs
The white king is too far away
The black pawns are too advanced

ex.prompt: White has played Kc1. Black to move. Walk in.
ex.why: The c pawn buys the entry square. The black king walks to f1, collects the knight and the f2 pawn, and the g pawn promotes.

lessons.title: Knight given a free hand
text: A closing example, and a warning. Black is lost here by any sensible assessment, and this was a one minute game, so the result should have been a formality.

What happened instead is the reason knights have a reputation. The black knight took the g pawn, then the a pawn, then the b pawn, then the bishop, forking something on almost every move along the way, and White lost.

The serious point underneath the comedy is that a knight is the hardest piece to keep track of. Its attacks do not run along lines you can see, so a knight left with open squares and no supervision will find forks that a bishop or a rook never could. Treat a loose enemy knight as an emergency, even when you are winning.

ex.prompt: Black to move and apparently lost. Set the knight loose.
ex.why: The knight attacks the bishop and the g pawn at once, and once it is moving it does not stop. Nc6 forks the king and the new queening square, and the a pawn falls next.

ex.prompt: What makes a loose knight so much more dangerous than a loose bishop?
ex.why: You can see a diagonal. A knight fork has to be checked for deliberately, which is exactly why it gets missed, and why it gets missed even by very strong players.
options: It is worth more
Its attacks do not run along visible lines
It cannot be attacked by pawns
It moves further in one go

lessons.title: Knights test 1, level 1200 to 1600
text: White to move. Read the position before calculating anything.
White has more space in every sector, two active bishops, an attack on the king, control of the centre, and the better structure, since e6 is weak. Both black knights are purely defensive.
Silman's note on the band is that the answer is straightforward and does two things at once. A 1200 might see only the attack on the king and miss what the move does to a piece.

ex.prompt: White to move. Find it.
ex.why: It entombs the knight on h8 and opens the attack in the same move. Finding one of those is good. Finding both is the test.

lessons.title: Knights test 2, level 1400 to 1800
text: Tal against Soloviev. White to move.
Black has just played the knight to f8 and intends Ne6, from where it reaches d4 or f4. Ask what that plan needs, and what would take it away.
The right move can be reached three ways: to gain space, out of worry about exd4, or because you saw Ne6 coming. Silman hopes it was the third.

ex.prompt: White to move. Stop the knight before it starts.
ex.why: It closes the centre, takes e6 from the knight permanently, and prepares h4 and h5, an attack that needs a closed centre to be worth playing.

lessons.title: Knights test 3, level 1600 to 1800
text: White to move. The key is the holes on d4 and d5.

Black wants a knight on d4 as fast as possible and White wants one on d5. White would love the route Nd2-b1-c3-d5, and cannot start it, because moving the d2 knight drops the e4 pawn. So deal with that first.
Silman raised the band to 1600 for one reason. Spotting the hole is the easy half. The position also demands the patience to prepare the journey rather than begin it.

ex.prompt: White to move. Free the knight for its journey.
ex.why: Defending e4 releases the d2 knight from guard duty. In the game White played Bc3, which took away the very square the knight needed.

lessons.title: Knights test 4, level 1800 to 2000
text: Fischer against Ibrahimoglu. White to move.
White has the bishop pair, and b5 and c4 are easy to take over. The important feature is d5, a genuine hole. Compare d4, which is not a hole at all, because c3 heals it.
Another knight retreat. Silman says he would have set the band lower, except that the knight already eyes c4 and moves like Qb5 look tempting, which makes it genuinely hard.

ex.prompt: White to move. The knight has somewhere better to be.
ex.why: All the way home, heading for c3 and then d5, the real hole. c4 is available and is the lesser square, which is exactly what makes this hard to find.

lessons.title: Knights test 5, level 1800 to 2000
text: Szelag against Radjabov. Black to move, and the position fools people in White's favour. Black's bishop looks bad, his knight looks harmless, and he even has more pawn islands.

The dynamic reading is different. Black's rooks press the f4 pawn, one of his so-called extra islands is a strong pawn centre, and White's knight has no useful move in either direction. Grabbing at f4 directly with e5 or g5 achieves nothing, so the question becomes which defender can be harassed.

The f3 rook is solid. The d4 rook is not, and the bishop can never touch d4, which leaves one piece to ask about. Silman's band note says the winning retreat probably would not occur to anyone under 1800.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Attack the loose defender.
ex.why: The knight reroutes to c6 where it hits the d4 rook, and f4 falls by force. Defending with g3 instead collapses to e5, d4 and g5, when the so-called bad bishop on b7 turns into a monster.

lessons.title: Knights test 6, level 1900 to 2200
text: Silman against Booth. White to move.

Both sides have loose queenside pawns, a6 for Black and b2 for White, but White's minor pieces are more active and the extra central space keeps Black worrying about both f5 and e5. The pride of the position is the knight on c4.

Black would dearly like to trade that knight off with Nb6, offering his far less impressive horse for it. Seen that way the move suggests itself, and Silman still rates it advanced, because White already has a knight on c4, so bringing a second one to bear on the same square feels wrong.

ex.prompt: White to move. Protect the best piece on the board.
ex.why: Heading for d2, so that when Black trades on c4 a second knight simply replaces the first. The octopus on c4 survives the exchange, which is the whole point.

lessons.title: Knights test 7, level 1900 to 2200
text: Benjamin against Silman. White to move.

Black's two bishops gave him a comfortable game earlier and he let it drift. The last move was the real error, and Silman notes that had Black seen the reply he would have taken on d6 and headed for a quick draw.
The knight is already on a fine square. The test is whether you can see that there is a better one.

ex.prompt: White to move. The knight has one more jump in it.
ex.why: A knight that already looks well placed can usually be improved once more. Being satisfied with a good square is how strong moves get missed.

lessons.title: Knights test 8, level 2000 to 2200
text: Black to move, and almost everyone reads this position wrongly. White has a lead in development, more space, a threat against c6, and the better pawn structure. Black has two rather inactive bishops and not much else that is visible.

Silman showed this to an audience of about two hundred players ranging from beginner to over 2200. The large majority said White was considerably better. Not one of them thought Black had more than equality.

His note on the band says he would not be surprised to see masters miss it, because the move is anti-intuitive twice over. It gives away the coveted bishop pair, and it hands White a protected passed pawn.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Do the thing that looks wrong.
ex.why: Black gives up the two bishops and gifts a protected passed pawn, in exchange for a blockading knight. Keeping the bishops with Qe8 runs into Nac4 and White is better for every reason listed.

lessons.title: Knights test 9, level 2000 to 2200
text: Xie Jun against Larsen. White to move.

The position favours White because of the holes on b6 and d6. By now the reflex should be to ask whether a knight can get to a hole, and a knight reaching c4 would cover both of them. So Nd2 heading for c4 suggests itself.

It does not work yet. Nd2 allows Nc5, and after Qc4 b6 and the trade on c5, Black is fine with Ba6 to come. Silman calls this an advanced players only problem for exactly that reason: seeing the manoeuvre is one level, and holding it back for one preparatory move is another.

ex.prompt: White to move. Prepare the knight journey before starting it.
ex.why: It prevents Nc5 first. Only then does the knight go to d2 and on to c4, arriving on a square Black can no longer contest.

lessons.title: Active, useful, or tall pawn
text: Where a knight crawls, a bishop crosses the board in one move. Give it a clear diagonal and anything standing on that diagonal is in danger from a piece that may be nowhere near it.

Bishops are traditionally called good or bad depending on whether your own centre pawns sit on the bishop's colour. Silman drops those labels, because they mislead. A so called bad bishop is often active and strong, and it is often the one piece holding your position together. Calling it bad tells you nothing about what to do.

Three labels replace them. A bishop is **active** if it is outside the pawn chain or on a reasonably clear diagonal. It is **useful** if it is doing a real job, defensive or dynamic, such that losing it would hurt. It is a **tall pawn** if it is doing neither, stuck behind its own pawns and serving no purpose. The best bishops are active and useful at once.

ex.prompt: Click the bishop that is active.
ex.why: It sits outside the pawn chain on a clear diagonal pointing at the black king. The c8 bishop has not moved and looks at its own pawns.

ex.prompt: What makes a bishop useful, as opposed to active?
ex.why: Active is about geography and useful is about function. A bishop can command an empty diagonal and be doing nothing that matters.
options: It sits on a long diagonal
It is doing a real job, so losing it would damage your position
It is outside the pawn chain
It is the same colour as your centre pawns

ex.prompt: Why does Silman abandon the good bishop and bad bishop labels?
ex.why: The label describes pawn colour, not what the piece is doing. Two bishops with identical pawn structures can be worth wildly different amounts.
options: They are too hard for beginners
A so called bad bishop is often active, or a vital defender
They only apply to endgames
Engines disagree with them

lessons.title: Activating the slacker
text: White has pressure against d6, and it is going nowhere. The knight defends it and the black rooks are about to join in. Piling more attackers onto a square the opponent can defend faster is not a plan.
The player of the white pieces noticed something else instead. His bishop on e2 was doing nothing at all, and he had been told often enough about leaving pieces out of play.

c5 solves both problems with one pawn. The bishop gets c4, where it is suddenly the best piece on the board, and the d file opens for the doubled rooks. The pawn is a small price for turning a spectator into an attacker.

ex.prompt: Click the white piece that is contributing nothing.
ex.why: It has no diagonal and no target. Before looking for a new threat, look for the piece that is not yet in the game.

ex.prompt: Give that piece a job, even at the cost of a pawn.
ex.why: c4 becomes available for the bishop and the d file opens for both rooks. Taking the pawn is already losing, and declining leaves White clearly on top.

ex.prompt: What is the general lesson?
ex.why: Pressure that the defender can match is not pressure. Adding a piece that was not previously in the game changes the count in a way another attack on the same square does not.
options: Always sacrifice a pawn for the initiative
When an attack stalls, activate your worst piece rather than adding attackers
Doubled rooks beat a knight
Trade when you have more space

lessons.title: Ruler of the diagonal
text: This position is deliberately absurd, and it makes the point better than a realistic one would. Black has four connected pawns marching down the board and White has one bishop and one pawn.

Look at where those black pawns need to go. The b pawn needs b1. The c pawn needs c2. The d pawn needs d3. The e pawn needs e4. Every one of those squares lies on the b1 to h7 diagonal, and the bishop on g6 owns all of it.
One piece, one diagonal, four pawns stopped. Meanwhile the white d pawn walks to d8 unopposed. Nothing about this is realistic, and everything about it is true.

ex.prompt: Click a square on the bishop's diagonal that a black pawn needs and cannot have.
ex.why: The b pawn needs b1, the c pawn needs c2, the d pawn needs d3 and the e pawn needs e4. All four sit on the same diagonal, and one bishop covers the lot.

ex.prompt: With the black pawns frozen, start the one that is not.
ex.why: Nothing can step onto the diagonal to interfere, so the pawn walks to d8 and promotes.

ex.prompt: What is the realistic version of this lesson?
ex.why: The bishop is doing its work from the far corner of the board. That reach is what you are buying whenever you open a diagonal for one.
options: Bishops are stronger than knights
A single clear diagonal can control an entire sector at long range
Passed pawns should always be blockaded by bishops
Four connected pawns beat a piece

lessons.title: Catapult
text: The bishop on d3 already points at h7, and on its own that is only a threat the defender can live with. Put the queen behind it and the same diagonal becomes a delivery mechanism.

Qe4 does exactly that. The queen lines up behind the bishop and prepares to arrive on h7 with decisive effect. Silman calls it riding the bishop's vapours, which is a better description of the idea than the usual word battery.
The defence collapses quickly. f5 is met by capturing en passant and doubling on the f file, and the alternative g6 runs into Bxh6 with a winning attack.

ex.prompt: The bishop points at h7. Bring up the artillery behind it.
ex.why: The queen uses the bishop's diagonal to reach h7. Black cannot cover the square and cannot afford to weaken the king further.

ex.prompt: Why put the queen behind the bishop rather than in front?
ex.why: The piece in front does the pushing and the piece behind does the damage. Reverse them and the bishop is blocked and the queen is a target.
options: The queen is safer there
The bishop clears and controls the path, so the queen arrives with support
It develops with tempo
It avoids a knight fork

lessons.title: Active is not the same as useful
text: White's dark squared bishop on e3 looks fine. It eyes two diagonals, which is more than most pieces manage.

Look at what those diagonals are worth. The long one is blocked by the b6 pawn, which is not moving. The other one points away from where the game is being decided, and the square that matters, d6, is screaming for attention that the bishop is not giving it.

So the bishop is active and useless at the same time. The cure is to admit it and go backwards. Bc1 heads for a3 and then d6, and suddenly Black has to worry about a king that cannot easily leave the centre. A retreat that improves a piece is not a loss of time.

ex.prompt: Click the white piece that is active but not doing anything useful.
ex.why: Two diagonals, one blocked by a pawn that will not move and one pointing away from the fight. Activity without a purpose is decoration.

ex.prompt: Send it somewhere it matters, even if that means going backwards.
ex.why: From c1 the bishop heads for a3 and then d6, the square the position is actually about. Black has to answer with e5 to keep the king safe.

ex.prompt: What is the dream bishop?
ex.why: Covering ground and doing a job that relates to the other imbalances in the position. Either one alone is worth much less than people assume.
options: One on the longest available diagonal
One that is active and useful at the same time
One outside the pawn chain
One on the opposite colour to your pawns

lessons.title: Ugly bishop that holds everything
text: On a quick look White is better. The white bishop is far more active than the awkward black one, the e6 pawn is weak on an open file facing two rooks, e5 is a hole, and it is White to move.
It is not so simple. The white d4 pawn is loose and Rxf3 shattering the king cover is a real threat. More to the point, ask what each bishop is actually doing.

The proud white bishop dominating the b1 to h7 diagonal does nothing about Rxf3, nothing about e5, and nothing about d4. The despised black thing on d7 is single handedly holding e6 against two rooks. One bishop is holding off two enemy rooks, and once e6 is safe it can emerge via b5, a4, or the route through e8. Ugly and indispensable beats handsome and irrelevant.

ex.prompt: Click the bishop that would be most missed by its owner.
ex.why: It holds e6 on its own against two rooks. The white bishop commands a diagonal that has no bearing on any of the position's real problems.

ex.prompt: What question separates a useful bishop from a merely active one?
ex.why: Remove the black bishop and e6 falls at once. Remove the white bishop and very little changes. That test cuts through appearances every time.
options: Which one has more squares?
What would happen to the position if this piece vanished?
Which one is outside the pawn chain?
Which one is on a longer diagonal?

ex.prompt: White has to deal with the threat of Rxf3. Play the game continuation.
ex.why: Re3 was the other way to sidestep the threat. Neither one addresses the real issue, which is that White's better looking bishop is not helping with any of it.

lessons.title: Tall pawn
text: A bishop that serves no useful function and is stuck behind its own pawns stops being a piece. Silman calls it a tall pawn, and this endgame is the extreme case.

White's bishop on h2 is entombed. It has no move that changes anything and no future, so White is playing a piece down while being level on material. That is why an entombed bishop usually loses both the middlegame and the endgame.

Black's only problem is getting the king to e2, where it will collect the white kingside pawns. There is exactly one way to arrange it, and it starts by giving away a pawn to create an outside passer that drags the white king to the wrong side of the board.

ex.prompt: Material is level. Why is White effectively a piece down?
ex.why: A piece with no useful move is not worth anything. Counting it as three points is the mistake the whole lesson is built on.
options: The king is badly placed
The bishop is entombed and takes no part in the game
Black has an extra passed pawn
The h pawn cannot be defended

ex.prompt: Black to move. Start the plan that gets the king to e2.
ex.why: Giving the pawn turns the a pawn into an outside passer. The white king has to go and deal with it, and by the time it has, the black king has a free road to e2.

lessons.title: Burying a bishop on purpose
text: The previous lesson showed a bishop that had been entombed by accident. This one shows how to do it on purpose, and it comes up often enough to be worth knowing as a device rather than a trick.
The setup is the Botvinnik system against a kingside fianchetto. White has advanced the f and g pawns, and Black has a bishop on g7 sitting behind its own e5 pawn.

f6 closes the lid. The bishop is driven to h8, where it stays for the rest of the game, buried alive. From that moment White can play on any part of the board he likes, because he is permanently a piece up in every fight that matters.

ex.prompt: Bury the g7 bishop for good.
ex.why: The bishop has to go to h8 and it never comes back. Everything after this is White playing with an extra piece wherever the game is decided.

ex.prompt: Why is this worth a pawn move that blocks your own position?
ex.why: One black piece is out of the game for good, so every subsequent skirmish is fought a piece up. That is worth far more than the flexibility the pawn move gives away.
options: It opens the g file
It removes a defender from the black king permanently
It wins the exchange
It prepares a knight outpost on f5

lessons.title: Tall pawn in a real game
text: Entombed bishops are the dramatic case. The ordinary tall pawn is just a bishop stuck behind its own pawns with nowhere to go, and this is what it looks like in a real grandmaster game.

The bishop on g6 is the problem, and what makes it a lasting problem is that it has no way out. h5 is covered by the white queen. Getting out through f7 or e8 needs the f pawn to move again, and that turns e6 into a serious weakness.

White plays around it. Ng2 stops the trade on h4, heads for f4, and prepares to torment the bishop further with the h pawn. The white bishop will operate freely in the centre and on the queenside for the rest of the game, knowing the lump on g6 can never challenge it.

ex.prompt: Click Black's problem piece.
ex.why: It has no safe square to move to and nothing to do where it stands. Everything in White's plan follows from that one fact.

ex.prompt: Why can the bishop not simply escape?
ex.why: Every exit costs something bigger than the bishop gains. A piece that can only be freed by wrecking your structure is not really free.
options: It is pinned against the king
h5 is covered, and going via f7 or e8 leaves e6 weak
It has no legal moves at all
Moving it loses the f5 pawn

ex.prompt: Play the move that stops the trade on h4 and starts making things worse for the bishop.
ex.why: It rules out Bxh4, heads for f4, and prepares h4 and h5 to harass the bishop further. Improve your good pieces while the opponent's bad one watches.

lessons.title: Trading your bad piece for their good one
text: Black has just played Re8, and the idea behind it sounds sophisticated. If White tries Bh6, Black answers Bh8, and because the rook has left f8 it is no longer hanging to the bishop on h6. The dark squared bishops stay on.

It is completely wrong. Black should be delighted to trade those bishops, because the g7 bishop is a tall pawn stuck behind its own chain. It guards a few squares, and beyond that it is an ugly piece with no prospects.

The rule underneath is one of the most useful in the book, and it is easy to apply. Do not hesitate to exchange your bad pieces for the opponent's good ones. Avoiding a trade because you have been told trades are for the defender is how bad pieces end up staying on the board for fifty moves.

ex.prompt: Black avoided the dark squared bishop trade. Was that right?
ex.why: The g7 bishop is stuck behind its own pawn chain with no future. Trading a piece like that for an active enemy bishop is a straight profit.
options: Yes, keeping pieces on helps the cramped side
No, the g7 bishop is a tall pawn and Black should welcome the trade
Yes, the bishop defends the king
It makes no difference either way

ex.prompt: State the rule.
ex.why: It sounds obvious written down, and it is routinely ignored at the board, usually because a general rule about trading gets applied without looking at which pieces are actually coming off.
options: Trade when you are ahead in material
Do not hesitate to exchange your bad pieces for the opponent's good ones
Never trade your fianchettoed bishop
Avoid trades when you have more space

ex.prompt: White improves the last piece that is not yet doing anything. Play it.
ex.why: The rook takes the open file while Black rearranges pieces to preserve one he should be trying to give away.

lessons.title: Bishops of opposite colours
text: Bishops of opposite colours are just a bishop against a bishop, but it is a strange fight, because the two pieces exist in different dimensions. They can never touch each other. Neither can defend what the other attacks or attack what the other defends.
The consequence is the one everybody half remembers. Put your pawns and your king on the opposite colour to the enemy bishop and that bishop can do nothing about any of it.

This position is deliberately ridiculous, and it proves the point beyond argument. White is two pawns and three pieces ahead, White's king is far better placed, and Black is completely passive. It is a dead draw, because every white bishop is dark squared and c6 is a light square. The whole armada cannot touch the one square that matters.

ex.prompt: White is two pawns and three pieces up. What is the result?
ex.why: Material is irrelevant when none of it can attack the squares that decide the position.
options: White wins easily
A dead draw
Black is winning

ex.prompt: Why can White not make progress?
ex.why: Four dark squared bishops cover no light square between them. The black king simply stands on a colour that the entire white army is blind to.
options: The black bishop defends everything
Every white bishop is dark squared, and c6 is a light square
The white king cannot approach
There are not enough pawns left

ex.prompt: What is the practical rule to take from this?
ex.why: It works both ways. Defending, it makes you untouchable. Attacking, opposite coloured bishops favour the side with the initiative, because the defender has no piece that can contest the squares being attacked.
options: Avoid opposite coloured bishops when ahead
Put your pawns and king on the opposite colour to the enemy bishop
Trade bishops whenever possible
Opposite coloured bishops always favour the attacker

lessons.title: Bishops test 1, level 1400 to 1600
text: Averbakh against Tal. Black to move. What combination of factors gives Black a decisive advantage?

Black is a solid pawn up, and by now you know that one pawn does not decide anything when the bishops are of opposite colours. So Black wants to keep pieces on and show that his bishop attacks things the other bishop can never defend.
Silman's note says the extra pawn and the grip on the e file are obvious, which leaves one feature as the thing being tested. That feature is a square.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Take the square the whole plan rests on.
ex.why: From d4 the bishop eyes f2 and blocks the d file at the same time. The extra pawn is what lets the bishop sit there safely, which White's bishop cannot match.

lessons.title: Bishops test 2, level 1400 to 1600
text: Sakaev against Malakhov. White to move.

Black is short of space on the queenside, and the worse problem is the bishop on b7, which is a true tall pawn. White's dark squared bishop can spring to life with Bf4, and the other one is hitting granite on d5.

Silman is explicit about what he is testing. Bf4 was tempting and he does not mind if you saw it. What he wants is for you to have noticed that your own g2 bishop is not doing enough, and then to have done something about it. More often than not you have to make a bishop active, because it will not happen on its own.

ex.prompt: White to move. Give the g2 bishop a life.
ex.why: It cracks the centre open for the bishop, and it has a second point: the d file opens for the rook and d6 becomes available to the white pieces.

lessons.title: Bishops test 3, level 1400 to 1600
text: Ivanchuk against Leko. White to move.

White has two rooks for the queen, which should be enough, but he is behind in development and Black's bishops look dangerous. The concrete worry is e3, opening the long light squared diagonal at the white king.

Silman's band note is a good hint about how to use the course itself. Most players at 1400 would sense the danger on that diagonal, and since this whole section is about bishops it stands to reason the answer involves one. That reasoning alone gets you there.

ex.prompt: White to move. Shut the dangerous diagonal before it opens.
ex.why: It blocks the e pawn, so the long diagonal never opens and the rooks get time to dominate the queen. Prevention, chosen over any active-looking alternative.

lessons.title: Bishops test 4, level 1400 to 1800
text: Ehlvest against Novik. White to move, and the position is a clean illustration of the rule about trading your bad pieces for the opponent's good ones.

One glance settles which bishop is which. White's on d3 is a tall pawn, locked behind its own c4 and e4 pawns with exactly two legal moves. Black's on d7 is patrolling two open diagonals at once, toward a4 on one side and toward h3 on the other.

So White wants precisely that trade, and the route matters. The direct offer on b5 is impossible, because White's own c4 pawn blocks the way. The bishop has to go the long way round, and Silman's band note says a careful read of the bishops material gives him complete faith the reader finds it.

ex.prompt: White to move. Start the journey that trades the tall pawn for the good bishop.
ex.why: Bc2 prepares Ba4, the offer the bishop cannot reach directly because c4 blocks b5. Black's best try was Qe8, so that after the trade the recapturing knight hangs to the queen down the freshly opened diagonal. In the game the trade went through, and b4 gave White his queenside play.

lessons.title: Bishops test 5, level 1600 to 1800
text: Black to move, and in trouble. The f5 pawn has just asked the e6 bishop a question, and there are only two answers. Capture on d5, or retreat to d7.

Retreating keeps the bishop and looks safe, and it loses. After Bd7 comes f6, the g7 bishop is driven to h8 and buried alive, and Bh6 picks up the exchange on top of the funeral. The f6 pawn cannot be taken by anything.

So the capture is forced even though it gives White a fine recapture either way. Silman's band note is about realism. You are already worse, and the skill being tested is damage control, choosing the least bad structure rather than searching for an equality that is not there.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Choose the least bad option.
ex.why: Giving up the bishop hurts, and the alternative buries a piece for the rest of the game. After the recapture Nd4 at least plants the knight. Never let your pieces be entombed.

lessons.title: Bishops test 6, level 2100 and up
text: Aronian against Svidler. White to move, and this one is rated for 2100 and up.

The obvious imbalance is White's central majority against Black's queenside majority. Amateurs tend to fear a queenside majority, and central pawns are usually worth more while pieces remain on the board.

There is a second battle running underneath it. Black's centre and kingside pawns all sit on light squares, and White has a light squared bishop. If those pawns could be fixed where they are, every one of them becomes a target. Silman's band note calls this finding subtle ways to create something that does not yet exist.

ex.prompt: White to move. Fix the enemy pawns on the colour of your bishop.
ex.why: It prepares g5, freezing the black kingside pawns on light squares where the bishop can work against them for the rest of the game.

lessons.title: Bishops test 7, level 2100 and up
text: Capablanca against Corzo, Havana 1900, played when Capablanca was twelve years old. White to move, in a position built from three features: opposite coloured bishops, two passed centre pawns, and a b2 bishop that is currently a tall pawn staring at its own d4 pawn.

Black's pieces are arranged to keep it that way. The queen blockades on d5, and the dream is a knight on e6 with the bishop landing on d5, a permanent dark square lock. The black king, meanwhile, sits on the same long diagonal as the sleeping bishop.

Silman's band note says the strategy is the test. If you saw that the b2 bishop was the problem, noticed the potential along the long diagonal, and did everything to open it, you did very well; the rest is tactics in service of that one idea. White gives the e pawn, then the queen itself, to strip every blockader off the diagonal.

ex.prompt: White to move. Start clearing the long diagonal, whatever it costs.
ex.why: The pawn clears e5 and the queen sacrifice on b5 drags the blockader off d5, so d5+ opens the diagonal with decisive effect. Qc4, offering the queen trade to the same end, wins more simply, and both moves serve the identical idea.

lessons.title: Two bishops, and the antidote
