text: A bishop cannot cover both colours, and that single weakness is what the bishop pair cures. Two bishops patrol everything between them, which is why the pair is worth more than the sum of its parts.

It follows that the way to deal with an enemy bishop pair is not to out-manoeuvre it but to break it up. Trade one of them off, by any means, and what remains is an ordinary bishop against bishop or bishop against knight fight that you know how to play.

White is under real pressure here and the bishop on f4 cannot be dealt with. The one on c6 is another matter, and Ivanchuk simply offers his own passive bishop for it. Black declines twice and White insists twice, and the game is drawn on the spot.

ex.prompt: Black owns two bishops. Click the one White can realistically do something about.
ex.why: The f4 bishop cannot be challenged. The c6 bishop can be met by a white bishop on the same diagonal, which is all the anti-pair formula needs.

ex.prompt: Offer the trade that breaks up the pair.
ex.why: White swaps a passive bishop for the dangerous one. Black says no twice, White insists twice, and the game is agreed drawn.

ex.prompt: State the anti-bishop-pair formula.
ex.why: Removing one bishop turns the problem into a fight you already understand. Your knight or your own bishop are both acceptable currency for the trade.
options: Close the position and wait
Trade one of the two bishops off, by any means
Attack on the wing where the bishops are not pointing
Trade queens to reach an endgame

lessons.title: Breaking the pair from the other side
text: Same principle, seen from the side that does not own the pair. White has two bishops, and Black has a central pawn majority to work with.

One detail decides the plan. White's queenside majority looks respectable and cannot actually do anything, because it can neither expand nor produce a passed pawn. Black's central majority can. So Black wants the position simplified into a shape where that majority tells, and the bishops are the obstacle.

Black wastes no time. Bh6 offers the dark squared bishop immediately, and once its partner is gone the remaining light squared bishop turns out to be remarkably ineffective. Do not wait for the perfect moment to break up a pair. Take the trade when it is available.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Break up the bishop pair.
ex.why: Black offers the trade at once rather than manoeuvring around the pair. Everything after this is a knight against one bishop, which suits the side with the central majority.

ex.prompt: Why is White's queenside majority worth less than Black's central one?
ex.why: A majority that cannot advance is not really a majority. Counting pawns on each wing tells you nothing until you ask whether they can move.
options: It has fewer pawns
It can neither expand nor make a passed pawn
It is on the wrong colour for the bishops
It is too far from the kings

ex.prompt: When should you take the chance to break up an enemy bishop pair?
ex.why: The chance is often available once and briefly. Black takes it on move 23 rather than improving the position first, and the game turns on that.
options: Only in the endgame
As soon as it is available
Only when you can win material by it
Only if you keep your own pair

lessons.title: Opening lines serves the bishops
text: Black has just played c5, blasting the centre open. White has the bishop pair and a superior pawn structure, and Black has handed the bishops exactly the open lines they were waiting for.

There is a real argument on the other side, and it is worth stating. White's king is still in the middle, and opening the position to punish a central king sometimes outranks any favour you do the enemy bishops. Here it does not, because Black gets nothing going at all.
White takes everything, castles as soon as the king needs it, and the dark squared bishop settles on the long diagonal where Black has nothing left to contest it. That bishop decides the game.

ex.prompt: Black has just opened the centre. Good idea or bad?
ex.why: Facing two bishops, keep the position shut and trade one off. Opening it up is doing the opponent's work.
options: Good, it activates Black's pieces
Bad, open lines are what the enemy bishop pair wants
Neutral, the structure is symmetrical

ex.prompt: Take what Black has offered.
ex.why: The exchanges leave White with two bishops, a better structure, and a king that gets castled a move later. Long term advantages, and nothing for Black in the short term.

ex.prompt: You are facing two bishops. What is your policy?
ex.why: Closed lines blunt bishops and a trade removes the pair. Those two ideas cover almost every practical case.
options: Open the position to create counterplay
Keep it closed and trade one bishop off
Trade all the rooks
Attack on the wing

lessons.title: Create the diagonal, do not look for one
text: White has just gone out of his way to prevent Black keeping the bishop pair, which tells you what the game is about. What is left is one bishop against one knight, and Black has to make that bishop matter.
The bishop on f6 is Black's worst piece, and there is no open diagonal anywhere for it to move to. Most players would settle for Bg5, going where there is at least some air.

Benjamin plays Bd8, which looks like a retreat to nowhere and is the whole point of the lesson. The bishop is not heading for a diagonal that already exists. It is going to build one, with c6 and then b6, and in the meantime it can hold d6 from c7 or hit c3 from a5. When there is no ready made diagonal for your bishop, make one.

ex.prompt: Click Black's worst placed minor piece.
ex.why: The knight on c5 is fine. The bishop has no diagonal, no target, and nothing to do where it stands.

ex.prompt: Improve it. The move looks like a retreat.
ex.why: From d8 the bishop supports c6 and then b6, building the diagonal it wants. It can also hold d6 from c7 or swing to a5 against c3, which is more flexibility than any forward move offered.

ex.prompt: What is the rule this illustrates?
ex.why: Looking for an open diagonal finds nothing here. Asking which diagonal you could build, and what pawn moves would build it, finds the move.
options: Retreat a bishop when it is attacked
If no useful diagonal exists, create one
Always keep the bishop pair
Trade a bad bishop at the first opportunity

lessons.title: Anti-knight strategy
text: Knights live on support points, so the way to fight one is to take its squares away with pawns. Silman calls this anti-knight strategy, and the reason it deserves a name is that the squares are usually given away by moves nobody thinks twice about.

b5 here is the main line of the Ruy Lopez. It gains queenside space, it hits the bishop, and it is entirely correct. It also permanently gives up a square, because the b pawn can no longer cover c5, leaving the d pawn as the only babysitter.

Pawns cannot move backwards. Every time one advances, some control is lost forever. That is not a reason to stop pushing pawns, since space is worth having. It is a reason to know what each push costs before you play it.

ex.prompt: Black has just played b5. Click the square it gave up.
ex.why: The b pawn covered c5 and no longer can. Only the d pawn is left to watch it, and a white piece landing there cannot be met by a pawn.

ex.prompt: What is anti-knight strategy in one line?
ex.why: A knight with no reachable support point is a knight with nothing to do. Pawns are what deny those squares, which is why the strategy is a pawn strategy.
options: Trade knights whenever possible
Use your pawns to deny the enemy knight advanced squares
Attack the knight with your bishop
Keep your knights closer than the opponent's

ex.prompt: What is the cost you accept every time you advance a pawn?
ex.why: Pawns do not come back. Push them for space and for activity, but know which squares you are handing over as you do it.
options: Nothing, space is always good
Control of the squares it can no longer cover, permanently
A tempo
The right to castle

lessons.title: Knight goes on a journey
text: This is the short range weakness from the knights part turned into a winning plan. White's position is close to comical. The c pawn is under assault and there is nothing constructive to do about it.

Fischer asks the question the whole course has been building towards. If the knight could land on one support point and hit c2 from it, which square would that be? The answer is d4, and the route is Nf6-d7-b8-c6-d4.

That is four moves to move one piece, and it is worth every one of them, because White cannot do anything in the meantime. The first move is not a knight move at all. The knight is currently defending h5, so g6 has to come first to free it.

ex.prompt: Click the square Black's knight is heading for.
ex.why: From d4 it hits c2 and cannot be driven off. The route is long, Nf6-d7-b8-c6-d4, and White has no way to use the time.

ex.prompt: The knight cannot leave yet. Free it.
ex.why: The knight was tied to defending h5. Once the pawn covers it the horse is free to travel, and g6 also opens a second route through h7 and g5 to e6.

ex.prompt: Four moves to reposition one piece. What makes that affordable?
ex.why: Time only costs you when the opponent can use it. Check whether they can do anything before deciding a long manoeuvre is too slow.
options: The knight gives check on the way
White has no constructive plan during those moves
It wins material immediately
The knight cannot be captured

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 1, level 1400 to 1600
text: Radjabov against Anand. White has just played Bd3 and a draw was agreed on the spot. The test is to explain why, because White has the bishop pair in an open position and a draw seems generous.

The answer is the anti-pair formula from earlier in this part. Black has a forced route to trading one of the bishops off, and nothing White does can stop it. Trying to prevent it with c4 even fails tactically to Bxg3.
Silman's band note says the idea of removing one of the two bishops is fully within a 1400's reach. The plan is a knight hop followed by offering the dark squared bishops.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Begin the plan that neutralises the bishop pair.
ex.why: The knight heads for f4 via d5, and Bf4 offers the trade White cannot decline profitably. One bishop comes off, and with it goes the whole point of White's position.

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 2, level 1400 to 1600
text: Haba against Pachow. White to move, and the whole position is a battle for one square, e4.

Count the fighters. Black's bishop and knight both bear on e4, and White's bishop already stands there with the c3 knight ready to recapture. Whoever wins the square wins a superior minor piece with it.

The band note says a battle for a single square should be within everyone's reach by this point in the section. The trick is the move order, because the obvious recapture at the end gives the square back.

ex.prompt: White to move. Win the fight for e4.
ex.why: The pin means the f6 knight cannot join the recapture. After the trades White's knight lands on e4 permanently, and the recapture with the knight first would have thrown the square away to Nxe4.

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 3, level 1400 to 1800
text: Varga against Bakre. White to move. The natural reading is that this position is about the weak d6 pawn, and that reading is wrong.

Look at it with a pure minor piece mentality instead. Black's knight has just arrived on c5 looking active, and his dark squared bishop is huddled on d8. White can convert the whole position into great knight against poor bishop.
The band note points out that the section is about minor piece battles, so the answer should involve one, and there is no cleaner battle than bishop against knight.

ex.prompt: White to move. Trade into the minor piece battle you want.
ex.why: The exchange removes Black's good knight, and Ne3 then offers to remove his good bishop as well. What remains is a flexible knight with four entry squares against a bishop with none, plus the open d file.

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 4, level 1400 to 1800
text: Amonatov against Zablotsky. White to move, in a Sicilian-like structure where d6 is backward and d5 is the hole.

Ask who guards d5 for Black. Only the knights can, since his remaining bishop is dark squared and will never touch the square. That observation is the whole plan: exchange both black knights and what is left is a knight ruling d5 against a bishop that cannot fight it.
The band note calls the strategy basic but extremely important. Trade pieces so that the minor piece you keep is better than the one they keep.

ex.prompt: White to move. Start removing the guardians of d5.
ex.why: The bishop pins itself to the job of trading a knight, and the follow-up manoeuvre brings the f3 knight into the fight for d5 through h2 and g4. Both black knights come off, and the surviving white knight takes d5 for the rest of the game.

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 5, level 1400 to 1800
text: Jakovenko against Aronian. Black to move, a pawn down with the two bishops. The question is whether the bishops are worth the pawn, and the honest answer is probably not, so long as White's knights keep their central homes.

That conditional is the test. Do not fixate on the pawn and forget the minor piece battle. The knight that just landed on d4 wants to be permanent, and anti-knight strategy says permanence is exactly what you deny.
In the game Black played a rook move instead, White answered b4, and the d4 knight became a fixture that eventually decided the game.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Deny the knight its home.
ex.why: The pawn strike undermines c3 and with it the knight's anchorage on d4. Bc8 then covers f5, and a later f5 push evicts the other knight too. The compensation for the pawn is real only while the knights have no permanent posts.

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 6, level 1900 to 2200
text: McDonald against Lukacs. White to move. Black has doubled f pawns and the two bishops, and White has bishop and knight with the queenside as his playground.

The plan has two halves. Seek queenside play, with a minority attack in the air, and optimise the knights, which means finding the post from which one of them influences that queenside fight. The post is c5, hitting b7, and if it is ever chased by b6 the c6 pawn falls weak on an open file.
The band note calls this hard, because the winning move is a jump that must also be compared with two slower routes to the same square, and one of those runs into a tactic on the f5 pawn.

ex.prompt: White to move. Start the knight's journey to c5.
ex.why: The route is e5, d3, c5. It beats routing the other knight through f4 or c1, and it carries a point: with the knight off c4 the reply Bd5 fails to Qxf5, since the queen no longer has to babysit c4.

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 7, level 2000 and up
text: Staunton against Loewenthal, Birmingham 1858. White is a pawn up and hits on an idea: give Black the two bishops with Bxc6, then close the position with e4 so the pair never breathes. Watch it happen, then find Black's reply.

The idea would be excellent if White had time to consolidate with castling, Qe2, d3 and f4. The flaw is that Black is not obliged to accept a closed position, and Silman draws the lesson for both chairs. If you give your opponent two bishops, be certain he cannot open things up. If your two bishops look dead, insist on bringing them to life.
The band note rates this for experts, because Black is a pawn down and the bishops genuinely look buried, so the right move requires trusting dynamics over material.

ex.prompt: White has just closed the centre. Rip it back open.
ex.why: The break shatters the wall the bishops were supposed to rot behind. Taking on f5 with the knight loses to Bxe4, and after the capture on e4 material is level with every black piece better than its counterpart.

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 8, level 2200 and up
text: Wang Yue against Radjabov. Black to move, holding a tall pawn on g7 and good queenside prospects with a4 and a rook lift to b4 coming.

Playing for the queenside alone would compensate for the inferior minor piece. Radjabov asked a better question, which Silman quotes as the reason this position is in the book. Why not win both battles?
The band note says spotting both battles deserves credit below 2200, and actually playing the move takes vision and courage, because it spends a pawn on a piece everyone has written off.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Spend a pawn to resurrect the tall pawn.
ex.why: The pawn clears the long diagonal and the bishop lands on d4 with check, driving the king away from the queenside before the a pawn starts running. One pawn for a piece brought back from the dead is a bargain.

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 9, level 1600 to 1800
text: Kamsky against Eljanov. Black to move, and the task is simply to assess. White has two bishops against bishop and knight, which usually reads as an edge.

Look at what the pieces are doing instead of counting them. Black's bishop owns the long light squared diagonal, his knight can reach e4 or d5, and White's c1 bishop is not merely passive, it cannot find a diagonal to live on at all.

Silman then makes the point with a thought experiment. Shift White's pawns to e4 and f3 and put the bishop on e3, and the assessment flips completely. Owning two bishops means nothing by itself. Black's job here is to keep the c1 bishop miserable and make sure that better version never happens.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Keep the sleeping bishop asleep.
ex.why: The rook takes the open file and, crucially, denies the c1 bishop its one developing square on d2. Simple, strong, and aimed entirely at the opponent's worst piece.

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 10, level 1400 to 2200
text: Krush against Xu Yuhua. Black to move, slightly worse against the bishop pair, with a knight stranded on h5. Neither side has a real weakness, so there is no cause for panic and no case for heroics.

The inferior side has two honest options in such positions. Accept that you are worse and improve piece by piece toward equality, or seek tactics, remembering that forcing matters usually creates weaknesses in your own camp. Here the aggressive f5 fails concretely, so the sober road it is.
That means the anti bishop pair ideas, every piece into play, and a wall with no entry points. The first candidate for improvement is obvious once you say it aloud.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Rescue the piece rotting on the rim.
ex.why: A knight on the edge of the board does nothing for the defence. Bringing it back is not glamorous, and it is exactly how a worse position gets held.

ex.prompt: What is the realistic plan for the worse side here?
ex.why: Being worse without weaknesses is uncomfortable and entirely holdable. The losing choice is usually the impatient one.
options: Attack before White consolidates
Tighten the position, trade one bishop off when possible, allow no weaknesses
Trade queens at any cost
Push the a and b pawns for space

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 11, level 1400 to 2200
text: Carlsen against Anand. White to move with the better structure and an active bishop against a tall pawn on e6. A small plus, and the question is how to grow it.

The natural instinct is to keep the knight, since Black's bishop is ugly. Carlsen reads the position one level deeper. The e6 bishop is inactive and useful, holding d5 and f5 together, which makes it a piece worth removing rather than a piece to laugh at.
Silman's band note splits the credit deliberately. Assessing the position is 1400 material. Choosing to trade your knight for the bad bishop is what pushes the band to 2200.

ex.prompt: White to move. Trade for the ugly piece that holds Black together.
ex.why: After the trade the king itself must babysit f5, and White's king and bishop squeeze while Black defends squares a bishop used to cover. Inactive does not mean useless, and useful enemy pieces are the ones to remove.

lessons.title: Minor piece war test 12, level 1400 to 1800
text: Dominguez against Nakamura, Cuernavaca Young Masters 2006. White to move, and the book asks whose minor piece is better, and by how much.

Count what the bishop can ever do. White's pawns will all end up on dark squares, so it can never attack one. The kingside space chokes it and its own king together, and it is chained to e6 for tactical reasons the next question makes you name. The knight, meanwhile, hops between colors, kicks the black king off any square it likes, and White's king can park on a dark square where the bishop can never touch it.

Silman's band note says everyone should have seen that the knight is better. The real test was the verdict. This is not a small plus to nurse, it is total domination, and the game score reads like the knight giving a clinic.

ex.prompt: Whose minor piece is better, and how much better?
ex.why: Every pawn the bishop could ever attack sits or will sit on a dark square, so the bishop is a permanent spectator while the knight torments both wings. Barring an accident this minor piece battle wins for the knight in middlegame and endgame alike.
options: The bishop, slightly, because the position may open
The knight, slightly, but Black should hold
The knight, totally, this structure is close to winning by itself
Neither, the minor pieces balance out

ex.prompt: Why can the bishop never leave the defence of e6?
ex.why: The f6 pawn is a promotion tactic waiting to happen. The moment e6 is taken with fxe6 the f pawn steps to f7 and touches down. One pawn on f6 sentences the bishop to lifelong guard duty.
options: Because e6 hangs to the queen
Because Nxe6 followed by fxe6 and f7 makes a new queen
Because the king needs the bishop for shelter
Because the d5 pawn would fall

ex.prompt: White to move. Start the winning plan on the queenside.
ex.why: First clear away the b4 pawn. That opens c3 for the pieces and prepares a later b4 push, and after the queen trade on c3 the white king walks in while the bishop watches from its cage.

lessons.title: Rooks need a file, so demand one
text: One statement covers most of what rooks need. A rook without an open file is worth less than a minor piece, sitting behind its own pawns dreaming of a future it will not get.

Everyone agrees with that and very few play like it. The trap is hoping a file will open by itself. Ask a player developing like this what the plan is for the rooks and the answer is usually that the rooks come later. Later tends not to arrive.

Nc3 here is the move that quietly ruins it. It blocks the c pawn, and the c pawn is the one that would have opened a file. Play c4 first and everything changes. The knight on c3 joins the pawn in the fight for d5, a rook comes to c1, and a later capture on d5 hands that rook the file it needs.

ex.prompt: White to move. Play the move that gives the rooks a future.
ex.why: c4 first, and only then Nc3. The pawn creates the tension that will open the c file, and the knight supports it instead of standing in its way.

ex.prompt: What actually creates open files?
ex.why: Files open where pawns meet and one of them captures. If your pawns never make contact, no file will ever open, and no amount of rook shuffling will fix it.
options: Trading pieces
Pawn tension and pawn breaks
Castling on opposite sides
Advancing the rooks early

ex.prompt: What is wrong with developing the knight to c3 first?
ex.why: The move looks like healthy development and quietly removes the plan. Ask what each developing move does to your pawn breaks before you play it.
options: It blocks the c pawn, which is the pawn that opens the file
It hangs the d pawn
It blocks the bishop
Nothing, it is a normal developing move

lessons.title: Stealing a file
text: Both sides have a rook on the c file, staring at each other. Neither can take, because whoever trades first lets the other recapture and own the file outright. The usual outcome is that the rooks sit there for the rest of the game and nobody gets anything.

Ivanchuk found the way past it, and the idea is worth stealing. Put a piece on the file between the two rooks. The connection breaks, the enemy rook is no longer defending anything down the file, and you are free to double or even triple behind your own.
Bc7 does exactly that. White follows with Rc3 and Rfc1, and only then moves the bishop back to d6. The rooks are stacked, the block lifts, and the file belongs to White.

ex.prompt: Neither rook can take on the c file. Break the deadlock.
ex.why: The bishop cuts the file in half. White stacks the rooks behind it in peace, then steps the bishop back to d6 and takes the file.

ex.prompt: Why can neither side simply trade rooks on the c file first?
ex.why: That mutual standoff is why contested files so often stay contested. Breaking it needs a third piece, not a better rook move.
options: The rooks are pinned
Whoever trades first lets the opponent recapture and own the file
The trade loses a pawn
It would allow a back rank mate

lessons.title: Waiting to pull the trigger
text: Sometimes you are the one who gets to decide when a file opens, because a capture of yours would open it. That is a real asset, and the mistake is using it too early.

White can play the capture on g5 at any moment. Doing it now would open the h file and share it equally. Holding it back, while stacking rooks behind the pawn, means that when the file finally opens it opens for one side only.

The count is the whole point. White has three squares to work with on the h file and Black has two, so White can triple and Black cannot. Capture first and Black gets as many squares as White. Capture last, after the rooks and queen are on their best squares, and the file is a gift to nobody but yourself.

ex.prompt: Queenside counterplay is dead. Start work on the other wing.
ex.why: The pawn arrives on h4 and then stays there. White brings the king out of the way and stacks rooks on the h file while the tension holds.

ex.prompt: Why does White avoid capturing on g5 straight away?
ex.why: White has three usable squares on the file and Black two, so White can triple. Capturing early evens that count and throws the advantage away.
options: It loses a pawn
It would give Black as many h file squares as White
It opens lines toward the white king
It allows a knight fork

ex.prompt: When should the file finally be opened?
ex.why: The capture is a one-time resource. Spend it when the rooks and queen are already maximised, not while they are still getting ready.
options: As soon as possible, to gain time
Once your own pieces are on their best squares
Only in the endgame
Never, the tension is the advantage

lessons.title: Alekhine's gun
text: The same idea as the previous lesson, on the other wing, played by Fischer. White can capture on b5 whenever he likes, and taking now would only produce a standoff with both sides equally placed on the a file.

So he does not take. Ra3, then the other rook to a1, then the first one to a2, and finally the queen behind both of them on a1. Stacking the queen behind two rooks is Alekhine's gun, and it is the maximum pressure a single file can carry.

Only then does the capture become worth making, because the file will open onto a fully loaded battery. Fischer follows with Nf1 heading through d2 and b1 to a3, adding a fifth attacker to a pawn that cannot run.

ex.prompt: Taking on b5 now only trades. Build up instead.
ex.why: Both rooks come to the a file behind the pawn, with the queen to follow. The capture waits until the battery is complete.

ex.prompt: What is Alekhine's gun?
ex.why: Queen last, rooks in front. The rooks do the pushing and the queen supplies the weight, which is the same logic as the bishop and queen catapult from the bishops part.
options: Two rooks on the seventh rank
The queen stacked behind both rooks on one file
A rook and bishop on the same diagonal
Doubled pawns supporting a rook

lessons.title: Two rooks on the seventh need help
text: Two rooks on the seventh rank is one of the strongest formations in chess, and here it is not enough on its own. The bishop on g1 blocks the damage, and if Black cannot generate something concrete the a pawn simply runs and wins.

The lesson is the one the knights part kept making about attackers and defenders. Rooks on the seventh are two attackers. Bring a third and the position collapses. Leave them to work alone and a single well placed defender holds them.

The knight comes in with Nh5 and then Ng3, and suddenly the white king has no shelter. Black is a piece down and completely safe, because control of the seventh rank plus one more attacker is worth more than the material.

ex.prompt: The rooks cannot break through alone. Send reinforcements.
ex.why: The knight heads for g3 where it tears open the king's cover. Rg5 was even simpler, and both work for the same reason: a third attacker.

ex.prompt: What was missing while the rooks sat on the seventh alone?
ex.why: Two attackers against one good defender is a stalemate of forces. This is the same counting rule that decided the weak pawn lesson in Part One.
options: An open file
A third attacker
A passed pawn
The bishop pair

lessons.title: Seventh rank with nothing to bite on
text: Read the position the way the course has trained you and White looks close to winning. The open d file belongs to White, a rook sits on the seventh attacking b7, and there is not an obvious weakness in the white camp.
The truth is that White has almost nothing. Maroczy was a magnificent endgame player and could not dent it. The reason is worth more than the position itself.

A rook on the seventh is not an advantage by itself. It is a delivery mechanism, and it needs something to deliver against. Black has no weakness that the rook can actually attack, so the impressive-looking rook achieves nothing, and Black calmly offers a trade of the bishop that defends b2.

ex.prompt: White has the open file and a rook on the seventh. How large is the advantage?
ex.why: The formation is right and there is nothing to use it on. Impressive placement with no target is worth very little.
options: Winning
Small, and Black holds comfortably
Black is actually better

ex.prompt: Black to move. Go after the piece that holds White together.
ex.why: The bishop offers to trade the one on a3, which is what defends b2. Removing a defender is the same idea as attacking a weak pawn, applied to a piece.

ex.prompt: What does a rook on the seventh actually need?
ex.why: Pawns it can eat, or an enemy king it can cage. Without either, the seventh rank is just a rank.
options: A second rook beside it
Targets it can attack
An open file behind it
The enemy king on the back rank

lessons.title: Rooks test 1, level 1600 to 1800
text: Elder against Hosmer, Cleveland 1871. Black to move, dominating the c file with both rooks and pressing c2.

The pressure achieves nothing yet, because White's knight on d4 guards the pawn and glues the position together. Your target is c2, his knight defends it, and your own knight is doing nothing about any of that.

Silman's band note says this one is solved by pure talking. Name the target, name the defender, ask how to remove the glue. He worried a 1400 would hunt for something violent and miss that a plain exchange does the job.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Start removing the defender of c2.
ex.why: The knight heads for b5 to trade off White's defensive horse. In a sense the retreat-looking move already attacks c2, because once the defender is gone the file wins by itself.

lessons.title: Rooks test 2, level 1400 to 1600
text: Trapp against Buggs, Las Vegas 2008, an amateur game chosen because the decision is so clean. White to move, and the book poses it as a three way choice between Qb3 check, Rd1, and g3.
Two things matter. Black wants permanent ownership of the d file, and d3 is a hole. Any candidate that ignores both is answering the wrong question.
The check even sets a devious trap, and Silman's point is that a trick is never a reason to play a move. After the calm reply the check has achieved nothing and Black lands on d3 anyway.

ex.prompt: Which move is correct: Qb3+, Rd1, or g3?
ex.why: Rd1 denies Black the file and holds the draw. g3 hands over both the file and d3. The check hopes for Qd5, when Rd1 would win the house, but one accurate king move ends the trick and Black takes d3 anyway.
options: Qb3+, setting a trap against Qd5
Rd1, contesting the d file at once
g3, making luft first

ex.prompt: What happens after 27.Qb3+ Kg7 28.Rd1 Rd3, if White trades on d3?
ex.why: The e4 pawn recaptures onto d3 and becomes a protected runner two steps from home. The hole and the file were the same problem, and the trade converts one into the other.
options: White wins the exchange
The recapture gives Black a monster passed pawn
It is a dead draw
Black loses the e4 pawn

lessons.title: Rooks test 3, level 1400 to 2200
text: Panno against Idigoras. White to move, and the book asks two questions. Is he in any hurry, and how do you see this game playing out?

Black is out of space in the centre and on the kingside and can only shuffle. That answers the first question. When the opponent cannot do anything, time stops mattering, and White may build up in any way he pleases. Note the g7 bishop, which has earned full tall pawn status, and a rook on h7 that is not far behind.

The second question is the master level half. A trained eye foresees that Black will eventually play g5, transposing into a known closed structure with known plans, and prepares for that future position now. Panno then tortured his opponent in the best cat and mouse style.

ex.prompt: Is White in any hurry?
ex.why: A space advantage against an opponent with no plan removes the clock from the position. Rushing is the only way White can go wrong.
options: Yes, Black is about to free himself with g5
No, Black can only shuffle, so White builds at leisure
Yes, the h4 pawn hangs

ex.prompt: White to move. Begin the unhurried buildup on the file that will open.
ex.why: The rook lifts toward the g file before it opens. When g5 finally comes, White has already massed against the structure he knew was arriving.

lessons.title: Rooks test 4, level 1400 to 1600
text: Polugaevsky against Bronstein. Each side has queen and rook, there is one open file, and everything reduces to a single question. Does the queen lead onto the d file head first, or does the rook lead with the queen behind?
Silman's rule of thumb is about what can be ignored. A queen arriving on the seventh rank can often be tolerated for a move. A rook arriving there cannot.

So the heavy pieces stack with the rook in front, the same logic as Alekhine's gun scaled down to two pieces. The band note says he expects 1400 players to find this easy and knows some will still choose the queen.

ex.prompt: White to move. Take the file feet first.
ex.why: The queen slots behind the rook, and Rd7 lands next with threats Black must answer. Leading with the queen also grabs the file, and allows Black to blunt it, since a queen alone on the seventh can be shrugged off.

lessons.title: Rooks test 5, level 1400 to 1800
text: Carlsen against Stubberud, from a ten board blindfold display. White to move with two quiet bishops, the better structure, and one clear target on d6.

The knight has just hit the queen, so there is a small decision about where she goes, and the answer is chosen by the plan rather than by the attack. White intends to triple heavy pieces against d6, rooks in front, queen at the back.
Silman's band note is cheerful about this one. Anyone who was paying attention when Alekhine's gun appeared in the rooks chapter will rush to set it up here.

ex.prompt: White to move. Step the queen back to where the gun forms.
ex.why: From d1 the queen backs both rooks as they stack against d6. Black's answer in the game was passive defence of the target, which is usually how positions with one fixed weakness get lost.

lessons.title: Rooks test 6, level 1800 to 2200
text: Taubenhaus against Schiffers, 1887. White is winning, and Black has staked everything on the b pawn, which is starting to look genuinely fast.

The defensive reflex is to bring a rook back and babysit the pawn, and it works, slowly, while giving Black endless chances to twitch. Silman's advice is to ask what your own best pieces are for before you volunteer them for guard duty.
Both white rooks own open files, and most of Black's army is a long way from its king. The band note says this is hard precisely because the running pawn makes players panic.

ex.prompt: White to move. Ignore the pawn and attack the king.
ex.why: The rooks double on the eighth rank, where with the e pawn and knight they bury the king before the b pawn matters. Rd8 works the same way, and racing beats defending here by several tempi.

lessons.title: Rooks test 7, level 1400 to 1800
text: Capablanca against Portela, Havana 1913. Black to move, two clean pawns up. The book's question is whether White is doomed.

He is not, and the reason is a bind rather than a tactic. The rook on the eighth rank and the knight freeze Black's king and bishop where they stand, and the black rook is chained to its third rank, because leaving it allows Ne6 winning the bishop. Two extra pawns with no way to use a single piece is a draw.

The game itself became famous for what happened when Portela refused the draw and grabbed the a4 pawn anyway. The knight reached e6 at last and ate the bishop, then g6, f4, h5 and g7 in one continuous rampage.

ex.prompt: Black is two pawns up. What is the correct result?
ex.why: Activity counts before material. King and bishop are frozen, and the rook may never leave its third rank. Nothing black can improve, so nothing black can win.
options: Black wins with the extra material
A draw, because the bind paralyses every black piece
White is actually winning

ex.prompt: What exactly is Black's rook doing on the sixth rank?
ex.why: The moment the rook abandons the rank, Ne6 wins the bishop, which is precisely how the real game ended when Portela grabbed on a4. A piece that cannot move without losing material is not really a piece.
options: Attacking the a4 pawn
Guarding e6 so the knight cannot fork its way to the f8 bishop
Preparing to double rooks
Shielding the king

lessons.title: Taking material takes courage too
text: Everyone knows that giving material up takes nerve. Silman's point is that taking it often takes just as much, because grabbing a pawn usually costs you something you can see clearly, which is time.

Look for the target first. The e5 pawn is the obvious one and it is comfortably defended, which makes it no target at all. Something is only weak if you can bring pieces to bear on it. The pawn Black can actually reach is a4, through Na6 and Nc5 with the queen coming to e8.

The capture is not free and Fischer knew it. Every move Black spends collecting on a4 is a move White spends developing, so the pawn is bought with time and central space. That is a deliberate trade of one imbalance for another, not a blunder, and it made the game sharp enough to win. Game 13 of the 1972 match is sometimes called the greatest ever played.

ex.prompt: Click the pawn Black can actually attack.
ex.why: The e5 pawn looks like the target and is easily defended, so it is not one. A weakness you cannot reach is not a weakness.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Start the journey to that pawn.
ex.why: Na6 heads for c5, the queen comes to e8, and the pawn falls. Four black moves to win a pawn while White develops, which is exactly the trade being made.

ex.prompt: What is Black paying for the a4 pawn?
ex.why: Naming the price is what separates a calculated grab from greed. Black accepts a real disadvantage in exchange for real material, and then has to handle the tension better than the opponent.
options: The bishop pair
Time and central space
King safety
The right to castle

lessons.title: Refusing to bow to their agenda
text: Black has weaknesses on a5, c5, c6 and c7, which is a lot of them. The a5 pawn is not sitting there quietly though. It attacks b4, and if White answers by taking on a5 then c5 comes and every one of those weaknesses disappears at once.
So Black has set a question, and the question has an implied answer. Deal with the threat to b4. Most players would be transfixed by the pawn and would spend the move defending or capturing.

Kramnik plays Nb3, which does not address b4 at all. It takes c5 away from Black permanently, which is the move Black needed to cure everything. White simply declines to accept that his opponent's idea is the important one on the board, and keeps his grip on the queenside.

ex.prompt: Black attacks b4 and threatens c5 to cure every weakness. Play the move that ignores the first and stops the second.
ex.why: Taking on a5 allows c5 and Black is fine. Nb3 denies c5 for good, and the weaknesses on a5, c6 and c7 stay weaknesses.

ex.prompt: What was the psychological trap in the position?
ex.why: Silman calls the alternative pushing your own agenda. When one side accepts that the opponent's idea matters more than his own, the position usually starts sliding.
options: Overestimating the attack
Answering the opponent's question instead of asking your own
Trading queens too early
Grabbing a pawn

lessons.title: Pushing your agenda under pressure
text: A three minute blitz game, which is the point. In a fast game there is no time to reason your way to a good frame of mind. Whatever your default is under pressure is what you will play.

Black stands well and is threatening two things at once, Qxe4 and Rxb2. The reflex is to pick one and deal with it, and once you start answering threats in a position like this you tend to keep answering them until the game is gone.

White brings the last rook to the centre instead. The move addresses neither threat and improves White's own position, which is the whole discipline in one move. Silman is explicit that this is trainable at any level, in tournament games and in blitz, by making a habit of asking what your position wants rather than what the opponent is asking of you.

ex.prompt: Black threatens Qxe4 and Rxb2. Play the move that does neither.
ex.why: The last piece joins the game. Answering one threat invites the next, and in a blitz game answering threats is how you lose without ever making an obvious mistake.

ex.prompt: Why does blitz make good training for this?
ex.why: Under time pressure you fall back on your default. Practising the habit in fast games is how it becomes automatic in slow ones.
options: Because the positions are simpler
Because there is no time to think, so your habit is what plays
Because opponents blunder more
Because material matters less

lessons.title: First one to crack
text: Two players around 1100, and the mistake about to be made is one that never fully goes away at any rating.

White notices that Ng4 is possible, imagines a knight running loose near his king, and plays h3 to prevent it. The move is not a blunder and loses nothing by force. It is a whole tempo spent on a problem the opponent had not actually created.

Nf3 was the move, and if Black really goes Ng4 then castling deals with it while doing something White wanted to do anyway. The habit worth building is to answer a threat with a move you were happy to play regardless. Reacting to what the opponent might do, rather than to what he has done, is the most common way a good position quietly turns into a worse one.

ex.prompt: White is worried about Ng4. Play the move that gets on with the game.
ex.why: If Ng4 comes, castling answers it and develops at the same time. h3 answers it and does nothing else, which is a tempo handed over for free.

ex.prompt: What was actually wrong with h3?
ex.why: Prophylaxis is fine when the threat is real and the move is otherwise useless. Here the threat was hypothetical and the move did nothing else.
options: It loses a pawn
It spends a move on a threat the opponent had not made
It weakens the king
It blocks the bishop

ex.prompt: What is the better habit when you sense a threat coming?
ex.why: A move that both answers the threat and improves your position costs nothing. A move that only answers it costs a tempo every time.
options: Prevent it immediately
Meet it with a move you wanted to play anyway
Trade pieces to simplify
Attack somewhere else

lessons.title: Psychology test 1, level 1800 to 2200
text: Karpov against Kudriashov, Moscow 1972. White to move, and for once the book does not ask for a move. It asks what White's two vastly different philosophical options are.

Black's king sits in the centre and his queenside pawns are wrecked, yet he dreams of castling and attacking down the b file with Rb8 and Qb7. White can rip the centre open with f5 and go for that king, or he can trade off the defenders of a4 one by one and simply win a pawn.

Silman's band note says anything that asks for the philosophy behind a position is advanced, and mixing two complete viewpoints makes it harder still. Neither road is wrong. The test is knowing that both exist, and knowing which player you are.

ex.prompt: What are White's two philosophical options?
ex.why: A tactical genius plays f5 and calculates a raging attack. Karpov played for suffocation instead, because a safe extra pawn asks nothing of the nerves. Both are fully justified, which is exactly what makes the question hard.
options: Attack the central king by opening lines with f5, or simplify with exchanges and collect the a4 pawn
Castle by hand or keep the king in the centre
Push the g and h pawns, the kingside attack is the only real plan
Trade queens at once or lose the initiative

ex.prompt: Play Karpov's choice, the move that begins the war on a4.
ex.why: Every exchange removes a defender of a4 and a piece from Black's b file dream at the same time. First the knight goes, then the light squared bishop, then the queens, and the pawn falls for nothing while Black watches.

lessons.title: Psychology test 2, level 2200 and up
text: A theory position from the Samisch King's Indian, reached after 8...Qh4 check 9.g3. The book asks whether taking on g3 is worthwhile.

The capture looks like a cheap pawn grab until you see 10.Qf2, when the knight appears trapped and the queen attacked. That is the point. Black walks in on purpose, because 10...Nxf1 begins a positional sacrifice of the whole queen.

Silman's band note admits that players who have not seen the idea will find it nearly impossible, and that many masters would feel, with some justification, that it simply cannot be sound. Once you count imbalance against imbalance instead of points, it starts to look like a bargain.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Play the critical continuation anyway.
ex.why: The autopilot brain rejects 10...Nxf1 instantly because it obviously loses the queen. Let it. The knight eats g3, f1, e3 and c4 in turn, and the queen goes for two bishops and two pawns.

ex.prompt: What does Black actually have for the queen when the dust settles?
ex.why: That material tradeoff is not bad at all for the second player, and even if c7 eventually falls, the time White spends winning it can let Black's army turn frighteningly active. Positions like this spit in the face of point count.
options: A rook and one pawn, which is not enough
Two bishops and two pawns, a solid position, and only c7 to worry about
A forced mating attack
Nothing, the line is a known blunder

lessons.title: Psychology test 3, level 1800 to 2200
text: Kramnik against Deep Fritz, Bonn 2006, from the man against machine match. Black to move with an uncastled king and the d5 pawn hanging.

The defences fail one by one. 16...Rd8 loses the a6 pawn to 17.Qxa6, and 16...d4 keeps the king in the centre while the queens invade. The robotic rule, it is threatened so I must guard it, leads straight into a death spiral.
Silman's band note says the vast majority of players will think only about saving the pawn, and that there is no effective way to do it. The machine refused the premise entirely.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Refuse to defend the pawn.
ex.why: So simple, and so easy to miss. Black hands over d5, develops, castles, and suddenly owns the lead in development, the queenside majority, and pressure on a2 and e5 while White nurses one extra pawn. The game was drawn without drama.

ex.prompt: What was the real cause of Black's trouble in the diagram?
ex.why: The pawn was the symptom. The king was the disease, so every tempo spent guarding material instead of curing the king made things worse. Cure the disease and the symptom stops mattering.
options: The hanging d5 pawn
The king still sitting in the centre
The missing light squared bishop
The backward b6 pawn

lessons.title: Psychology test 4, level 1400 to 1800
text: Blau against Fischer, Varna Olympiad 1962. Black to move, and Fischer is dying to chop the c4 pawn. This is not raw greed. It is the last step of a long campaign, create the weakness, surround it, feast.

The immediate grab spoils it. After 1...Rxc4 comes 2.Nc6, and the fork on e7 wins everything back with interest. The greed is right and the move order is wrong, which is why the book asks which minor piece has more impact in the battle along the c file.
Silman's band note is one line. Would a 1400 want to prevent Nc6? No doubt about it.

ex.prompt: Why does the immediate 1...Rxc4 fail?
ex.why: After 1...Rxc4 2.Nc6 Rxc1 3.Nxe7+ Kh8 4.Rxc1 the knight has taken a pawn and the exchange comes back. One tricky knight defends the whole queenside by itself, which tells you exactly what to remove.
options: The c1 rook simply recaptures
2.Nc6 forks its way to e7 and wins the exchange back
White wins the d6 pawn in return
It walks into a back rank mate

ex.prompt: Black to move. Remove the defender, then feast.
ex.why: Giving up the fianchetto bishop hurts, and it is the piece with less impact on the only battle that matters. With the knight gone c4 falls cleanly, and the centralizing Qe4 holds e7, kills the counterplay, and starts a siege of a2 and d5. Fischer took his pawn on his own terms and won.

lessons.title: Psychology test 5, level 1800 to 2000
text: A King's Indian structure where everything seems to be going White's way. He leads in development, f5 is attacked, and his king is the safer one. All of it is true, and the book asks what Black can do about his apparent inferiority.

No normal move stops the pain. 1...f4 hangs h7 the instant the f5 pawn steps off the b1 diagonal, and the computer retreats Nb8 or Nb6 merely hold things together, guarding f5 by unmasking the c8 bishop while fighting for nothing.

Silman's band note says the correct move is instant for anyone who has met the idea before, and fairly hard to find otherwise. Being a bit worse with no play rarely ends well. Being a bit worse with lots of play keeps all three results alive.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Make something nice happen by force.
ex.why: One pawn buys a litany of imbalances. The e5 square turns any black piece into a monster, the g file opens for the rooks, the f4 pawn forever threatens f3, and the extra e4 pawn is a traitor that buries White's queen and bishop while robbing the c3 knight of its best square.

ex.prompt: What is actually wrong with the sturdy retreats 1...Nb8 or 1...Nb6?
ex.why: Waiting moves ask the position to improve by itself, and it will not. When a sacrifice creates real play in a position where everything else is misery, you play it even if the engine calls you slightly worse.
options: They lose material by force
They defend f5 and fight for nothing, which is survival rather than play
They allow White to win the h5 knight
Nothing, they are the safest practical choice

lessons.title: Psychology test 6, level 1800 to 2200
text: Fischer against Evans, United States Championship 1963. A King's Gambit where both sides have played with fire, and now Black must decide whether 17...Qxh4 is wise.

Count what the capture really buys. The h1 rook was out of the game and inherits a half open file. The h2 knight was a bystander and finds honest work. Black already suffers along the f file, where f4, f5 and f6 are weak and f7 can become a target, and the pawn grab develops nothing.
Silman's band note points at White's reply, the kind of quiet move that many players never consider, and at how hard the position is to assess with so many ideas floating around.

ex.prompt: Is 17...Qxh4 wise?
ex.why: Fischer answered with the quiet 18.Kg1, defending h1 and threatening Nxg4 against the loose h8 rook. After 18...Nh6 19.Nf1 the sad knight developed with tempo, 20.Nxh5 took the pawn back and clamped f6, and the position was a rout.
options: Yes, a clean extra pawn is a clean extra pawn
Yes, because it drags White's king into the open
No, it activates the h1 rook and the h2 knight, wastes time, and does not even keep the pawn

ex.prompt: What should Black have done instead of grabbing on h4?
ex.why: A pawn grab is fine when you actually win the pawn and give little back. Here Black gave activity to two sleeping white pieces, lost time his shaky position could not spare, and the pawn came back anyway. That combination is simply a disaster.
options: Traded queens immediately
Played Qd7 and followed with Ne7, Kb8 and c5, developing and shoring up the weaknesses
Pushed the h pawn to h4 himself
Sacrificed on f4 for an attack

lessons.title: Psychology test 7, level 1400 to 1800
text: Larsen against Fischer, a little known Copenhagen exhibition game from 1962 between two legendary giants. Larsen has just recaptured on e5, and the book asks whether taking that pawn is wise.

Black could keep a pleasant edge with simple moves, castling or Be6, banking on the better structure and the weak squares in White's camp. Fischer did the Fischer thing instead. He measured White's coming activity, judged that it would eventually dry up, and took the pawn.
Silman's band note hopes that everyone reading the book understands the principle. If you can take something, and you cannot see why you should not, then by all means chop away.

ex.prompt: Is grabbing the e5 pawn wise?
ex.why: This is calculated greed, not hope. Fischer knew White would get play for the pawn and judged that the material would outlast the initiative. Both quiet moves were also fine, and the point of the test is that fear alone is never a reason to decline.
options: No, Black should complete development first
Yes, if your calculation says the activity dries up, greed is just good judgement
No, the g7 bishop is Black's best piece and must not move
It loses by force to the check on b5

ex.prompt: Black to move. Do the Fischer thing.
ex.why: White gets his burst, a check on b5, the bishop stabbing at h6, some pressure against f7. Black meets each threat calmly, keeps the extra pawn, and the activity drains away exactly as calculated. Fischer converted the ending.

lessons.title: Psychology test 8, level 1800 to 2200
text: Panarin against Pevzner, Russian Championship 2007. Black sacrificed a pawn for activity and now faces a choice between 23...Na4, winning the exchange, and 23...Be6, developing with a threat against c4.

The book asks whether 23...Na4 is a good idea, and the answer sits in what White gets back. Overwhelming space, a monster rook landing on d6, two laser beam bishops, and a black bishop that goes to a1 to die. With two pawns for the exchange, Black is not even ahead on material.
Silman's band note says the move wins material and that this in itself does not make it good, then guesses that most players under 1800 could not resist. In the game Black could not resist either.

ex.prompt: 23...Na4 wins the exchange. Is it a good idea?
ex.why: Black played for the exchange and got his wish, and everything else in the position turned white. Two pawns came with the deal, so the material ledger was level while every imbalance pointed one way. The rest of the game was a slaughter.
options: Yes, material is material and the rest is technique
No, after 24.Nxa4 Bxa1 25.e5 White gets space, the d6 rook, both bishops, and the a1 bishop never comes home
Yes, but only if Black finds the follow up Be6
It is equal either way

ex.prompt: What was the better choice, and on what grounds?
ex.why: Be it good or bad, the developing move deserved the nod, since lines like 24.Bf1 d5 turn every black piece active. The moral is Silman's own. Never play for material without carefully pricing every imbalance the opponent gets in return.
options: 23...Be6, because activity for every piece outranks a material gain that buries your own bishop
23...Qf6, hitting d4 and f4
23...b5, breaking the queenside open
23...Na4 anyway, but declining the rook

lessons.title: Psychology test 9, level 1800 to 2000
text: Rustemov against Movsesian, Moscow 2004. White stands beautifully, with a coming kingside attack, a bind on e5, more space everywhere, and pressure against the weak pawns on a6 and c6. Black has just offered one of them.

The book asks whether 14.Rxc6 is a good idea. Taking gives Black exactly what he prayed for, since 14...Nf6 and 15...Ne4 spring the passive pieces to life, and White keeps at most a shadow of his advantage.

Silman's band note appreciates the greed and understands why the capture would be given a go, then suspects that experienced players would hold off. When you own every imbalance on the board, why buy a pawn at the price of counterplay?

ex.prompt: Is 14.Rxc6 a good idea?
ex.why: After 14.Rxc6 Nf6 15.Nc5 Ne4 the formerly dead pieces jump into the game. The defender offered material precisely to buy activity, and refusing the bribe is the respectful answer. White played 14.h5 and pressed on with his own agenda.
options: Yes, a free pawn and the a6 pawn falls next
No, it trades a strangling grip for a pawn and hands Black the counterplay he was begging for
No, because the rook gets trapped on c6
Yes, but only after inserting h5 first

ex.prompt: Two moves later, after 14.h5 a5 15.hxg6 fxg6, the same capture was on offer again. What had changed?
ex.why: Circumstances decide, not habits. With the king newly airy, 16.Rxc6 Nf6 17.Nc5 Ne4 18.Nxe4 dxe4 19.Bc4+ e6 20.Ng5 is overwhelming. White chose the quiet g3 instead and still won, a very human decision when a positional lock is already in hand.
options: Nothing, taking on c6 was still wrong
The recapture toward the centre fixed Black's structure
Black's king cover had been damaged, so 16.Rxc6 now won material and kept the attack
White no longer had the h file

lessons.title: Psychology test 10, level 2000 to 2200
text: Christiansen against Silman, exhibition match 1978, told against himself in the book's mental breakdown section. White has just captured on h7 with check, and the book asks what is going on.

Both players had been trading delusions for moves. Silman, sure he was lost, sank into the self talk of I cannot survive this, while Christiansen kept playing this has to win moves without checking them. The rook grab on g7 a move earlier was the last of those, and it threw away a forced win for this.
During the game Silman found a third option beyond the two legal king moves. He resigned. Christiansen stared at him in shock, because he had been about to offer a draw.

ex.prompt: Silman's actual choice here was to resign. What is the truth of the position?
ex.why: The negative frame of mind made it impossible to see what was really on the board. Silman later traded phrases like I cannot and it is hopeless for a single belief, there is always a defense, and credited that swap with much of his later career.
options: White mates in a few moves, resignation was correct
It is a dead draw by perpetual check or stalemate
Black is winning because the a2 pawn queens
Black survives only by giving the queen for the rook

ex.prompt: Black to move. Play the defense Silman never looked for.
ex.why: Either king move draws. White wins the queen, the a pawn promotes with check, and the new queen and rook chase the king up the board until Rxh2 and Qg4 force either perpetual check or the stalemate that ends this line. Christiansen played it all out afterward and slammed down the final move.

lessons.title: Psychology test 11, level 1600 to 2000
text: An internet blitz game, Empire against girl-brain, ICC 2007. Black has grabbed the g2 pawn and stands clearly better, and White has just attacked a7 with the queen.

The move Black would love to play is the simple king step to b8, guarding a7 and tucking the king away. In the game Black promptly said I cannot, spotted a scary looking sequence, and returned the pawn with a knight retreat instead, handing the advantage straight back.
Silman's band note suspects a 1400 would play the right move instantly and only then discover White's idea. The test is refusing to be psyched out of your dream move by a threat nobody has proven.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Defend a7 the way you want to.
ex.why: This is the dream move, so it deserves a real defense at the board. White's bishop check and hop to c7 look terrifying, forking rook and knight, and that picture is exactly what scared Black out of playing it. The threat lives in the head until it is proven on the board.

ex.prompt: Play has gone Kb8, Bf4 check, Ka8, Bc7, hitting rook and knight at once. Save everything with one move.
ex.why: The rook steps out of the fork and attacks the queen on a5 in the same breath, so White never gets time to take the knight. Ask the position a calm question, how do I save the rook with tempo, and the answer hits you square between the eyes. Black keeps the pawn and the game.

lessons.title: Psychology test 12, level 2000 to 2200
text: Kasparov against Karpov, world championship 1985. White has just attacked the d7 rook, and defending it while creating a threat of your own looks like the most natural decision ever made.

The position waves every tactical red flag at once. White's pieces are more active, the back rank is delicate, f7 is under pressure, and the b7 bishop stands loose. Flags like these demand that a move be proven tactically, not just logically. Karpov checked one capture, satisfied himself, and played the rook to d8.

It became one of the biggest blunders of his career, born of the phrase after I defend my rook he cannot take it. Announcements that stop the thinking process are the main source of tactical oversights at every level, world champions included.

ex.prompt: The natural 22...Rcd8 defends d7 and threatens the d1 rook. Does it hold up?
ex.why: Karpov calculated only 23.Re8 check, which indeed fails to Rxe8 and Re7. Kasparov instead took the rook at once, and after 23...Rxd7 24.Re8+ Kh7 25.Be4+ g6 26.Rxd7 White had two rooks for the queen and won a piece by force, since taking the bishop on c6 walks into mate on f7.
options: Yes, every capture on d7 loses material for White
No, 23.Qxd7 wins on the spot, since after Rxd7 comes Re8 check and the bishop check picks up the house
Yes, though White keeps a small pull
No, because of the quiet 23.Re8 check first

ex.prompt: Black to move. Batten down the hatches instead.
ex.why: Now the queen guards d6, everything defends c6, and stacking on d8 becomes safe next move. Black had fully equalized, and the game would have fizzled into the drawn endgame it eventually reached in analysis. One prophylactic rook move was the whole difference.

lessons.title: Psychology test 13, level 2000 to 2200
text: Edward Lasker against Bogoljubov, New York 1924. The book asks you to assess, in your head, the position after Rd5, Qb6 and the pawn recapture on b5.

Alekhine annotated this game in the classic tournament book and gave exactly that line as easily winning for Black. His analysis is a complete mess. The recapture on b5 walks into a forced mate, and his follow up capture on c7 misses that mate entirely. One of the greatest calculators ever fell to the phrase he has to, twice in a row.

Silman draws a training recommendation from the wreck. Annotate your own games in depth before any engine sees them, write down why you made every decision, and then watch how often the words I cannot and he had to appear in your notes.

ex.prompt: Alekhine gave 40...Rd5 41.Qb6 cxb5 42.Qxc7 as winning for Black. What actually happens after 41...cxb5?
ex.why: After 42.f6+ Kf8 43.Qb8+ the king is run down by force. Once the mind announces Black has to take on b5 and White has to take on c7, both blunders follow effortlessly, and even the man annotating the game never checked either one.
options: Black wins with the two extra pawns, as claimed
White mates in four, starting with the pawn check on f6
White regains the pawn with equality
Black must bail out with perpetual check

ex.prompt: Play has gone Rd5, then Qb6 attacking rook and queenside. Find the move that really wins for Black.
ex.why: The exchange sacrifice trades every attacker off the board. After the queen trade and the knight's return to f5, Black's connected passed pawn and active pieces leave White in serious trouble, which is what Alekhine's easily won for Black should have said in the first place.

lessons.title: Psychology test 14, level 1400 to 2200
text: Czebe against Koneru, Budapest 2001. Black gave away most of a winning advantage but still controls the game, and the book asks you to calculate a forcing line in your head. Rook to c2, rook to e2, take the rook, White has to take back, then bishop to c5 and grind forever.
Koneru calculated exactly that sequence at the board and played it, having judged the resulting endgame to offer decent winning chances against the two bishops.
Silman's band note admits to setting a trap for the reader and asks, with tough love, whether you fell in. The whole line rests on three innocent words, has to take.

ex.prompt: How should you assess Black's winning chances in the line Rc2, Re2, Rxe2, Bxe2, Bc5?
ex.why: Every assessment of the final position is wasted effort, because the position is never reached. The recapture on e2 felt forced only because the line began with the words she has to take back, and once that lie is embraced you see nothing else.
options: Good practical chances, White must grovel for the draw
Roughly balanced, the two bishops hold
The assessment never matters, because after Rxe2 White is not forced to take back
Winning for Black, the b4 knight dominates

ex.prompt: After 29...Rc2 30.Re2 Rxe2, what does White actually play?
ex.why: The check on c4 ends the game at once. The e2 rook must block on e6, the bishop takes it with mate, since the b2 bishop rakes g7 and h8 while Black's own f8 bishop entombs the king. Koneru resigned on the spot, and many players have been put on suicide watch by less.
options: 31.Bxe2, and the grind begins
31.Bc4+, and it is mate after Re6 32.Bxe6
31.Re8, trading into a lost ending
31.Bd4, saving the bishop pair

lessons.title: Psychology test 15, level 1900 to 2200
text: Schlosser against Fish, Bundesliga 2005. Black has just captured a knight on c3, so White is a piece down and must obviously get it back. The book adds that analysis is not necessary, which is itself a clue.

There are exactly three moves that do not simply lose a piece for nothing, the two recaptures and one move that is neither. Seeing all three is the entire test. Most players never notice the third, because I have to recapture mode shuts the search down the moment a recapture is found.

Silman's band note calls the game itself extremely advanced and insists the example is not about finding the star move. It is about how a blanket I have to blinds players of every level, a disease few even realize exists.

ex.prompt: White is a piece down. Which moves deserve consideration?
ex.why: Even deciding that e5 must be garbage counts as solving the problem, because you noticed it existed. The pawn push attacks the f6 knight while the c3 bishop stays short of squares, so the piece comes back anyway, on White's terms.
options: Only 13.bxc3, keeping the pawn front intact
13.bxc3 and 13.Qxc3, the two recaptures
13.bxc3, 13.Qxc3, and the non recapture 13.e5, and noticing the third is the whole point
Only 13.Qxc3, since bxc3 wrecks the structure

ex.prompt: White to move. Regain the piece the third way.
ex.why: After the bishop grabs e5 and the f pawn recaptures, the f6 knight must retreat and White has the piece back with a bind. The quiet regrouping ending in Bh5 leaves White clearly better in every line, and the greedy Bxb2 or Bb4 alternatives lose to a prison sentence or a direct mating attack.

lessons.title: Psychology test 16, level 1600 to 2000
text: Kretchetov against Faber, American Open 2008, opening the book's macho chess section. Black has just played the rook to e7, threatening to take the e3 pawn with check.

A capture with check would convince many players to obey and defend the pawn. Kretchetov gave the threat no respect at all, because a threat is only a threat if the consequences actually hurt you, and here the doubled rooks have bigger business on the seventh rank.

Silman's band note says the check would freak out many players, and that any number of solid choices would be perfectly understandable. Understandable, and each one slower than simply asking what happens if Black actually does it.

ex.prompt: White to move. Ignore the threat and end the game.
ex.why: The rook lands on the seventh and every defense collapses. Taking on e3 with check is suicide, since the king walks to h4 and the g pawn delivers mate, while trading on d7 loses the a7 pawn and the game without even a check to show for it.

ex.prompt: Why was the threatened Rxe3 check never a real threat?
ex.why: One check is not an attack. After Kh4 the black rook has said everything it will ever say, and the g and f pawns mate on the other wing. Measure a threat by what follows it, not by the fact that it comes with check.
options: Because the e3 pawn was poisoned by a back rank trick
Because after the check the white king simply steps up the board and Black has no follow up while the mating net closes
Because White could defend the pawn in time
Because Black loses a rook to a fork immediately

lessons.title: Psychology test 17, level 1800 to 2000
text: Videki against Tiger Hillarp Persson, Budapest 1996. White has just pushed to d5 and intends c4 next, when the b7 bishop becomes a nonentity and Black's queenside dreams go dim.

The reasonable move is e6, striking at the centre, and it gives Black a fine game. Tiger, one of the most aggressive players of his generation, felt he was owed more than reasonable, and looked for the move that turns hoped for play into actual play.
Silman's band note says a 1400 might well toss out the excellent e6, but the move he is really looking for is a much harder proposition.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Take your fate into your own hands.
ex.why: The pawn offers itself to open the c file. A retreat hands Black a tempo, the capture hands him the file plus a tempo after Rc8, and either way the c5 square becomes a permanent home for the d7 knight. In the game White declined with Bc2 and was slowly buried, a finish the book titles death by bishops.

ex.prompt: What exactly does 12...c4 buy?
ex.why: Before the push Black had wishes. After it he has a file, a square, and the initiative, at the price of one pawn that White dares not hold. Macho chess is not violence, it is refusing to wait for permission.
options: A direct attack on the d3 bishop and nothing more
It converts hoped for queenside play into reality, clears c5 for the knight, and gains time however White reacts
It wins a pawn by force
It locks the queenside so Black can attack the king

lessons.title: Psychology test 18, level 2000 to 2500
text: Miles against Silman, Lone Pine 1979, confessed by the author as the worst psychological dive of his career. Black to move, and Silman had prepared the active b5 with a full supporting line.

Then he spotted White's quiet f3 idea at the end of his analysis, decided all his calculations were garbage, and reasoned that Miles, being the stronger player, had surely seen and refuted everything. Filled with self loathing, he raised the flag with the lazy capture on b3 and died slowly with no play and no hope.
After the game he showed Miles the intended line. Miles said he had not seen any of it. If you do not defend your analysis, who will?

ex.prompt: Black to move. Play the move Silman prepared and then abandoned.
ex.why: The combative push gives Black active pieces and an unstable white king to gnaw on. The feared f3 is answered by a6, when the counterplay holds the balance, and the game move cxb3 was simply bad, trading everything Black had for three pawn islands and a lifetime on the c file rack.

ex.prompt: After 13...b5 14.a4, what did the panicking Silman never even consider?
ex.why: A confident eye finds a whole world in a position. After Qxb4 Rb8 and cxb3 the b pawn runs to b2 and cements itself with Qd6 ideas. Fear does not just reject lines, it stops you from looking for them at all.
options: Trading queens on c3
14...b4, when the queen grab on b4 lets cxb3 create a monster passed pawn on b2
Retreating the knight to b8
Sacrificing on a4

lessons.title: Psychology test 19, level 1400 to 2200
text: Christiansen against Sanz, National Open 2004. Black has just captured on e5 and expects the recapture, the old I take you and you take me paradigm.
Christiansen recaptures only when a lull appears that costs no momentum. Right now there is no lull, because the eighth rank is available and Black's pieces are away from their king.

Silman's band note calls the spread surprising on purpose. Refusing the autopilot recapture is 1400 material for readers of this book. The tactical follow up that justifies it can be missed by players of a very high class.

ex.prompt: White to move. The pawn can wait. Play the move that cannot.
ex.why: The rook trade drags the king into the open, and then comes the point, the queen gives itself on h5. Taking it allows Bf5 and mate two moves later, so Black must decline, and only now does White take the e5 pawn, with the queen also hitting c7, threatening mate on h8, and stopping every check.

ex.prompt: The raid has netted a pawn and Black regroups with Bg7. The c7 rook hangs. Take it?
ex.why: After the greedy capture the queen check on e1 and the knight jump to e6 hand Black real counterplay with opposite colored bishops around an airy king. Qe2 stops every trick first, and the game stays won. When your pieces stop working together, regroup before you grab.
options: Yes, a rook is a rook
No, retreat the queen to e2 first, since a successful raid leaves pieces scattered and the king must be secured before new gains
No, but only because of a direct mate threat
Yes, but only after trading rooks

ex.prompt: The game ended 37...e6 38.f5 exf5. What did White play?
ex.why: Either acceptance mates, gxh5 runs into Bxf5, and Bh6 into Qxh6. One queen offered twice on the same square in one attack is the kind of thing that gives the spectators a thrill, and it all grew from refusing one automatic recapture.
options: 39.Bxf5, winning a third pawn
39.Qh5+, offering the queen on h5 for the second time in one game, with mate next move
39.Rd7, doubling on the seventh
39.Qe5, centralizing again

lessons.title: Psychology test 20, level 1400 to 1800
text: Atalik against Likavsky, Ottawa 2007. White is running the classic minority attack, two queenside pawns marching against three to create a permanent weakness on c6. Black has answered with a scary looking kingside demonstration and now threatens h4.
The book asks how to deal with that threat, and answers with a question of its own. Is it real yet? If not, the correct response is to push your own agenda and let your play race his.
Silman's band note has full confidence that readers of this section will show Black who is boss rather than fall to their knees in the face of the attack.

ex.prompt: White to move. Send the message.
ex.why: Neither side blinks, and that is fine, because White's play arrives with threats while Black's arrives with hopes. The retreat Ne2 is the position in miniature, an attacking move that lets the queen hit c6 and a defensive move that stops g3 in the same breath.

ex.prompt: How did Black's attack actually end?
ex.why: Every white defender did double duty while every black attacker abandoned the rest of the board. After Ke2 the threat of Rh1 was a showstopper, and the knight check on h5 won the queen outright. An attack made of wishes ends exactly this way against calm hands.
options: Black broke through on h2 and won
The queen and knight wandered too deep, the king stepped to e2, and the rook lift to h1 trapped the queen
White gave perpetual check
Black bailed out into a lost endgame

lessons.title: Psychology test 21, level 1800 to 2200
text: Saidy against Russell, National Open 1999. Thoroughly outplayed and about to lose the a5 pawn, Black threw the Hail Mary g5, and the book asks whether he went berserk and how White should respond.

The sacrifice is not madness. After the natural capture Black gets the g5 square for his knight, the e5 square for his bishop, and dark squares around White's king, real trumps bought for one pawn. Saidy took, gave his opponent all of it, and eventually lost to exactly those dark squares.
Silman's dialogue for such moments runs, why should I give my opponent anything of worth, why does he deserve that activity, and he suggests throwing in the word kill for good measure.

ex.prompt: Was 23...g5 berserk?
ex.why: Objectively Black is worse after any sane reply, and the move still deserves credit, because it announces that he does not intend to go quietly. The test is whether White respects the idea enough to take it away from him.
options: Yes, it loses a second pawn for nothing
No, it is a practical sacrifice buying the e5 and g5 squares and dark square play, in other words hope
No, it wins material by force
Yes, resignation was more honest

ex.prompt: White to move. Deprive him of every trump before taking anything.
ex.why: The insertion changes everything about the position Black dreamed of. His bishop bites on the e5 pawn instead of ruling the long diagonal, e5 is no longer a square, White's own bishop owns h1 to a8, the knight gets e4, and the queen reaches f5. A fairytale position instead of a fight.

lessons.title: Psychology test 22, level 1400 to 1800
text: Finegold against Sarkar, United States Open 2007. Black's aggressive flailing has bought him kingside space, kingside weaknesses, and now a second attacker on the d4 pawn. The book asks how White should defend it.
He should not. Both captures on d4 fail, one to a queen check on g6 and the other to the recapture ritual that ends with the queen taking on d5, so the threat is pseudo and the pawn defends itself.
Silman's band note lists the themes, king in the centre, refusing to bow to enemy threats, pushing your own agenda, and declares full faith that his 1400 readers will shine.

ex.prompt: White to move. Defend d4 by ignoring it.
ex.why: Castling long answers the fake threat, solves the central king, and keeps every option open, e3 to tighten, Nf3 to develop, or e4 to blast the centre. In the game Black cracked almost immediately, drifting with Kf7 and then losing a clean pawn with the e5 break.

ex.prompt: Why exactly was the attack on d4 a pseudo threat?
ex.why: Count the punishment before you defend. When you stand up to a threat and force the opponent to master the position or drown in it, more than a few players crumble, and Sarkar did exactly that within two moves.
options: Because the d4 pawn was defended twice
Because either knight capture loses material or concedes a grip, one to Qg6 check and the other to the queen recapturing on d5
Because Black cannot afford to open the position
Because White threatened mate first
