lessons.title: Psychology test 23, level 2200 and up
text: Grefe against Biyiasas, American Open 1974, a battle for first place. Grefe, the reigning United States champion, has outplayed his opponent, stands three pawns up, and the book asks whether there is any difference between Ra8 and Ra7.

Biyiasas was famous for never say die defence, and this position is why the reputation existed. Ra7 wins without a story. Ra8, with its obvious threats of Rf8 and Qa8, looks even more forcing, and walks into one of the most beautiful swindles ever played.
Silman's band note calls this one extremely tough, demanding calculation, inspiration, and a devious mind. You get to sit in the defender's chair and supply all three.

ex.prompt: Is there any difference between Ra8 and Ra7?
ex.why: Grefe played Ra8 expecting resignation. After Nf4 check, the bishop takes, the rook recaptures, and the stage is set. The spectators later insisted the bishop capture was the losing moment, but the analysis shows the game was drawn against every defence once the rook left the seventh rank.
options: No, both win routinely with three extra pawns
Yes, Ra7 wins, while Ra8 allows a forced draw by stalemate machinery
Yes, Ra8 wins faster because of the mate threat on the eighth
Yes, Ra7 loses time and lets Black escape with checks

ex.prompt: Play has gone Ra8, Nf4 check, Bxf4, Rxf4, then Rd8, expecting the queen trade to end it. Begin the save.
ex.why: The rook gives itself with check, and when the queen takes, Qg3 offers the second piece. Taking either way is immediate stalemate, and declining with Kf1 loses to the queen check on a6. Biyiasas had seen the whole machine moves earlier, while paying attention to every trick the position held for him.

lessons.title: Psychology test 24, level 1800 to 2200
text: Silman against Hurdle, Amateur Team West 1998, told against himself once more. White has a far superior structure, a huge queenside space advantage, and a powerful knight against a tall pawn. Silman was so certain of victory that he stopped paying attention, and his last move handed Black a chance.
The first thing Black must do is admit he is on death's door. Once he accepts that, he can embrace guiltless desperation, and the position offers exactly one way to fight.
Silman quotes Lasker on why such swindles keep working. The player with a slight disadvantage plays more attentively and more boldly than the antagonist who takes it easy or aspires after too much.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Refuse eternal passivity.
ex.why: A star move that computers dislike and humans should love. For one pawn the tall pawn bishop gets b5 and a working diagonal, the rooks get the b file, and Black gets the only thing that matters in a lost position, a chance to fight. Blood in the water turned the defender into a shark.

ex.prompt: Twelve moves of pressure later White has drifted, and his king has wandered to a4 to meet your queen head on. Finish him.
ex.why: The queen sacrifice strips the shelter, and the doubled rooks take everything back with interest. Silman describes imagining a teleport to a kinder, gentler place while a dozen spectators watched him get gutted. He had written his opponent's obituary a little early.

lessons.title: Psychology test 25, level 1800 to 2200
text: Altounian against Vande Mortel, US Chess League 2008. Black is a pawn down with an airy king, and his one trump is that White's king is still in the middle, with the h1 rook undefended and x-rayed by the c6 queen. If White ever castles, the tactics die and the extra pawn decides. Black must strike right away.

The game move was f5, clearing the long diagonal by hitting the knight. It looks like a tactical bomb and it is a dead end, because the knight simply steps to g5 and the attack turns out to be one move of noise.

Silman's band note says the mistake would attract a lot of players while the correct move is easily missed. The old maxim applies, when you see a good move, sit on your hands and look for a better one.

ex.prompt: Two attractive moves fight for attention, f5 and Rb8. Which is the real one?
ex.why: The rook offer cannot be accepted, Qxb8 walks into Qc1 mate, and the retreats are a minefield, Qd1 loses to the knight fork discovery and Qb1 to Nc3 and Nxe4. In the game f5 was answered by Ng5, and White consolidated, won the black rook, and took the point.
options: f5, blasting open the long diagonal at once
Rb8, hitting the queen when taking the rook allows mate on c1
Neither, Black should trade queens and grovel
Both work, it is a matter of taste

ex.prompt: Black to move. Play the move that was most likely overlooked.
ex.why: The rook chases the queen around the corner while mate on c1 hangs over every capture. Black has a guaranteed perpetual against the queen whenever he wants it, and every attempt by White to keep the game leaves the first rank tactics alive. A pawn down, Black holds the draw with counterplay to spare.

lessons.title: Psychology test 26, level 1400 to 1800
text: The same game a few moves later, offered as one final trick. Black is a rook and a pawn down, and the position is completely hopeless.
Resignation, as the book notes, is an option that will always be available. Before using it, Black sets one last trap, and the trap costs absolutely nothing.
Silman's band note admits the title is a huge hint, and hopes his 1400 readers would spot the idea even though the move does not objectively work.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Give it one last shot.
ex.why: Every capture loses or draws for White. Taking with the queen meets Qg1 check and the queen offer on h2 with stalemate, taking with the king walks into Qf1 check skewering the f8 queen, and taking with the pawn allows Qg1 check when the greedy king walk to h3 gets mated on h1. Altounian calmly played Kf2 and won, which is the other lesson, look around before you snap anything off.

ex.prompt: What happens if White grabs the pawn with 2.Qxf3?
ex.why: The lone g6 pawn is frozen and the king on g5 has no squares once the white queen watches from f3, so removing Black's queen removes his last legal move. People fall into tricks like this far more often than you might imagine, which is exactly why you set them.
options: White wins a second pawn and the game
Qg1 check, then the queen sacrifices itself on h2 and taking it is stalemate
Black gives perpetual check on c1 and g1
Black trades queens into a drawn ending

lessons.title: Listing every target
text: White's position is a wreck and the exercise is to say exactly why, out loud, before playing anything. The white pieces are doing nothing. The king is still in the centre. The e pawn is backward on an open file and blocks its own light squared bishop. The c4 pawn is under the eye of a fine knight on e5. The pawns on a3 and c3 are both loose.

That list is the skill. Silman is blunt that the move Black plays here is obvious and is not the point. The point is training yourself to produce the inventory quickly, in every position, whether or not anything comes of it.

Once the list exists the move writes itself. Qa5 hits a3 and c3 at the same time and one of them has to fall. Target consciousness is not a tactic. It is the habit of always knowing what there is to attack.

ex.prompt: Click one of White's two loose pawns.
ex.why: Both are undefended by pawns and both sit on the same diagonal as squares the black queen can reach. Two loose units in one line is an invitation.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Attack both of them at once.
ex.why: One queen move, two targets, and White cannot hold both. The move is easy once the targets have been named, and invisible until then.

ex.prompt: What is the skill this position is teaching?
ex.why: The move here is obvious. What is not obvious is doing the inventory in positions where nothing jumps out, which is where the habit actually earns its keep.
options: Finding a queen fork
Producing a full inventory of targets before choosing a move
Attacking the uncastled king
Winning a pawn in the opening

lessons.title: Central king, and the drill
text: Most amateurs treat the enemy king as the target from move one, which is a mistake that blinds them to everything else in this book. Having spent a whole part arguing that, Silman then names the case where you genuinely must drop the positional niceties and go for the king. The most common one by far is the uncastled king sitting in the centre.

The drill has four steps. Notice that the king has stayed in the middle too long and get excited about it. Stop it from castling to safety. Bring as many pieces to that sector as you can. Then rip lines open and go for the throat.

It starts with recognition, not calculation. You train yourself to see red when the enemy king is still in the centre, label it a target, and then play with as much energy as the position allows. Here Black is fully developed and castled, White is neither, and everything follows from that.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Bring another piece to the fight and prepare the blow.
ex.why: The knight takes a strong post and sets up Nd3, which rips open the e file straight at the king. Castling was already too late, since O-O runs into Nf3 and mate follows.

ex.prompt: What is step two of the drill, after noticing the central king?
ex.why: A king that reaches safety takes your whole advantage with it. Deny the escape first, then bring pieces up, then open lines.
options: Trade queens
Stop it from castling to safety
Win a pawn
Double rooks on the open file

ex.prompt: When is a king in the centre not a death sentence?
ex.why: Closed centre, no roads in, and a longer stay is affordable. Look hard for a punishment anyway. If there is none, the opponent's judgement was sound and you carry on normally.
options: When it is only for a few moves
When the centre is closed and the enemy pieces cannot get in
When material is level
It always is a death sentence

lessons.title: Two central kings are not equal
text: Both kings are in the middle, so on a symmetrical reading neither side can claim anything. That reading is wrong, and seeing why is the whole lesson.

White's king is still tucked behind an intact set of pawns. Black's has been opened up by g5 and h6, which were played for reasons that had nothing to do with king safety. Same square, completely different degree of exposure.

So White is the one who gets to attack, and the h file is already half open with a rook behind it. Black's reply in the game was to grab on b2, an act of greed the position could not support. Taking material while your own king is the exposed one is the combination that decides most amateur games.

ex.prompt: Both kings are uncastled. Who is actually worse off?
ex.why: Count the pawn cover rather than the square the king stands on. White's shelter is intact and Black's is not, which is what makes one central king a target and the other merely slow.
options: White, the king is on an open file
Black, the pawn cover has already been given away
Neither, the position is symmetrical

ex.prompt: Open the file toward the weaker king.
ex.why: The h file opens with a rook already behind it. Black answered by taking on b2, which is more material than a position this loose can afford.

lessons.title: Targets test 1, level 1600 to 2199
text: Linderman against Ruggiero, from a clock simultaneous on the internet. White has an obvious lead in development against a king stuck in the centre, and the position screams for immediate dynamic play. Wait, and Black consolidates with Ne7 and castles into a good game.

In the game White played the quiet Nf1, a move the book says has nothing whatsoever to do with the position, and the game fizzled to a draw. The section is called target consciousness because the first job is recognition. If you do not see what you possess, you cannot use it.

Silman's band note grades by depth. Noticing the central king and lead in development and reaching for a fight scores at 1600. The tactics that follow are for experts, and nobody is required to calculate them to pass.

ex.prompt: What does this position demand of White?
ex.why: Both of White's advantages are temporary. Every developing shuffle lets Black play Ne7 and castle, so the moment demands moves that open lines toward the king that cannot yet run.
options: Quiet consolidation, the queenside pawns need care
An immediate fight with moves like b4, a4, or Nb3, before Black castles
A kingside pawn storm
Trading queens to exploit the structure

ex.prompt: White to move. Start the fight at the king's expense.
ex.why: All three fighting moves pass. After b4 the a5 knight is chased into tactics, the queenside opens, and White emerges with two rooks for a queen and a superior structure in the main line, while Nb3 aims at c5 and cracks e6. Only the do-nothing move fails the test.

lessons.title: Targets test 2, level 1400 to 1600
text: Rives against Staunton, Brussels 1853. White to move, and the book asks whether c3 to c4 is a good idea.
The push attacks the queen, and that is the whole of its resume. One tempo, paid for with a gaping permanent wound on d4 that a knight will sit in for the rest of the game.
Silman's band note fully expects 1400 players to understand that obvious one move attacks are to be avoided unless the threat has a deeper point beyond hoping the opponent misses it.

ex.prompt: Is c3-c4 a good idea?
ex.why: The queen steps aside and the wound remains forever. Staunton's knight duly landed on d4, the light squared bishop chopped f3, and the attack that flowed through the holes ended in a mating net. One move threats are questions, and this one had a losing answer.
options: Yes, it gains a tempo on the queen and space
No, it buys one tempo with a permanent hole on d4
Yes, but only with a3 and b4 to follow
It is equal either way

ex.prompt: What is the test to apply before any pawn move that attacks a piece?
ex.why: A tempo is only worth what the resulting position pays back. Pawns cannot retreat, so every square they abandon is a permanent gift, and d4 was the most expensive square on the board.
options: Whether the piece has a safe retreat
Whether the pawn move helps you after the piece simply steps aside
Whether it gains time on the clock
Whether it can be defended twice

lessons.title: Targets test 3, level 1400 to 1600
text: Silman against Nocon, National Open 1998. White is a pawn up in a rook endgame, which is often not enough. The book asks you to list Black's weaknesses.

The real advantage is the shattered black structure. The pawns on a7, f7, f6 and h6 are all targets, and the squares they no longer guard are highways. White's only care in the world is the little pawn on a3.
Silman's band note hopes his 1400 readers have embraced their inner greed by this point in the book and are already drooling in the direction of every black pawn.

ex.prompt: List Black's weaknesses.
ex.why: Every half of the board offers White something to hit, which is what lets one rook do the work of two. The plan is not one threat but a rotation of threats, each pawn taking its turn under the lamp.
options: Only the a7 pawn is genuinely weak
The pawns a7, f7, f6 and h6 are all targets, four islands of misery
The back rank is the only real problem
Black has no weaknesses, the extra pawn decides

ex.prompt: White to move. Put the rook where it tickles everything at once.
ex.why: From b4 the rook can swing to a4, f4 or h4 as the defence commits. Black chases the a3 pawn, the only target he owns, while White doubles, ties every black piece to a7 and f6, and finally weaves a mating net around the cornered king.

lessons.title: Targets test 4, level 1400 to 1800
text: Grischuk against Ivan Sokolov, Poikovsky 2004. White has just played a4. Black will not simply let the b pawn fall, so the book asks what the point of the move is, and whether it is any good or just a one move threat.

This is the sound version of the previous test's blunder. After the forced b4 the single pawn thrust has created three items, a loose pawn on b4, pressure against a6, and a hole on c4 that a white knight can call home.

Silman's band note adds the honest fine print. Black gets the c5 and c3 holes in exchange and White's b3 pawn turns delicate, so it takes the higher end of the rating band to see the ledger for both sides.

ex.prompt: What did a4 actually accomplish?
ex.why: The difference between this and the Staunton test is everything. There the attacked piece stepped aside and the attacker gained nothing. Here the forced reply commits a pawn forward, and every square it abandons becomes a White asset for the rest of the game.
options: Nothing, it is exactly the one move threat the previous test warned about
After b4 it leaves Black with a loose b4 pawn, a pressured a6 pawn, and a c4 hole for a knight
It wins the b5 pawn by force
It prepares to trade off White's bad bishop

ex.prompt: What does Black get in return after 16...b4?
ex.why: Real positions pay both sides. Sokolov offered the b4 pawn for kingside play, the game turned into a fight over mutual weaknesses, and Grischuk's extra assets won out only after further errors. Counting the opponent's share is part of counting.
options: Nothing, the position is simply worse
Holes on c5 and c3, plus a delicate white pawn on b3
A direct kingside attack
The bishop pair

lessons.title: Targets test 5, level 1400 to 1800
text: Baird against Weiss, New York 1889. White has just played the strange retreat to h8, trusting a fortress. The bishop babysits c3 from the long diagonal, the king shields the kingside pawns, and Black seems to have no way in.
Count the targets honestly and White is almost right. Only c3 and g2 are vulnerable, and both are covered. The question the book poses is whether Black can create a third.
Silman's band note says that by now his 1400 readers know the necessity of creating targets rather than wishing they would appear.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Manufacture a new weakness.
ex.why: Since c3 cannot be undermined, the pawn cracks b4 instead, and the recapture turns a5 into a second queenside invalid. Black regains the pawn with check, keeps both bishops, and the bishop's return to c7 begins the siege that costs White the a5 pawn and the game.

ex.prompt: Why does the defensive try Bb6, guarding a5, fail?
ex.why: After the trade and axb6, Bxe2 followed by Kf6 to f5, f4 and g3 eats g2 and h3 while White watches. Two weaknesses stretched the defence past breaking, which is the whole arithmetic of target creation.
options: It loses the bishop to a fork
Black trades on b6, wins the e2 knight with the other bishop, and the king march to the kingside pawns decides
It allows mate on the back rank
It does not fail, White holds the fortress

lessons.title: Targets test 6, level 1400 to 2000
text: A position with a story. Fischer, reviewing Yudovich's King's Indian book in 1969, dismissed it as 229 pages of nothing, then admitted he learned exactly one thing of value. This position is that thing.

Black to move, and the idea Fischer did not know rewrites the position. The fianchetto bishop, the piece amateurs are taught never to surrender, gives itself up for the c3 knight to destroy White's pawn formation.

Silman's band note expects some readers to blanch at the solution, and trusts that everyone else has learned to love moves that hand you long term weaknesses to attack. White's attacking chances without the dark squared counterpart, Fischer notes, are not real.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Play the move Fischer learned from a book he hated.
ex.why: The capture saddles White with crippled doubled c pawns, and the rook slides to a4 where it fixes both c4 and a2 in its sights. Two years later Velimirovic played exactly this and stood much better, rook camped on the fourth, knights circling the wreckage.

ex.prompt: What makes giving up the fianchetto bishop correct here?
ex.why: The rule about keeping the fianchetto bishop assumes an attack that can exploit its absence. With the light squared bishops traded and no pieces aimed at the king, the exchange is simply structure for nothing, the purest form of target creation.
options: It wins a pawn immediately
The doubled c pawns are permanent targets and White has no real attack to use the dark squares
It forces a favourable queen trade
It is a known theoretical draw

lessons.title: Targets test 7, level 1800 to 2000
text: Short against Ni Hua, Beijing rapid 2003. White's g4 was a bold, greedy bid to annex the e4 square, so the obliging captures toward e4 would give him exactly what he wants.

Black refuses to donate the square, and instead annexes one of his own. Weak squares do not magically appear. A player has to create them, and a pawn is a small price for winning the strategic battle.

Silman's band note starts the level at 1800 because g4 could easily strike fear into many players, and because the solution looks wrong at first sight, opening the f file straight at Black's own queen.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Answer a square grab with a square grab.
ex.why: The pawn gives itself to buy e5 for the knight forever. After f4 the extra white pawn on e4 is a traitor that entombs the d3 bishop and evicts the c3 knight from its dream square, while the f4 pawn joins the attack. The knight reached e5, the f pawn reached f2, and Short resigned within twenty moves.

ex.prompt: Why not the natural 19...fxg4 or 19...f4 at once?
ex.why: Strategy is a negotiation over squares. Capturing on g4 or closing with f4 signs White's proposal, while e4 tears it up and writes Black's own. Ask what the opponent's last move wants before you give it.
options: Both lose material to tactics on the f file
Both hand White the e4 square, which is precisely what g4 was played to win
Because the queen hangs on f6
They are equally good, just less flashy

lessons.title: Targets test 8, level 1400 to 1600
text: Donaldson against Lucas, David Collyer Memorial 2001. Black has just blocked the check on e7 rather than accept the ugly but tenable Kf8, and now his king is one castling move from safety.
The target is the king in the middle, and the task is to keep it there. There is a standard device for exactly this job.
Silman's band note congratulates anyone who noticed the central king and went out of the way to detain it, and hopes the example becomes a catalyst for the rest.

ex.prompt: White to move. Keep the king in the centre.
ex.why: The queen adds a third attacker to e7, so castling stays illegal and every developing move Black wants remains on hold. It is a common device worth owning forever. In the game the routine Rc8 ran into Ne5 and the c6 bishop fell, leaving White a clean pawn up.

ex.prompt: What was Black's best chance back in the diagram?
ex.why: When castling is held hostage, walk the king out by hand. The game move prepared to castle two moves too late, and the e5 knight plus the pin turned the queenside into a shooting gallery before the king ever reached g8.
options: 14...Rc8, preparing Rc7 and castling
14...f6, keeping the knight out of e5 and planning Qd7 and Kf7 by hand
14...Bb5, trading the bad bishop
14...h6, making luft first

lessons.title: Targets test 9, level 1400 to 2000
text: Silman against Speelman, Aaronson Masters 1978. White has a lead in development against a king still in the centre, and by now you know what that screams for.
Both advantages are temporary. The king will eventually castle and the development will eventually equalize, so the moment is use it or lose it, and recognition must come before calculation.
Silman's band note asks only for two things, seeing the central king, and reaching for the move that starts a war before the king escapes. Nothing deeper was required to pass.

ex.prompt: White to move. Use it or lose it.
ex.why: The pawn rips at e6 and g6 before Black completes his setup. Silman confesses he then hurried and missed the strongest follow ups more than once, but the pawn lever itself was the exam, and the initiative it bought eventually carried the game against a future top ten player.

ex.prompt: What is the correct order of operations when you spot a king in the centre?
ex.why: Silman's phrase is a primal desire to kill, tempered afterward by calm analysis. The order matters, because a player who calculates without the desire finds reasons to wait, and waiting is precisely the move that loses a temporary advantage.
options: Calculate every line first, then decide whether to attack
Recognition, then the desire to punish, then a cool look at what is really going on
Develop every piece before considering action
Trade queens to reach a safe endgame

lessons.title: Neither style is enough on its own
text: Players like to describe themselves as attacking or positional, and it is a pleasant thing to believe and a poor thing to rely on. A positional player with no feel for dynamics gets flattened. A tactician who cannot tell a static plus from a hole in the wall gets ground down. You need both, because the opponent gets a vote.

This position is the argument in miniature, and it is a normal line of the Nimzo-Indian. White has two active bishops and a lead in development, which are dynamic assets and will not keep. Black has the better pawn structure, because White's c pawns are doubled and weak, and structure is static and keeps forever.

So each side knows what to do. White has to make something happen while the bishops still have open lines. Black has to trade one of them off or blunt them, and then the doubled pawns decide the game. Same position, two completely different clocks.

ex.prompt: Click one of the pawns that gives Black a long-term advantage.
ex.why: The doubled c pawns are the static feature. They will still be doubled in fifty moves, which is exactly why Black is in no hurry.

ex.prompt: Which side holds the dynamic assets?
ex.why: Two active bishops and faster development are things that fade. Whoever holds the dynamic side is the one working against a clock.
options: White, with the bishop pair and a lead in development
Black, with the better structure
Neither, the position is balanced

ex.prompt: What does Black need to do to make the structure tell?
ex.why: The same anti-pair formula from the minor-piece parts, used here as a way of converting a static advantage. Remove the dynamism and only the pawn structure is left.
options: Attack the king
Trade one bishop off or restrain the pair
Open the position
Win a pawn

lessons.title: Choosing which side to be
text: An ordinary isolated d pawn position, and the roles look settled. Black gets the long-term static plus, meaning play against the isolated pawn and the fine square in front of it. White gets dynamic compensation, meaning active pieces and chances against the king. Everyone knows the script.
The natural move is c6, supporting d5 and preparing Nbd5, and it is a perfectly good move that plays the script as written. Most players would choose it and be right to.

Morozevich decides he does not have to accept the static role at all. Be6 invites the capture that wrecks his own pawn structure, and buys iron control of d5 and the newly opened f file with it. The personalities swap. White now has a static target on e6 to nag at, and Black has the active pieces. Both readings of the position were available, and which one you take is a choice.

ex.prompt: In the standard reading of this structure, who holds the static plus?
ex.why: Isolated pawn positions almost always divide this way. The owner of the pawn plays fast and the other side plays slow.
options: White, with active pieces
Black, with play against the isolated pawn and the d5 square
Neither, it is symmetrical

ex.prompt: Black to move. Refuse the script and take the dynamic side instead.
ex.why: It damages Black's own structure on purpose, in exchange for permanent control of d5 and an open f file. Silman calls it a non-dogmatic move, which is a good name for the whole idea.

ex.prompt: What did that move actually change?
ex.why: A moment earlier White was the active side. Now White has a static weakness to work against and Black has the initiative. Roles in a position are not always fixed.
options: It won a pawn
It swapped which side is static and which is dynamic
It prevented an attack
It forced a queen trade

lessons.title: Turning one kind of advantage into another
text: Black holds both kinds of advantage here, which is worth pausing on. The big pawn centre is static and will still be there in the endgame. The pressure the rooks will generate down the open b and c files against White's queenside is dynamic and will not be.

What happened in the game is the most useful idea in this chapter. White used his own dynamic chances not to deliver a knockout but to change the nature of the position, and ended up with an extra pawn, which is static, while Black was left with two bishops and a rook on the seventh, which is dynamic. The two sides had traded roles entirely.

That transformation, static into dynamic or dynamic into static, is extremely common and worth watching for. A dynamic advantage that is about to expire has to be converted into something permanent. Cashing it in for a pawn, a structural weakness, or a permanent square is usually how.

ex.prompt: Click the pawn at the head of Black's static advantage.
ex.why: The centre pawns are the part of Black's position that keeps. Everything else Black has here depends on activity that may not last.

ex.prompt: A dynamic advantage is about to run out. What should you do with it?
ex.why: Either it produces a knockout or it buys a static asset. An unconverted dynamic advantage simply disappears, and you are left having spent the moves for nothing.
options: Hold on and defend
Convert it into something permanent, such as a pawn or a weakness
Trade queens
Repeat moves

ex.prompt: How does the position in the game end up?
ex.why: White finishes a pawn up with the long-term plus, and Black holds two bishops and a rook on the seventh as compensation. Reading a position once is not enough, because the roles move.
options: Black keeps both kinds of advantage
The two sides swap roles, White static and Black dynamic
All the imbalances disappear

lessons.title: Statics against dynamics test 1, level 1900 to 2200
text: Rubinstein against Colle, Liege 1930, and the book simply says assess this position. Out of a Nimzo Indian, Black has built the thematic two piece battery against c4, bishop on a6 and knight on a5, the setup every Nimzo player is taught to aim for.

The setup has hit its ceiling. No third attacker can ever join, since the ideal queen trek to a4 or c6 is slow, can be stopped by a4, and invites Bg5 miseries along the way. Meanwhile White owns a monstrous pawn centre and his pieces are already poised for a kingside attack. The centre and the kingside belong to White, so Black must break through on the other wing or, ultimately, perish, and there is no healthy way to do it.

Silman's band note reserves this one for 1900 and up, because it takes a sophisticated player to recognise when a well known setup is not working, and when one side's famous plan is simply overshadowed by the opponent's. Rubinstein never analysed any of it. He knew from experience that this structure without proper counterplay favours White.

ex.prompt: Click the pawn Black's whole setup is besieging.
ex.why: Bishop and knight both hit c4, and the whole opening was played to put them there. The question the test asks is whether the siege amounts to anything.

ex.prompt: Assess this position.
ex.why: Every attempt to add an attacker or induce d5 costs more time than Black has, and the book's sample lines all end with the kingside washed away. A famous setup is only worth what it does in the position in front of you.
options: Black is better, the c4 pawn will fall
White is better, the siege of c4 has hit its ceiling while the centre and a kingside attack belong to White
Equal, one wing each
Black is slightly better once the queen reaches a4

ex.prompt: In the game Black lashed out with c5. What is the verdict?
ex.why: With the pawn still on c7, a later d5 could at least be met by c6, opening the file for the rooks. After c5 and d5 that lever is gone, a4 stops the queen trek, and Black had nothing left to do while White improved at leisure and broke through on the kingside.
options: Correct, it gains space and fixes c4 forever
It ends all counterplay, since after d5 the c file can never open and the c5 square is dead
A blunder because d6 hangs
Fine, but only after h6 first

lessons.title: Statics against dynamics test 2, level 1400 to 2200
text: Spiller against Silman, West Valley Open 1987, the same structure as the previous test seen from the other side of the board. This time White has played the opening without enough panache, the battery against c4 arrived in full force, and the pawn is about to fall.

Castling and shrugging the pawn off gives no compensation, and Qa4 is refuted by d5, when c4 falls anyway and the queen move turns out to be a wasted tempo. That leaves one honest try. The advance c5 sells the doomed pawn for dynamism before it is simply lost, even though the doubled isolated c pawns it invites would spook most club players.

Silman's band note expects a solid 1400 player to notice that c4 hangs and to realise White does not really have a choice, it is c5 or bust. He rates Black's side of the game considerably higher, because declining to double the white pawns and then recapturing away from the centre both break rules that most players obey blindly.

ex.prompt: Assess the position.
ex.why: The two piece battery has won the fight for c4, and this time there is no kingside attack to outweigh it. When the static battle is lost, the imbalances demand that you hunt for dynamic compensation while it still exists.
options: White is fine, castling keeps everything defended
White is strategically worse, c4 cannot be held, and his one chance is to sell it for dynamics
White is better thanks to the centre pawns
Equal, the a6 bishop bites on granite

ex.prompt: White to move. The pawn cannot be saved for free. Make it count.
ex.why: Not ideal, but best. Black swaps off the dangerous d3 bishop, pries at the chain with d6, and recaptures on b6 toward the edge on purpose, intending to own the c4 square and press on c3 down the newly opened file.

ex.prompt: Black has just recaptured on b6. Teachers everywhere would now say castle. Here that loses the strategic battle. Play the right move.
ex.why: The pawn refuses to be fixed on c3 as a target and becomes a dynamic force instead, in the best static against dynamic tradition, with rough equality to follow. The game instead saw the natural, lazy castling move from a very experienced master, and that single tempo decided the fight over c4. Black dominated the light squares, snuffed out all counterplay, and won.

lessons.title: Statics against dynamics test 3, level 2100 and up
text: Ponomariov against Papaioannou, Plovdiv 2003, the hardest test of the set. Black's doubled f pawns hand White the static ledger, but the same ruined structure opened the g file and put e5 and g5 permanently off limits to white pieces. A structure like this is made for dynamics, and dynamics run on a clock. White has just played h4 and intends h5.

Black wants the c5 break, and the way to get it is h5, played with the express purpose of giving the pawn up. The pawn covers g4, so the knight route through e3 to g4 dies, and when the knight goes the long way round to collect on h5 it ends up stranded on the rim with the queen for a babysitter while c5 arrives and every black piece goes to work. The timid h6 fails the position, since after h5 and Ne3 the bishop is buried on h7, h6 is a target, and c5 becomes nearly impossible to arrange.

Silman's band note puts this at 2100 and up, because noticing h5 is one thing and playing it as a deliberate pawn sacrifice is another. The one lesson he wants every reader to take away is that you cannot play a position properly until you know whether your chances lie with statics or dynamics, and once you know, you insist on the moves that promote your side of the argument.

ex.prompt: Black to move. The position is made for dynamics, so raise the tempo of the game.
ex.why: White would love to slow the game down, reroute the knight through e3 to g4, and quietly bank his better structure. The pawn thrust takes g4 away forever and makes the c5 break real. The price is the pawn itself, because Nf4 simply wins it, and how to answer that is the second half of the test.

ex.prompt: White has found the best reply, hitting the bishop and the loose h pawn at once. Keep every piece on its best square.
ex.why: The bishop keeps its diagonal and the pawn is abandoned with a clear conscience. After the knight collects on h5, c5 lands, and this is exactly the position Black played for, a pawn down with a sidelined white knight and total piece activity. The game stayed razor sharp, Black went astray much later, and the extra h pawn eventually decided, none of which changes the verdict on the idea.

ex.prompt: What is the one lesson Silman insists every reader absorb here?
ex.why: The side with the static edge tries to impose the slow game, the side with the dynamics does everything to keep the fire burning, and the first player to cave to the other's agenda usually loses. Both grandmasters here understood their roles perfectly, which is what made the game so hard.
options: Doubled pawns are always a losing weakness
Know whether your chances lie with statics or dynamics, then insist on moves that promote your side
Never sacrifice pawns without a forced win
Opposite side castling always means mutual attacks

lessons.title: Statics against dynamics test 4, level 1800 to 2200
text: Van der Wiel against Yusupov, Reykjavik 1985. White has an obvious advantage in central and kingside space, can open the a file whenever he pleases, and kingside pawn breaks hang in the air, static pluses that could turn dynamic at the drop of a hat. A long passive defence beckons, and Yusupov does not relish it.

The move is the capture on a5, which most players reject on sight because it saddles Black with doubled isolated a pawns. That is the price. The purchase is the open b file, which turns the dead rook on b8 into the most active piece on the board, hitting c3 a move later and filling the position with tricks. The analysis is littered with mating nets for both sides, a testament to what active pieces can do.

Silman's band note admits the capture goes against most players' training, but hopes that class A players would be attracted to the rook's newfound activity and would find the courage to cast their structural fears aside. In the game the activity held the balance comfortably until Black, not White, blundered in the complications and lost, which changes nothing about the idea.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Refuse the passive defence.
ex.why: Statics are sold for dynamics at the cost of Black's own structure. The rook lands on b3, c3 is attacked at once, and White already has to step carefully, since the natural push of the e pawn leads to lines where the rook and the two bishops weave mating nets around the white king.

ex.prompt: What exactly did Black pay, and what did he buy?
ex.why: White's static score actually improves, better structure and more space, but the dynamic swing is bigger. Silman's point is that this bargain appears far more often than it is taken, because the training that says never wreck your own pawns speaks louder than the position.
options: Nothing, the capture simply wins a pawn
He accepted doubled isolated a pawns and bought an open b file for a rook that was doing nothing
He gave up the bishop pair for structure
He bought a passed a pawn

ex.prompt: A sideline. Rooks were swapped on a3 and White grabbed the a7 pawn with his bishop. Punish the greed.
ex.why: The quiet bishop move attacks the c2 rook, and there is no good square, since the two bishops cover c1, b2, a2 and d1 between them, and the wriggle to d2 meets Bc1 with the chase continuing until material drops. The book's verdict is short, the rook is trapped.

lessons.title: Statics against dynamics test 5, level 1400 to 1600
text: Costa against Bagirov, Debrecen 1992, from a Semi Slav where Black grabbed on c4 and chased the knight with his b pawn. White has genuine pressure against the backward pawn on c6, a static advantage that will not evaporate. His problem is the king stuck in the middle, a dynamic disadvantage, and the a6 bishop rakes the very diagonal the king needs cleared for castling.

White's plan is Bd2, Rc1 and Bc4, adding to the pressure on c6 while trading off the nuisance bishop. Since White enjoys the static plus, Black should answer in as dynamic a fashion as possible, and the move is c5, turning the potentially weak pawn into a battering ram. The point runs deep, because White can even win a pawn with a little combination on e6, and Black simply castles into tremendous compensation against the king that never found shelter.

Silman's band note fully expects 1400 players schooled in the imbalances to spot the static against dynamic split, since the a6 bishop would make anyone uncomfortable and wariness of weak pawns should be autopilot this far into the course. The actual play turns out to be very advanced, and all he asks for is the basic understanding.

ex.prompt: Click the pawn that carries White's long term hopes.
ex.why: Backward on a file White half owns, it is the one target that will still be a target in thirty moves. Every white plan starts from pressuring it.

ex.prompt: Assess the position.
ex.why: Statics tend to last and dynamics tend to expire, so the side facing the king in the middle sets the pace. Given time for Rc1, Bc4 and castling, White's position would play itself, which is exactly why Black cannot grant the time.
options: White is clearly better, c6 falls within a few moves
A clean static against dynamic bargain, White owns the weak c6 pawn and Black owns the stranded white king, and the race is on
Black is worse, the b4 pawn is overextended
Equal and quiet, both sides will castle and regroup

ex.prompt: White has started the plan with Bd2. Answer in as dynamic a fashion as possible.
ex.why: The weak pawn refuses to be weak and the position bursts open with the white king still in the centre. Taking on e6 wins a pawn, since recapturing runs into a queen check on a4 that picks up the a6 bishop, but after castling Black's activity was worth far more than the pawn. Bagirov's initiative carried the game all the way to mate.

lessons.title: Statics against dynamics test 6, level 1400 to 2200
text: Ganguly against Short, Mumbai 2006, a standard Exchange Lopez position, and Short's own published verdict is a model of honest assessment. The statics favour White, because the doubled c pawns are a losing disadvantage if a pure king and pawn endgame is ever reached. The dynamics favour Black, because the e4 pawn is genuinely vulnerable and can only be defended at some inconvenience. Adding it up gives approximate equality.

The endgame claim is the engine of the whole evaluation and is worth owning. In the model king and pawn ending White plays a3 at the right moment, the crippled queenside majority freezes, and Black is effectively a solid pawn down, after which a kingside passer decides. There is one trick to respect, because if Black ever gets the a3 push in first, capturing with the b pawn is answered by b3 and a black pawn promotes. Alertness, not material, is the whole story there, and the frozen majority is why White dreams of trading every piece while Black must never allow it.

Silman's band note says the position mixes ideas any 1400 can grasp, pressure against a pawn and a love of active pieces, with nuances in the actual game that are considerably more advanced. Short soon fixed the white knight out of its best squares with c5, later unbalanced the game on purpose with an ugly and anti positional pawn push, and won when White cracked under the piece activity.

ex.prompt: Assess the position.
ex.why: Short's formula deserves memorising. Name who owns the statics, name who owns the dynamics, and only then produce a verdict. Neither player is worse here, they are playing different games on the same board, and the result depends on whose game gets imposed.
options: White is better, the doubled c pawns are dead weight
Approximate equality, the statics belong to White and the dynamics to Black
Black is better, e4 is already lost
White is winning as soon as the queens come off

ex.prompt: Why does White dream of exchanging every single piece?
ex.why: Four healthy kingside pawns against the doubled ruin means White creates a passer at will and Black cannot answer in kind. The one alarm to keep switched on is Black's own a3 break, when taking with the pawn loses to the b3 trick and a promotion, so the freeze has to come first.
options: Endgames are always safer for the better structure
The pure king and pawn ending is winning, since a3 freezes the crippled majority and Black is effectively a pawn down
Because knights beat bishops in closed endings
To relieve the pressure against e4

ex.prompt: Short soon played c5, giving one doubled pawn a job. Click the white piece the move takes the squares from.
ex.why: With c5 covering d4 and the f6 pawn already covering e5 and g5, the knight's dream tour through d4 to f5 is cancelled, and h4 is watched by the g6 knight as well. A doubled pawn is not weak while it controls the squares the opponent needs.

lessons.title: Why space is worth having
text: Amateurs respect material, attacks, and weak pawns, because all three are things you can point at. Space feels like an abstraction, and it is one of the most prized imbalances in modern grandmaster chess.

Silman explains it with a hotel room. A large person in an ordinary room is comfortable for a day. Put the same person in an aeroplane toilet and they fall apart, not because anything is attacking them but because there is nowhere to go.

That is what a space advantage does to an opponent. The pieces have no scope, they get in each other's way, and you improve your position at leisure while they sit and hope. Karpov takes his first spatial gain here with d5, and the move does two jobs, claiming the centre and shutting the b7 bishop out of the game.

ex.prompt: White to move. Take the first bite of territory.
ex.why: The pawn claims central space and closes the long diagonal on the b7 bishop at the same time. Karpov built the whole game from a series of gains like this one.

ex.prompt: What does a space advantage actually do to the opponent?
ex.why: Nothing is attacked and nothing is won. The opponent simply runs out of useful moves, which is why players like Petrosian and Karpov collected space the way others collect pawns.
options: It wins material slowly
It leaves their pieces with no scope and in each other's way
It creates passed pawns
It exposes their king

ex.prompt: Besides claiming the centre, what does this pawn move achieve?
ex.why: A space-gaining move that also entombs an enemy piece is doing two jobs. Look for the pawn advance that gains ground and blunts something at the same time.
options: It attacks a piece
It shuts the b7 bishop out of the game
It prepares to castle
It creates a passed pawn

lessons.title: Space means avoiding exchanges
text: White has much more central space, and the cramped side has one reliable cure. Trade pieces. Fewer pieces means the ones that remain have room, and the shortage stops mattering. That is the Volkswagen principle: twenty-seven people in the car is intolerable and four is fine.

It follows that the side with space should avoid unnecessary exchanges, and this position puts the rule to an immediate test. The white light squared bishop is attacked and must move, so the only question is where.

Bc4 looks natural and is the mistake. It gives Black time for Nb6 and then Bg4, trading the bishop that is currently in the way of his own pieces, and the cramp is cured. Bf1 looks passive and is correct, because Black keeps the piece he most wants to give away and keeps suffering.

ex.prompt: The bishop is attacked and must move. Play the move that keeps Black cramped.
ex.why: Retreating all the way home refuses the trade. Black stays short of room, and White has given up nothing that matters.

ex.prompt: Why is the natural Bc4 wrong?
ex.why: Nb6 and Bg4 follows, the bad bishop comes off, and Black's remaining pieces suddenly have room. The trade cures exactly what the space advantage was inflicting.
options: It loses a pawn
It gives Black time to free and trade his light squared bishop
It blocks the c file
It walks into a knight fork

ex.prompt: State the rule for the side with more space.
ex.why: Every trade helps the cramped side. This is the mirror of the rule from the space lesson in Part One, seen from the other chair.
options: Trade pieces to simplify
Avoid unnecessary exchanges
Advance on the wing
Keep the position closed

lessons.title: Cracking the wall with a pawn break
text: Being short of space is not a sentence, and Silman lists four ways out. Exchange pieces so the room you have is enough. Use pawn breaks to crack the wall. Prove that the space-gaining advance left weak squares behind it. Or treat the enemy pawn centre as a target in its own right.
The previous lesson covered the first. This is the second, and it is the most direct. White has just clamped the queenside with c5, and left alone that pawn will strangle Black by itself.

So Black hits it at once with b6. Note what does not work: White cannot support the clamp with b4, because a5 breaks it up. The wall looks solid and depends on one pawn, and finding which pawn is holding an advance together is how you know where to strike.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Attack the pawn that is doing the clamping.
ex.why: The break comes immediately, before White can consolidate. Supporting the clamp with b4 does not work for White, since a5 undermines it.

ex.prompt: Which of the four antidotes to a space disadvantage is this?
ex.why: Pawn advances that gain space also fix pawns in place, and fixed pawns can be attacked by other pawns. The break is usually available if you look for it early enough.
options: Exchange pieces
Use a pawn break to crack the wall
Target the weak squares left behind
Attack the centre with pieces

ex.prompt: How do you find where to break?
ex.why: A space-gaining chain usually rests on one pawn. Remove that and the whole structure loses its grip, which is why White here would love to prop c5 up with b4 and cannot.
options: Break wherever you have most pieces
Find the pawn holding the advance together and hit that
Always break in the centre
Break on the side where the king is

lessons.title: Treating the centre as a target
text: Reti against Lasker, and the fourth antidote. White has given Black a big pawn centre on purpose and has not tried to claim any space of his own. Both bishops are on long diagonals pointing straight at it, and the rook has just come to the open file.

The idea is that a large pawn centre is not only territory, it is also a set of targets that cannot easily move. Pieces can attack it from a distance while the pawns that make it up stay exactly where they are.

This is the hypermodern argument in one position, and it belongs here because it completes the list. Faced with an opponent who has more space, you can trade pieces, break with a pawn, occupy the squares the advance left behind, or simply refuse to compete for territory and shoot at the centre from long range.

ex.prompt: Click one of the centre pawns White intends to attack rather than imitate.
ex.why: Both are the space advantage and both are the targets. That double nature is what makes a big centre a commitment rather than a free asset.

ex.prompt: What is White's strategy here?
ex.why: Two fianchettoed bishops and a rook on the open file, all bearing on a centre that cannot run. Territory conceded deliberately in exchange for targets.
options: Claim equal space in the centre
Refuse the territory and attack the centre with pieces from a distance
Attack on the kingside
Trade into an endgame

ex.prompt: Name all four ways to handle a space disadvantage.
ex.why: Silman's list, and it is worth memorising because a cramped position feels like it has no plan. It has four, and usually more than one of them is available.
options: Attack, defend, trade, wait
Trade pieces, break with a pawn, use the weak squares left behind, attack the centre
Castle, develop, break, counterattack
Close the position, blockade, sacrifice, promote

lessons.title: Space test 1, level 1600 to 2200
text: Porper against Mikhalevski, Canadian Open 2009, and the widest question in the book. In prose, what is this position all about, and what kinds of moves and themes would be most logical? White has built a large Grunfeld centre and is one tempo away from expanding it further with f4.

The position is about that centre and nothing else. Black cannot afford to play quietly, because f4 and e5 would turn the territory into a steamroller, so the logical moves are the breaks that chip at it, e6 hitting d5 and b5 hitting c4, in some lines mixed together. The immediate capture on d3 is an unnecessary hurry that only narrows Black's options, though it is forgivable if the b5 and e6 follow up is intended.

Silman's band note admits the supporting analysis is so complicated that even strong masters would struggle through it over the board. The point of the problem was never the analysis, it was whether you understood what the position demands, and you pass if you named the centre destroying pawn breaks.

ex.prompt: In prose, what is this position all about?
ex.why: Every theme in the position runs through the centre. If it stands, White wins the game on territory alone, and if it is dismantled Black's pieces and queenside pawns come alive.
options: Black's queenside majority against White's kingside chances
White's huge centre against Black's duty to tear at it with the e6 and b5 breaks before f4 arrives
The two bishops against the knight
A closed position where both sides manoeuvre slowly

ex.prompt: Black to move. Start the demolition.
ex.why: Both breaks pass the test, and the book's main line mixes them, e6 first and b5 two moves later, in full pawn break mode. The analysis stays fine for Black everywhere it matters, which is all the assessment a position this sharp will give you.

ex.prompt: The game saw Rab8 instead, preparing b5 the slow way. What is the verdict?
ex.why: After f4 the e5 knight was pushed to the side, e5 and f5 came with tempo, and White's centre trumped Black's queenside majority in the endgame that followed. Against a mobile centre the break has to come at once, preparation is a luxury the position never grants.
options: Sensible preparation, breaks need support
Too slow, White got f4 in, the centre rolled forward and squashed the queenside play
Wrong rook, the d8 rook belonged on b8
Fine, it transposes to the b5 break anyway

lessons.title: Space test 2, level 1400 to 2000
text: Ivkov against Carvalho, Sao Paulo 1973, a King's Indian where the usual bargain has gone wrong for Black. The book asks you to assess the position and then find White's best move.

Black's position looks solid and is actually in terrible trouble. The King's Indian trade is queenside space for a kingside pawn storm, and Black has already spent his storm, the f file was opened and exchanged away and no attack remains. Without kingside counterplay, White's queenside space play has no counterweight, and the thematic c5 advance, pressing d6 and preparing Nc4 behind it, starts an attack that nothing slows down.

Silman's band note expects a 1400 who read the space material to crave c5 on sight. Seeing how grim things really are takes a stronger player, because visually Black's game does not look bad at all, which is exactly what makes the position instructive.

ex.prompt: Assess the position.
ex.why: A space advantage is decisive precisely when the opponent has no play of his own, and Black traded his play away on the f file. Every white gain on the queenside now comes free of charge.
options: Roughly equal, Black is solid everywhere
Black is in terrible trouble, he has no kingside counterplay and the queenside attack will roll him off the board
White is a little better but Black holds comfortably
Black is better, the e4 pawn is a long term weakness

ex.prompt: White to move. Expand where the winning is.
ex.why: The pawn presses d6, Nc4 doubles the pressure, and b5 followed by c6 wedges the queenside open. Ivkov even missed a faster kill along the way and it changed nothing, because Black never got a single active move all game.

lessons.title: Space test 3, level 1800 to 2100
text: Shirov against Leko, Ljubljana 1995, a Breyer Lopez where White has been annexing territory for ten moves, first the centre with d4, then the queenside with a4, b4 and a5, and just now c4. The book asks which is better, Bg7, exd4, or Nh5.

The threat behind the last move is to take on e5 and follow with c5, a spatial clamp across the whole board. Suffocation is only tolerable when the advancing pawns leave weak squares to occupy, or you have play in another sector, or the pawns themselves become targets, and quiet play here collects none of the three. So Bg7 simply submits, and Nh5, though more aggressive, still lets White consolidate. Taking on d4 first and then playing Nh5 keeps the position fluid, with the c5 and d5 breaks in hand and pieces poised to jump to life.

Silman's band note grades this one high because White's quiet intention is easy to miss, while hoping his lower rated readers notice the coming envelopment and prove the spread wrong. In the game Black played the bishop move, White clamped with c5, and the squeeze ran unopposed to resignation.

ex.prompt: What is better, Bg7, exd4, or Nh5?
ex.why: The capture is the only move of the three that fights the clamp before it exists. After exd4 and Nh5 Black gets his full share of the play, while both alternatives let White take on e5 and play c5 with a strangling bind.
options: Bg7, finishing development before committing to anything
exd4, keeping the position fluid, with Nh5 to follow and the c5 and d5 breaks in hand
Nh5, heading for the f4 hole at once

ex.prompt: When is it acceptable to sit in a spatially inferior position?
ex.why: Silman's three part list, and the whole test in one sentence. After the passive bishop move Black had none of the three, which is why a single quiet developing move was enough to lose the strategic battle on the spot.
options: Never, space must always be contested immediately
When the advanced pawns leave weak squares to use, or you have play elsewhere, or the pawns are attackable targets
When you hold the bishop pair as compensation
When the queens have been exchanged

lessons.title: Space test 4, level 1400 to 1800
text: Buslaev against Petrosian, Leningrad 1946, a closed Lopez. The book asks you to point out the imbalances and then find Black's most logical move.

White has central space and two normal plans, a kingside attack with Bh6 and Ng4, or pressure against the loose pawns on a6 and c4. Black has queenside space and the b file. The real story is the price White paid for d5, because the advance released its grip on c5, and a knight arriving there radiates onto two more weak squares in the white camp, b3 and d3. Once you see the c5, b3, d3 triangle, the move picks itself.

Silman's band note says that if you noticed the holes and found the knight manoeuvre you should take a bow, and he trusts his 1400 readers to manage it with ease. His image is worth keeping, on f6 the knight is a rather unimposing critter, on c5 it is a mighty octopus with tentacles reaching in all directions.

ex.prompt: Click the hole that connects everything for Black.
ex.why: The d5 advance bought space and paid with this square. A black knight there hits the a4 rook, eyes b3 and d3, and turns the whole queenside into a minefield for White.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Begin the short journey.
ex.why: The f6 knight was doing nothing, and two moves later it is an octopus on c5 preparing the leap to d3. In the game White answered with f4, blind to the invasion and opening his own diagonal, and both knights poured into b3 and d3 while Petrosian collected the full point.

ex.prompt: What was White's only decent defence against the incoming octopus?
ex.why: A knight this strong cannot be evicted, so it has to be exchanged before it settles, even at the cost of the dark squared bishop, after which White could still play against a6 and c4. The game's f4 instead handed Black the g1 to a7 diagonal on top of everything else.
options: f4, gaining kingside space first
Trade it off the moment it lands, Be3 and Bxc5
Race for mate with Bh6 and Ng4
Grab the a6 pawn while there is time

lessons.title: Space test 5, level 1400 to 1800
text: Jacobsen against Yates, London Olympiad 1927. White has just grabbed space with c5, and the book asks which three moves should stand out above all others here, and which of them is best.

The advance ignored the two questions every space grab must answer, whether the pawn can be maintained and whether the position behind it is ready, and White's king is still in the centre. The three candidates are Ne4, to be cemented by f5, b6, tearing the space gaining pawn down, and e5, nuking the pawn chain and opening the centre while the king sits in it. Yates chose e5, the most punishing, though all three are fully playable.
Silman's band note is blunt, these ideas were clearly discussed and an alert 1400 should know them, and any reader who does not should reread the space section until the lessons fully sink in.

ex.prompt: Which three moves should stand out above all others?
ex.why: Each one confronts the overextension differently, the knight anchors on the square the pawn abandoned, b6 attacks the advanced pawn's existence, and e5 rips open the centre where the white king still lives.
options: Ne4, b6 and e5
b6, a5 and Qa5
Ne4, h6 and Re8
e5, Qe7 and Rd8

ex.prompt: Play the most punishing of the three.
ex.why: It rends the pawn chain limb from limb and starts a fight while the king is stuck in the middle, which is exactly the fight White cannot afford. The book's line wins the pawn back with a lead in development and a lasting initiative, and the quieter b6 and Ne4 were fully playable runners up.

lessons.title: Space test 6, level 1800 to 2200
text: Ehlvest against Nakamura, Philadelphia 2001. Black has held the initiative the whole game, pried open the h file, and just planted a knight on d3, the classic square behind the space gaining pawns. It looks for all the world as if Black has won the argument.

White's central space advantage still exists, and the black king is a little drafty, so this is the moment to cash the static centre for dynamics. The advance e5 blocks the h8 bishop out of the game, frees e4 for the knights and the bishop, one pawn move activating three minor pieces, and prepares e6 and f5 to crack the king open.

Silman's band note calls it a tough one, because Black really did achieve something by landing the knight on d3, and anyone who still saw that the centre could strike at the enemy king should consider himself a very good player. The change of momentum proved psychologically unbearable, and Black was gobbled up within ten moves.

ex.prompt: White to move. The knight on d3 looks terrifying. Change the subject.
ex.why: Statics are spent the moment they buy something bigger, and here the fine centre buys a direct attack. In the game the en passant capture and f5 tore the cover off, the octopus never got a say, and White mated within a dozen moves.

ex.prompt: What did the single pawn move accomplish?
ex.why: Silman lists exactly these three dividends. A space advantage does not have to be nursed forever, at the right moment it converts into open lines and attacking squares, and the conversion is usually irreversible for both sides.
options: It won the d6 pawn by force
It shut the h8 bishop out, freed e4 for three minor pieces, and set up e6 and f5 against the king
It sealed the centre and secured a draw
It trapped the d3 knight behind its own lines

ex.prompt: Black got his knight to the square behind the pawns and still stood worse afterward. Why?
ex.why: The d3 square was real compensation, but compensation has to arrive in time. Once e5 and f5 hit the king, every tempo belonged to the attack, and the knight on d3 spent the rest of the game watching from the wrong wing.
options: The knight was on the wrong colour square
A positional trophy means little while your king is being cracked open, the octopus never influenced the fight
White's extra pawn decided
The knight should have gone to b4 instead

lessons.title: Space test 7, level 1400
text: De Riviere against Chigorin, Paris 1883. The plans are mapped out, White's huge queenside space advantage translates into an eventual b5 advance, while Black's only play is on the kingside with h6 and g5, the centre being completely dead. The book asks a single question, is grabbing space by a5 worth considering?

Silman wants the move to cause a scream of horror, and physical pain in any spectator passing by. Space is not an end in itself, it is worth exactly the penetration it enables or the enemy play it prevents, and a5 does neither. It buries White's own b5 break forever, deprives him of his only active plan, and gives Black the green light to assemble the perfect attack at leisure. Never accept, let alone willingly create, a position where you are helpless.

Silman's band note sets the level at 1400 flat, because he expects every reader of the book to feel revulsion at the sight of the move. White played it anyway, and Chigorin lowered the boom only after every single piece had reached its ideal square.

ex.prompt: Is grabbing space by a5 worth considering?
ex.why: Space that enables no penetration and stops no enemy play is scenery. After a5 the b5 advance can never be supported again, so White volunteered to watch the kingside attack build for eighteen moves and then die by it.
options: Yes, more space is always a plus
No, it should cause a scream of horror, it kills White's own b5 break and with it his only plan
Yes, it fixes a6 as a target for the pieces
Only after the queens come off

ex.prompt: White's real plan lives on one square. Click it.
ex.why: The b5 break is the only way this queenside territory ever turns into something concrete, and every white move should have served it. The game's space grab buried the break for good, which is why the move deserves its double question mark.

lessons.title: Passed pawn as an attacking piece
text: The usual reason to love a passed pawn is that it might become a queen. That is not the only job it can do, and this one has no interest in promoting at all.
Black is a pawn down and facing a serious attack. The natural instinct is to look for the piece move that adds another attacker. Bisguier pushes the pawn instead.

d6 does not threaten to promote in any meaningful sense. It rips a hole in the black position, opens lines for the pieces behind it, and joins the hunt for the king as a full attacking unit in its own right. Every move that follows is forcing, and Black never gets a breath.

ex.prompt: White to move, attacking. Bring the pawn into the assault.
ex.why: The pawn is not going for the eighth rank. It is opening lines and clearing squares for the pieces, which is worth more here than promotion ever would be.

ex.prompt: What makes this passed pawn valuable in this position?
ex.why: A passer in an attack is a piece that the opponent's pieces cannot capture without opening more lines. Its promotion value is almost incidental.
options: It will promote by force
It is an extra attacker against the king
It blockades an enemy pawn
It gains space for the endgame

lessons.title: Handing over a protected passed pawn on purpose
text: A protected passed pawn is the pawn everyone wants. Nothing can touch it and at any moment it might run. Silman opens this chapter by warning that a passed pawn, protected or not, can be a serious disadvantage, and this is the position that proves it.
White looks well placed. The pieces are more active, the pawns are healthier, and f5 is coming, which would both create a far advanced passer with e6 and threaten f6 against the black king.

So Black plays f5 himself and gives White a protected passed pawn on e5. That sounds like a gift and it is the point. The moment the pawn becomes a passer it stops being a majority, and with it goes the space-gaining f5 advance and the f6 smash against the king. All that dynamism is converted into one pawn that sits there. Ask what a majority is threatening to do before you help it become a passer.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Kill White's kingside plans, even at a cost.
ex.why: By force, White's central majority becomes a protected passed e pawn. Gone with it are f5 gaining space and f6 crashing into the king.

ex.prompt: Why would anyone hand the opponent a protected passed pawn?
ex.why: A majority is a threat that can still choose how to advance. A passed pawn has already chosen. Fixing it can be worth more than the pawn it costs.
options: To win a tempo
Because it ends the dynamic potential of the majority it came from
To open a file
To trade queens

ex.prompt: What is Silman's name for a passed pawn that sits there looking good and doing nothing?
ex.why: A nimble Louie is the one that runs. Deciding which of the two you are actually holding is the whole skill this chapter teaches.
options: A nimble Louie
A posing Polly
A tall pawn
A baby queen

lessons.title: What a majority is for
text: The reason passed pawns get their own chapter is that they are what every pawn majority is trying to become. Understand one and you understand the other.
Here each side has a majority pointing in a different direction. White's is central and Black's is on the queenside, and both are racing toward the same goal of producing a passer.

A majority can be a purely static asset, sitting quietly for forty moves and then producing a queen out of nowhere. It can also be dynamic, gaining space and squeezing the opponent as it advances, which is what White's central pawns are doing here. Knowing which kind you have tells you whether to hurry.

ex.prompt: Click a pawn belonging to the majority White is planning to advance.
ex.why: The central pawns are both the space advantage and the future passed pawn. Advancing them squeezes Black and works toward a passer at the same time.

ex.prompt: What is a pawn majority ultimately trying to do?
ex.why: That is the whole purpose, and it is why understanding passers improves your handling of majorities. Everything else a majority does on the way is a bonus.
options: Control the centre
Produce a passed pawn
Shelter the king
Open a file for the rooks

ex.prompt: A majority that gains space as it advances is which kind of asset?
ex.why: A quiet majority can wait forever. One that takes territory as it advances is doing damage on the way, which changes how fast you should be pushing it.
options: Purely static, so there is no hurry
Dynamic as well as static, so it can squeeze while it works
Neither, until a passer actually appears

lessons.title: Passed pawns test 1, level 1400 to 1900
text: Taimanov against Khasin, Moscow 1957. Black has just played b6, inviting the c5 pawn forward in the belief that it will be surrounded and eaten. The book asks the only question that matters, is the c-pawn a goner or a monster?

It is a monster, but only because White refuses to defend it. The pawn marches to c6, and when the knight tries to round it up with Nc5, White gives up the exchange on c5, because a passed pawn on the sixth supported by a king is worth far more than a rook. In the game Black checked instead, and the white king simply walked up the board, d5, d6, c7, shouldering everything aside in front of its own passer.

Silman's band note says a 1400 will see that c6 is forced, but pushed the scale toward 1900 for those who also see the exchange sacrifice coming and stay calm about it. Everyone, he hopes, will appreciate the follow up, one powerful king plus one sixth rank pawn against a helpless army.

ex.prompt: Is White's c-pawn a goner or a monster?
ex.why: Standing still loses the pawn, so it advances into the attack. Every defensive resource Black owns fails to one tactical point or another, and the pawn's supporting cast, king included, turns it into the whole game.
options: A goner, b6 wins it by force
A monster, it runs to c6 at once and White backs it with the exchange sacrifice and his own king
Neither, White should defend it with the rook and hold
A goner, but White gets drawing chances

ex.prompt: White to move. Answer the threat.
ex.why: The pawn is defended by advancing it. Black's checks only drew the white king forward, d5, then d6, then c7, a dynamic king marching in front of its own passer. The critical defence Nc5 is answered by taking on c5 with the rook, when the supported sixth rank pawn overpowers the extra rook.

ex.prompt: What does the pawn's arrival on c7 actually win?
ex.why: In the game the c-pawn cost Black his rook, and the ending with an extra exchange was routine. A passer this deep converts every threat into a material transaction on White's terms.
options: The b6 pawn
The game, the blockade square c8 falls next and the rook must give itself up for the new queen
A draw by perpetual pursuit
The knight

lessons.title: Passed pawns test 2, level 1800 to 2200
text: A hypothetical position from the analysis of Laurier against Sharif, Port Barcares 2005. Count the material and Black is up two minor pieces for a pawn, so the book's question, who is better and by how much, looks like it answers itself.

The real answer is a concept, not a calculation. White can force a queen against queen endgame in which he owns a far advanced passed pawn, and the theory section already taught that such a pawn in a pure queen ending is close to decisive. Playing for that position on faith is good enough, and the faith is justified, since the d-pawn costs Black his queen or promotes outright in every line.

Silman's band note says the flash is not the obstacle, the faith is. Questions like whether Black has a perpetual, or whether the black king can walk over and help stop the pawn, nag at most players below class A, and experience with this exact endgame is what silences them.

ex.prompt: Who is better, and by how much?
ex.why: Material counts only if the pieces survive the next three moves, and these do not. The combination wins knight, bishop and rook for a rook, and what remains is the one endgame every passed pawn dreams about.
options: Black, two minor pieces for a pawn is decisive
White is winning, a forced sequence reaches a queen endgame where the far advanced d-pawn decides
Roughly equal, Black returns material for a perpetual
White is slightly better at most

ex.prompt: White to move. Start the sequence.
ex.why: The knight falls with check, and the king must step into the corner, since f7 belongs to the queen. Now comes the move the whole combination rests on.

ex.prompt: Finish the thought.
ex.why: The rook removes the defender, the check on e7 forks king and rook, and the queen endgame arrives exactly as advertised. The greedy Qe7 instead lets Black fight on a rook down in activity, and the book's verdict is blunt, why settle for that when taking on g7 is gin. From there the d-pawn, helped by a few precise checks and one quiet luft move, walks through every defence.

lessons.title: Passed pawns test 3, level 1800 to 2200
text: Navara against Kramnik, Prague 2008. White looks lovely, a lead in development, central space, and a kingside majority with the f5 and f6 expansion programmed into its DNA. Kramnik now shows that the whole picture is an illusion.

The move is f5, and it hands White a protected passed pawn on a platter. What it buys is everything else. The white majority's dynamism dies on the spot, the e6 square in front of the passer becomes the blockade square Black will own, and Black's untouched queenside majority becomes the only mobile pawn mass on the board. A few moves later c5 evicted the white knights from d4, e6 fell permanently into black hands, and the blockading war was over.

Silman's band note admits the idea psychologically disturbs a whole range of players, and that even masters sometimes cannot bring themselves to play it, which is why a move discussed at length in the theory pages still earns the top of the rating band here.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Give White what he thinks he wants.
ex.why: The protected passer is a gift with a curse on it. The pawn on e5 now blocks its own pieces, the majority can never advance again, and the knight begins the journey to e6, the square in front of the passer, where a blockader radiates activity.

ex.prompt: What is Black's two part plan after the pawn is fixed?
ex.why: The passer is not a target, it is a prisoner. Once e6 belongs to Black the pawn influences nothing, and the game is decided by the only majority that can still move.
options: Trade every piece and win the endgame
Own the e6 blockade square, then advance his own healthy majority
Attack the king down the g file
Win the e5 pawn itself

ex.prompt: The knights hover near d4, keeping e6 contested. Win the blockading war.
ex.why: Taking d4 away from the knights forces them to squares that no longer touch e6, so the blockade becomes permanent. The dream setup follows, two bishops, a knight on e6, a mobile majority, and White's own pawns blocking his pieces. Kramnik went on to win.

lessons.title: Passed pawns test 4, level 2000 to 2200
text: Von Bilguer against von Heydebrand und der Lasa, Berlin 1837, one of the oldest positions in the book. White has an extra pawn, and not a weak one, the g3 passer is protected and passed. He has two bishops. The queens are already off, which usually ends all talk of an attack. Surely White is much better?

The answer is no, Black has excellent compensation, and the reasons are simple. Black has all the play while White must defend for a long time to come, the passed pawn is frozen and going nowhere, the light squares around the white king are chronically weak, and Black's plan is effortless, double rooks on the h file and hunt the king on g1. Engines will proclaim white's advantage all day, and the book's advice is to not become a slave to a soulless number.

Silman's band note says an extra protected passer plus two bishops plus queens off would make almost anyone lean White, and that handing White the move on top of it was a deliberate act of cruelty. Only a rare and very strong player gives Black his due here, which is what the 2000 and up label is for.

ex.prompt: White has an extra protected passed pawn, the bishop pair, and no queens to fear. Assess.
ex.why: Every white asset is static and every black asset is active. The passer cannot move, the bishops defend rather than bite, and the h file comes to Black for free. Compensation does not mean advantage, but it absolutely means White is the one suffering.
options: White is much better, the material and the pair decide
Black has excellent compensation, all the play, a frozen passer to laugh at, and weak light squares to invade
White is winning outright
Black is better because of the e4 pawn

ex.prompt: Click the black piece that keeps the passed pawn frozen.
ex.why: The bishop sits directly in front of the pawn and owns the square it needs. A blockader this comfortable turns the proud passer into scenery for the rest of the game.
