ex.prompt: White has just retreated his knight to h2, attacking the bishop. Show why the game ended on the spot.
ex.why: The exchange sacrifice rips the king's cover, the second rook arrives with check, and the quiet bishop move seals the mating net on the light squares that were weak all along. White resigned, an abrupt end that the position had been promising Black for some time.

lessons.title: Passed pawns test 5, level 1800 to 2200
text: Kofidis against Tzenniadianos, Athens 1997. Black already owns a protected passed d-pawn, but it is firmly blocked by the d3 bishop, and a bishop is a poor blockader, all defense and no activity, a tall pawn wearing a mitre. Meanwhile White's queenside majority is mobile, and a4 to a5 would set it rolling.

The move is a5, and it hands White a protected passed pawn with pleasure. The point is the blockader. A knight lands on b6, and from there it stops the pawn dead while attacking a4 and c4, active in every direction, while White's bishop blocks d4 and defends c4 and does nothing else. Compare the two blockaders and the position explains itself. After that comes the second half of the lesson, the f5 break, because a firm blockade means nothing without active play elsewhere.
Silman's band note is the same confession as the previous test, the idea was covered in the theory pages and it remains something most players simply cannot bring themselves to do.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Hand it over.
ex.why: The a-pawn will be passed and protected and completely irrelevant, because the knight reaches b6 where it blockades and bites at a4 and c4 at the same time. The pawns White must defend are the real story, and the coming f5 break gives Black play across the whole board.

ex.prompt: Both passers end up blockaded. Why is Black clearly better anyway?
ex.why: A blockader is judged by what else it does. The b6 knight is a tollbooth on the whole queenside, the d3 bishop is a wall, and the f5 break converted the difference into a winning central majority in the game.
options: The d4 pawn is further advanced
His knight blockades with threats while White's bishop blockades as a tall pawn, and only Black has a pawn break coming
The bishop pair was exchanged
White's king is exposed

lessons.title: Passed pawns test 6, level 1600 to 2000
text: Silman against Strauss, California Championship 1990, told against nobody, for once, since the idea worked. White got nothing from the opening and nothing from the brief middlegame. The one asset left on the board is the queenside pawn majority, and the question is how to make anyone care about it.

The answer is Bf3, offering a trade that cripples White's own kingside pawns. It looks like an anti-positional joke, and it is the whole point of the test, because a passed pawn reaches its peak strength in a queen endgame. After the bishops come off, c5 arrives, the majority produces its passer, and the doubled f-pawns turn out to form an oddly effective shelter for the king. White risks nothing and massages the position forever, and in the game the defender eventually cracked.

Silman's band note doubts that anyone under 1600 would willingly wreck his own structure this way, and hopes his readers prove him wrong. The immediate c5 instead lets Black free himself with e5 and e4, which is why the bishop trade comes first.

ex.prompt: What does White still own, and where does it cash?
ex.why: One asset, one plan. Every piece trade raises the value of the future c-pawn, and the endgame knowledge that queens plus passers favour the passer is what makes the next move thinkable at all.
options: Nothing, the position is dead equal
The queenside majority, and it cashes best in a queen endgame, so White should trade the bishops even at the cost of his structure
The better bishop, so avoid all trades
A kingside attack with g4 and h4

ex.prompt: White to move. Set the problems.
ex.why: Crippled pawns bought a queen endgame with a running c-pawn, and the doubled f-pawns quietly shield the king from the checks that usually save the defender. Pushing c5 at once fizzles against e5 and e4. From here White probed without risk until Black lashed out with h5 and lost quickly.

lessons.title: Passed pawns test 7, level 1600 to 2200
text: Ivkov against Milic, Sombor 1957. Black has just played c5, and the pawn passing his d5 neighbour poses White a question with a deadline attached. He must either capture en passant right now or keep his passed d-pawn forever, and the book asks you to describe both choices and the philosophies behind them.

Keeping the passer is a real plan, but only an active version of it, striking at the queenside majority with Rc1 against c5 or with a4, creating weaknesses before Black settles. What fails is mindless development, since after Rd1 and Nc3 Black plants a knight on d6 and the blockaded pawn becomes furniture. Taking en passant is the other philosophy, ripping the centre open to make maximum use of the superior minor pieces, with the d5 hole waiting for the knight and the d-file for the rooks.

Silman's band note hopes a class B player would appreciate the strength of a d6 blockade and choose the capture, and admits that plenty of masters would fail to feel the position's nuances. Ivkov chose the capture, vintage prime Ivkov, turning the screws without ever risking incoming fire, and won the resulting grind.

ex.prompt: Describe White's two legitimate philosophies.
ex.why: The choice is between a pawn structure asset and a piece activity asset, and either can be right. The one losing option is the passive one, because a blockaded passer does nothing while Black completes his ideal setup.
options: Develop quickly and let the passer win on its own
Take en passant for piece play against the d5 hole, or keep the passer and immediately harass the queenside majority with Rc1 or a4
Trade queens and grind the endgame
Sacrifice on b5 for an attack

ex.prompt: Why does quiet development fail here?
ex.why: One tempo of routine play and the knight path c8 to d6 closes the discussion. Passed pawn owners must always ask what the pawn will actually be doing three moves from now.
options: It loses the d5 pawn
After Rd1 and Nc3 Black reroutes his knight to d6, and the blockade turns the proud passer into a bystander
It allows a kingside attack
It concedes the c file

ex.prompt: White to move. Play Ivkov's choice.
ex.why: The centre opens while every white piece stands better than its counterpart. The bishop trade on c6 looks strange until you see that the knight was heading for d4, and afterwards the d5 hole, the d file and the two bishops ground Black down move by move, ending a clear pawn up.

lessons.title: Passed pawns test 8, level 1400 to 1800
text: Silman against Lawless, San Francisco 1982. Material is dead level, queen, rook and four pawns each, and the book asks how large White's advantage actually is.

The answer is that it is winning, for four stacked reasons. White's passer is far more advanced than Black's would-be b-pawn. The material mix of queen plus rook with no minor pieces is the ideal escort for a runner. The black king is far from safe. And Black never built a blockade, so d6 is available, after which d7 conquers the last stop and paralysis sets in.

Silman's band note gives full marks to anyone who appreciated the passer plus the queen and rook mix, the combination that keeps checks, threats and escort duty all in one package. The one trap to avoid afterwards is retreating the rook to babysit the pawn, since answering a fake threat by turning your best attacker into a defender is how winning positions go stale.

ex.prompt: Material is equal. How large is White's advantage?
ex.why: Each factor alone is an edge, together they are a verdict. The passer occupies the blockade squares one by one while every black piece is chained to defence, which is exactly what queen and rook do best.
options: Small, Black holds with accurate defence
Winning, the advanced passer, the ideal queen and rook mix, the airy black king, and the free d6 square add up to paralysis
Only a draw with best play
White is worse, the b-pawn runs faster

ex.prompt: White to move. Claim the first blockade square.
ex.why: The pawn takes d6 because Black never organised a piece to sit there, and three moves later d7 falls as well, leaving Black completely paralysed. Along the way White ignores the fake threat against d6, since Rd1 would turn the attacking rook into a nursemaid, and the e7 invasion decides.

lessons.title: Passed pawns test 9, level 1600 to 2100
text: Denker against Smyslov, Moscow 1946, the final test of the set, and it asks for a verbal breakdown plus Black's correct first move. White has a protected passed d-pawn and some kingside gestures coming with h4 and h5. So why does Smyslov look so comfortable?

The breakdown runs like this. The d-pawn wants a blockader, and d6 is the square, freshly vacated and begging for a knight. The pawns on c4 and e4 are weak, and a knight on d6 attacks both while it blockades. And if White ever grabs space with a4, Black answers a5, accepting a backward b6 pawn in exchange for a permanently weak white a-pawn. See all of that and the first move picks itself, the g6 knight starts the journey to d6 through e7 and c8, the one route that also keeps b6 defended.

Silman's band note calls the required attitude the I insist mentality, rarely found under 1600 and often missing far above it. Knowing you want a horse on d6 is one thing, spending four moves making it happen while the opponent pushes pawns at your king is another.

ex.prompt: Give the verbal breakdown.
ex.why: The passer looks imposing and is actually the least mobile thing on the board. Once the blockading knight doubles as an attacker of c4 and e4, every white pawn on a light square is a long term patient, and the kingside gestures never add up to real threats.
options: White's passer and space give him a pull
Blockade d6 with a knight, hit the weak c4 and e4 pawns from there, and meet a4 with a5, Black has a great game
Black must trade queens to survive the attack
The position is equal and drawish

ex.prompt: Black to move. Start the journey.
ex.why: The knight heads for d6 by way of c8, and the route matters, since from c8 it also guards b6, which the alternative path through h8 and f7 would abandon. Insisting on the ideal square is the entire lesson of the position.

ex.prompt: White grabbed queenside space with a4. Punish the pawn that moved.
ex.why: The move accepts a weak b6 pawn, which was falling to a5xb6 anyway, and in return fixes a4 as a target forever. Smyslov then traded the light squared bishops on purpose, tall pawn or not, because the trade highlights c4 and e4, and the knight duly reached d6 with a clear advantage. White's pawns on a4, c4 and e4 all fell ill, and Black won the long game.

lessons.title: Know what your opening gives both sides
text: Radjabov summed this position up in one sentence. White has gained a lot of space on the queenside, but Black has a lot of play on the kingside. That is the whole assessment, and it is all either player needs.

It sounds too simple to be worth saying, and here is the test. Pick your favourite opening, imagine fifteen moves have been played, and explain what the line gives you and what it gives your opponent. Most players cannot, which Silman calls a tragedy, because the information is easy to acquire and decides everything that follows.

In a sound main line neither argument wins outright. Both sides get their chances and the better player usually prevails. That is exactly why knowing the terms of the argument matters more than memorising the moves.

ex.prompt: Click the pawn at the head of Black's counterplay.
ex.why: Black's play is on the kingside, and the f pawn is what opens it. White's play is on the other wing, which is why both sides can push at full speed without ever meeting.

ex.prompt: What is the position giving each player?
ex.why: Radjabov's one sentence. Both sides have somewhere to go, and the game is a race between two plans that barely touch.
options: White is simply better
White queenside space, Black kingside play
Black is simply better
Nothing yet, it is symmetrical

ex.prompt: What should you be able to do with every opening you play?
ex.why: Theory runs out and the assessment does not. If you cannot say what the line is offering both sides, you are following moves rather than playing a position.
options: Recall twenty moves of theory
State what it gives you and what it gives the opponent
Name the players who invented it
Avoid all known traps

lessons.title: Choosing openings that suit you
text: Silman calls this heaven for him and hell for others, which is the honest way to describe an opening choice. White has walked into it deliberately, and what he has bought is small.

Central and queenside space, a queenside majority, and a king that is perfectly safe on d2 because the queens have already come off. There is no attack here and there never will be. What there is, is a safe and pleasant grind that lasts as long as White wants it to.

The point is the fit. This is theory both players knew, and Black allowed it expecting to draw. White chose it because the resulting position matches his strengths, then converted the small plus in a queenless middlegame and the middlegame into an endgame win. Picking openings that produce positions you enjoy playing is worth more than picking the ones with the best reputation.

ex.prompt: White's king is on d2 in the middlegame. Why is that acceptable?
ex.why: Queenless middlegames change the rules about king safety completely. The central king that Part One warned about is a liability while queens are on and often an asset once they are not.
options: It is well defended by pieces
The queens are already off the board
White intends to castle by hand
Black cannot reach it

ex.prompt: What did White deliberately buy in the opening?
ex.why: Space and a queenside majority, then a grind. The opening was chosen for the kind of position it produces rather than for its evaluation.
options: An attack against the king
A small, permanent positional plus that suits his style
A material advantage
A dangerous initiative

lessons.title: Same position, two philosophies
text: This exact position had been reached before, against Nunn, and Black had handled it quietly with h6. White won that game, and Black's assets never got a chance to say anything.

A couple of months later Karjakin arrived at the same position and disagreed. Ng4 is the move of a player who intends to make Black's two bishops and dynamic potential count rather than wait to be squeezed.

Silman's observation is that high-level opening battles come down to a philosophical difference of opinion. Both sides know the position. What they disagree about is whose imbalances matter more, and each one plays to prove his own case. That is the same argument this course opened with, arriving in the opening rather than the middlegame.

ex.prompt: Black to move. Play for the bishops and the dynamics rather than waiting.
ex.why: Nunn's h6 was quieter and left Black's advantages theoretical. Ng4 forces the issue while the dynamic assets still exist to be used.

ex.prompt: What are high-level opening arguments actually about?
ex.why: Both players know the moves. The disagreement is over the assessment, and each one plays the rest of the game trying to prove his reading was the right one.
options: Who has memorised more theory
Whose imbalances matter more in the resulting position
Who gets the first attack
Material

lessons.title: Opening imbalances test 1, level 1900 to 2200
text: Britton against Donaldson, Rhodes International 1980, a Maroczy Bind endgame every Accelerated Dragon player thinks he knows. White threatens Nb6 and Nxe7 with a capture on f6 looming, so the knight on d5 must be taken. The whole test is with what, since Bxd5 concedes the two bishops, while Nxd5 appears to hang e7, a pawn that in analogous positions is often indirectly protected.

Here the indirect protection is a mirage, and taking with the knight is the trap. After Nxd5, exd5 and Bd7, White grabs e7 anyway, and the standard punishment Bh6 runs into the cold shower Rad1, handing back the exchange on White's terms. Two bishops, two extra pawns and a monster majority added up to a technical win. So Bxd5 is right, a small concession that keeps the position solid, with a5 or b5 and b4 to challenge the bishops later.

Silman's band note calls this deceptively difficult, since players under 2000 avoid the knight capture for the wrong reason and experienced players avoid the bishop capture on principle. His closing moral is the point of the whole chapter, you cannot play known positions with your eyes closed, because the slightest change turns every assessment on its head.

ex.prompt: What is the right way to capture on d5?
ex.why: The familiar motif fails by exactly one tempo in this exact position, which is what the rating band is measuring. Knowing the setup is not the same as verifying it on the board in front of you.
options: Nxd5, keeping the two bishops, since e7 is indirectly protected as usual
Bxd5, conceding the bishop pair, because here the usual e7 trick fails and the knight capture loses material
Either capture, they transpose
Neither, Black should ignore the knight with Re8

ex.prompt: Black to move. Capture correctly.
ex.why: White keeps a pleasant pull with space and the pair, but Black is solid and has real plans, a5 to fix the queenside or b5 and b4 to secure c5 for the knight. A small minus with a future beats the tactical adventure that loses material.

ex.prompt: In the game Black took with the knight, and after exd5, Bd7, Bxe7 he uncorked Bh6, apparently winning material. What had he missed?
ex.why: Both rook retreats lose a piece, but the quiet developing move turns the tables completely. Black got the exchange and White got everything else, including a pawn majority the size of a weather system. The trap was set for whoever stopped calculating first.
options: Bxd6, saving the bishop with a third pawn
Rad1, calmly returning the exchange on d2, after which two bishops and two connected extra pawns won
Rc2, defending laterally
Nothing, White was lost after Bh6

lessons.title: Opening imbalances test 2, level 1600 to 2000
text: Rozentalis against Jones, Queenstown 2009, an Exchange Lopez. The schema says White plays against the crippled majority while Black leans on the two bishops, the e file and the f5 break. The question is how White should actually handle it.

The honest answer is that the famous majority is unusable here, Black is too solid and too active for White to extract a drop of honey from it. So White changes the terms, Rd1 followed by taking on d6, undoubling Black's pawns and abolishing his own majority story in the same stroke. What he gets instead is a pawn on d6 that his whole army can reach and pressure, plus a central space edge after c4. A target you can attack beats a static plus you can only admire.

Silman's band note says players fall in love with whatever positive imbalance they own and never notice it offers no active plan, and that undoubling the opponent's pawns is something most players reject out of hand. Rozentalis milked the d6 pressure into an endgame squeeze and eventually the full point.

ex.prompt: How should White handle this position?
ex.why: The majority cannot advance against this much piece activity, and the pawn ending is thirty trades away. Giving up one theoretical asset to gain one concrete target is the mature trade, and it is exactly the kind of move ownership pride prevents.
options: Advance the healthy majority with c4, e5 and f4
Trade on d6, undoubling the black pawns on purpose, to create a target the pieces can actually reach
Attack on the kingside with Qg3 and f4
Trade pieces toward the winning pawn endgame

ex.prompt: White to move. Begin the plan.
ex.why: The rook takes the file first so the recapture on d6 lands under immediate pressure. Three moves later White has central space, a fixed target on d6, and a clear scheme of Nc3, Rd2 and Rad1, while Black is chained to defence, which is precisely the situation the undoubling was designed to create.

lessons.title: Opening imbalances test 3, level 1400 to 2000
text: Leko against Radjabov, Morelia 2008, a Sveshnikov Sicilian where both sides have played logically. The book sets the goals for you. White has designs against a5, but his immediate job is to stop the freeing d5 push, so that the d6 pawn stays a static weakness rather than becoming a dynamic plus, and then to pile on it. The question is which moves serve those two goals.

Four moves have been tried by strong players, and the goals sort them instantly. Qa1 hits a5 but abandons both d squares, and in practice Black played d5 and won the resulting mess. Taking on f5 surrenders control of d5 for nothing. Qd2 fits the brief and earns full credit, though it has not proven especially effective. The star is Ra2, sliding the rook to d2, adding a heavy piece to both d5 and d6 while keeping every other option alive.

Silman's band note says a 1400 who has absorbed the book should find at least one goal-fitting move, because that is the entire method, read the imbalances, set logical goals, and the strong moves start suggesting themselves. Leko's follow up, queen to a1 and a3 only after d6 was fixed, dragged down a superstar and is worth replaying for pleasure.

ex.prompt: Which candidate moves actually serve the two stated goals?
ex.why: Qa1 answers a question nobody asked and let Black free himself with d5 in a stem game, while the capture on f5 loosens White's grip on d5. Matching the move to the goal is the test, and two of the four candidates pass it.
options: Qa1 and Nxf5, hitting a5 and grabbing the bishop pair
Qd2 and Ra2, both adding force against d5 and d6
Only Nxf5, removing a defender of d6
None, White should play f4 at once

ex.prompt: White to move. Play the most exact of the goal-fitting moves.
ex.why: The rook lift is the move that does nothing except the job, doubling on the d file square by square. Only once d6 was pinned down did Leko switch the queen to a1 and a3, hitting a5 as a bonus, and the picture after Qa3 is the book's own illustration of a team of pieces sharing one plan. Radjabov never got d5 in and lost.

lessons.title: Opening imbalances test 4, level 1400 to 1600
text: Bosch against Gufeld, Telex Finals 1978. White's opening was so tame that after seven moves he has absolutely nothing, and neither player is in book. The test asks for Black's most pronounced favorable imbalance, promising that once you name it, every move that follows will explain itself.

The nice-to-haves are a small lead in development and the safer king. The answer is the central pawn majority, d and e pawns against a lone e pawn, and everything Gufeld plays flows from it. He rolls the majority forward, d5, then e5, then d4 and the freeing e4, converting spare pawns in the middle into space, a passed pawn and finally a mating attack, a command performance built on one imbalance noticed at move seven.

Silman's band note trusts any 1400 conversant with the imbalances to spot the majority, and that is the entire ask. Respecting it, instead of shrugging that a central majority is somebody else's abstraction, is what separates finding the plan from watching it happen to you.

ex.prompt: What is Black's most pronounced favorable imbalance?
ex.why: Development evaporates and the c file is shared, but the majority is permanent and it is central, meaning every advance gains space that matters. Name it and Black's next ten moves become predictions rather than surprises.
options: The lead in development
The central pawn majority
The fianchettoed bishop against Bb2
The half open c file

ex.prompt: Black to move. Put the imbalance in motion.
ex.why: Central space first, then the rook slides behind the coming e pawn, and by move ten Black has a dream position, big centre, more space, everything developed to natural squares. No tactics yet, just a majority doing what majorities do.

ex.prompt: White has challenged the centre with c4 and, after your advance to d4, has just captured on d4. Keep the wave rolling.
ex.why: The point of the whole sequence, the pawn that recaptured on d4 is pinned to its square while e4 buries White's kingside knight and wins the d4 pawn back with interest. Gufeld's pieces poured through the space the majority had bought, and the game ended in a collapse on the light squares.

lessons.title: Opening imbalances test 5, level 1400 to 1800
text: Kozul against Varga, Pula 2002, and another position from an opening nobody has studied, because nobody should. The book asks for an assessment and for the specific features of Black's position that catch your attention.

Two things should stand out with multi-coloured clarity. White has a sizable lead in development, and Black's f6 has gutted the e6 square, which White's knight already eyes from f4. Together they add up to a winning advantage this early, and the move that serves every goal at once, development, castling, the e6 invasion and getting the pawn back, is the most natural one on the board, taking on c4.

Silman's band note says the development gap is easy to see and e6 should strike your brain like a gong, and that the resulting move is one any player from 1000 up would find. The joke of the answer is that White himself played d5 instead, gave the advantage back, and drew, proving that seeing the imbalances and trusting them are different skills.

ex.prompt: Click the square in Black's camp that should strike your brain like a gong.
ex.why: The f6 push abandoned it, the c5 push means the d-pawn cannot cover it either, and a white knight already attacks it from f4. A hole this deep, this central and this early decides the character of everything that follows.

ex.prompt: Assess the position.
ex.why: Six moves in, one side has played chess and the other has played hooky. When a lead in development points at a permanent hole, the advantage is not positional seasoning, it is the whole meal.
options: Roughly level, Black is solid if ugly
White is already winning, the development lead plus the wrecked e6 square are decisive this early
Black is fine after regaining space with e5
White is slightly better, one pawn down

ex.prompt: White to move. Play the move that serves every goal at once.
ex.why: It develops, regains the pawn, prepares castling, and after the trade the knight pair aims at e6 and d5 with ideas like Ne6, d5 and Qh5 hanging over Black permanently. In the game White played d5 instead and let Black wriggle to a draw, which is why the test rewards trusting the assessment you just made.

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 6, level 1400 to 1900
text: An anonymous internet game from 2009, and the first of the mixing tests, where the imbalances pull in different directions and you must decide which side of the argument you are on. White is a pawn up, a static plus. Black has active pieces and pressure against a2, b4 and e5, a position that runs entirely on dynamics.

White wants to castle, prop up e5, and only then cash the queenside. Black, a pawn down, has to turn the game into a fistfight before any of that happens, and his attacked g4 bishop tells him how. Taking on f3 removes the main defender of e5, wrecks White's kingside structure, and opens f5 as a permanent hole for the g8 knight to reach through e7. In the game Black retreated the bishop to h5 to keep the light squares, a thought that pays rent in other positions and hands White a free move in this one.

Silman's band note gives full marks for three observations, that Black must play actively being a pawn down, that the bishop is hanging, and that the capture on f3 gains time, ruins pawns and wins the f5 square all at once. Energy is the entrance fee when dynamics are your life blood.

ex.prompt: Read the position. Who owns what?
ex.why: Every mixing test starts with this sorting step. Once you know your position runs on dynamics, retreating moves that hand over free tempi stop being candidate moves at all.
options: White owns statics, the extra pawn, while Black owns dynamics, active pieces against a2, b4 and e5, and must attack before White consolidates
White owns both, the pawn and the initiative
Black is simply lost a pawn down
The position is quiet and equal

ex.prompt: Black to move. The bishop is attacked. Use the moment.
ex.why: One capture does three jobs, it removes the e5 pawn's best defender, cripples the kingside pawns, and digs the f5 hole the knight settles into two moves later. The game's Bh5 retreat kept a bishop and lost the thread, exactly the light square thinking that belongs in a different position.

ex.prompt: A few moves later, with the knight on f5, the book endorses the violent g5 over quiet development. Why?
ex.why: The calm route offers Black solid compensation, but the thrust is more in the spirit of the position, and the sample line ends with every black piece swarming the white king. Dynamic positions reward the player who keeps asking forcing questions.
options: It wins the h4 pawn
It tears at e5 and opens the g file, and a pawn down position built on dynamics has to keep raising the temperature
It prepares to castle kingside
It stops White from playing g4

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 7, level 1800 to 2200
text: Christiansen against girl-brain, an internet clock simultaneous from 2007. Black has held her own against a three time United States champion for twenty four moves, and now the heat is on, the d5 bishop is pinned against the queen and attacked, and if it falls she is a pawn down for nothing.

Her comment afterward was that she had to defend the bishop, so her move was forced. That sentence is the whole test. The bishop does not need defending, it needs to move with tempo, and taking on b3 does it, since after the rook grabs the queen on d7 the bishop takes the queen on d1, and when the dust settles material is level and only Black, thanks to the passed c pawn, can even think about winning.

Silman's band note sends anyone who defended the bishop back to the psychology chapter on the curse of I have to. The game itself is a museum of the disease, since even after the passive rook move her later notes said she could not take on e4, and analysis shows that capture led to a defensible game too. None of those resources exist for a player whose first sentence is I have to.

ex.prompt: The d5 bishop is pinned and attacked. Is defending it forced?
ex.why: The phrase I have to shuts the search down before it starts. Every capture and counterattack deserves one honest look before you accept servitude, and here the very first one works.
options: Yes, the pin leaves no choice
No, forced is a word to distrust, the bishop can move with tempo and the tactics work out level or better
Yes, but only with Re5
No, Black should give the pawn and fight on

ex.prompt: Black to move. Refuse the pin.
ex.why: The queens and bishops come off in one forced sequence, and the rook slides behind the passed c pawn in the final position. Silman's dry verdict is that Black is the only one who can even consider playing for a win, which is a strange fate for a piece that supposedly had to be defended.

ex.prompt: What is the deeper lesson the game teaches?
ex.why: Even after missing the shot, her later defence contained saves she talked herself out of, including a capture she declared impossible that analysis holds together. The position kept offering escapes and the words kept refusing them.
options: Never allow pins against your queen
Behind every I cannot and I have to hides a world of unexamined resources, and only the player who insists on looking finds them
Avoid simultaneous games against grandmasters
Passed pawns beat bishops

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 8, level 1800 to 2200
text: Cheparinov against Yusupov, Amsterdam 2007, and the book simply says assess this position. Black's tripled c pawns stand out like a sore thumb, and White's kingside majority with the f4 and f5 cascade looks like confirmation that the assessment writes itself.

It does not. The tripled pawns control b5, b4, b3, d5, d4 and d3, a fistful of squares that matter, and the d5 square in particular is a fine home for the bishop. Black is also a pawn up, though that counts for little since the single white pawn on c3 freezes all three trips. Add it up honestly and Black's position is perfectly acceptable, ugly pawns and all.

Silman's band note suspects many masters would automatically give White the nod, and awards pride to anyone who looked past the wreckage and counted Black's assets too. In the game Black stood well for six more moves and then melted down for unrelated reasons, which changes the assessment not at all.

ex.prompt: Assess this position.
ex.why: Ugly is not the same as bad. Every doubled or tripled pawn is a case, and this case pays Black in squares, a file, and a unit of material, while the famous f pawn cascade never actually achieves anything by force.
options: White is much better, the tripled pawns are a ruin
Black is perfectly fine, the trips control a fistful of squares, the bishop gets d5, and he is a pawn up besides
White is winning after f4 and f5
Dead equal and drawish

ex.prompt: Black to move. Put the best piece on the square the trips bought.
ex.why: The bishop is untouchable on d5, watching both wings while the b file rook trades itself into White's camp. From here Black had a comfortable game and even the more pleasant side of it, until a later collapse that had nothing to do with the structure.

ex.prompt: Black is a pawn up. Why does the book shrug at that?
ex.why: Frozen pawns are square controllers, not runners. The honest ledger reads, no usable extra pawn for Black, no usable majority for White, and a pile of central squares that only Black controls, which is why acceptable is the right verdict.
options: Because the c4 pawn will fall
Because one white pawn on c3 freezes all three trips, so the extra unit never becomes a passed pawn
Because material never matters in middlegames
Because White's majority is faster

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 9, level 1400 to 1800
text: Ni Hua against Morozevich, Beer-Sheva 2005, assess the position. The minor pieces are bishops of opposite colours, which whispers draw to everyone who has only heard half the rule.

The book borrows grandmaster Greenfeld's explanation of the other half. With major pieces still on, opposite bishops sharpen the game, because nothing can ever challenge a bishop on its own diagonals, so each side attacks on his own colour and two things decide everything, king safety and pawn structure. Measured that way the verdict is clear, White carries two permanent weaknesses on c3 and a2 while Black's formation is rock solid, so Black is better and can press for a long time at no risk.

Silman's band note expects every reader to notice White's inferior structure, gives extra credit for coveting the c4 and d5 squares, and full marks for realising that Black's bishop will simply enjoy a better diagonal than White's. Morozevich squeezed exactly as promised and won the long game.

ex.prompt: Opposite coloured bishops with queens and rooks on. What actually decides such positions?
ex.why: The drawing tendency belongs to the pure bishop ending. With majors aboard the bishops become one way attacking pieces, and the game is decided by the terms each side attacks on, which is Greenfeld's whole point.
options: Nothing, they are drawn with any material
King safety and pawn structure, since each side attacks unchallenged on his own colour
Whoever has the knight
The side with more pawn islands wins

ex.prompt: Apply the rule here and assess.
ex.why: Two targets against none, plus the c4 and d5 squares as furniture for Black's pieces. Morozevich's technique, f6 to blunt the dark squares, a5 to freeze a4 on the fatal colour, is the model of pressing an opposite bishop middlegame.
options: White is better, he has the e5 square and the h file
Black is better, White nurses weaknesses on c3 and a2 while Black's structure is rock solid
Equal, the opposite bishops cancel everything
White is better, Black's g pawns are doubled

ex.prompt: Black to move. Start the press.
ex.why: The queen takes the light squares White can never contest, and the rooks pile onto the open files. Within a few moves every black piece stood actively while White defended c3 and a2 forever, and the a5 freeze later fixed a third pawn on the doomed colour.

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 10, level 1800 to 2200
text: Bouaziz against Miles, Riga Interzonal 1979. White is up an exchange and his passed c pawn is one square from promotion. The game is all but over, which is precisely when the book demands one last ounce of caution, because positions that are won and positions that are finished are not the same thing.

The quiet g5 wins on the spot, and its only point is prophylaxis, giving the king an escape on g4 so that Black's one trick, the rook sacrifice on h3, comes to nothing. Bouaziz, certain Black was about to resign, pushed the pawn instead, and Miles uncorked Rxh3. Capturing the rook loses by force, queen check on h1, capture on f3, and the bishop joins with check until the g pawn mates, one of the most famous swindles ever played. Even after the shock White could still have drawn with the cold Qf1, but hysteria chose the king grab.

Silman's band note calls this a pay attention moment. When you think the game is yours, that is exactly when you must look long and hard for counterplay, and his prescription is to let the clock tick, absorb the position, and only then cash the point.

ex.prompt: White is winning easily. What does this exact moment demand?
ex.why: The habit being tested is the last look. Black has exactly one idea in the position, and one move of prophylaxis kills it forever, after which any plan wins. Winning positions are lost in the moment the winner stops looking.
options: Push c7 immediately, nothing can stop the pawn
Stop and hunt for enemy tricks first, the quiet g5 defuses everything and wins trivially
Trade a pair of rooks to be safe
Check on c5 first

ex.prompt: White to move. Win with the careful move.
ex.why: The pawn step opens g4 for the king, so the sacrifice on h3 no longer comes with mate attached, and Black, as the book puts it, really would have resigned. One tempo spent on the opponent's idea is the cheapest insurance in chess.

ex.prompt: In the game White pushed c7 at once. What followed?
ex.why: Even after Rxh3 White could have bailed out with the icy Qf1, returning material for a perpetual. Instead the king took the rook, and five checks later the spectators watched a won game end in mate. Silman suggests poor Bouaziz left on a stretcher.
options: Black resigned
Rxh3, and after the greedy capture the queen check on h1, the capture on f3 and the bishop check led to a forced mate by the g pawn
Black gave perpetual check
Black promoted his own b pawn first

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 11, level 1400 to 1800
text: Kremenietsky against Sidorov, Russian Championship 2007, assess the position. The centre is closed and the queenside is in a perfect state of balance, White presses the backward c6 pawn, Black presses the backward b3 pawn, White fights for the c5 square while Black grips b4.

The c5 square is the hinge of the whole queenside, because if Black ever achieves the c5 break his weaknesses evaporate while b3 stays sick forever. Since neither side can make progress on that wing, White's only try for an advantage lives on the kingside, and the capture on f5 is the critical move, opening lines toward the black king while the queenside stands frozen. The game's knight jump to c5 instead led nowhere, and White was gradually outplayed.

Silman's band note says the easy half is seeing White's assets, the pressure on c6 and the kingside chances, and the test is whether you also counted Black's, the b3 target and the b4 grip. Positions in perfect balance punish the player who only reads one side of the ledger.

ex.prompt: Click the square whose ownership decides the whole queenside.
ex.why: If Black gets c5 in, his backward pawn vanishes and White's b3 remains, so the assessment would flip on that single break. White's pieces crowd the square for exactly that reason.

ex.prompt: Assess the position.
ex.why: Symmetrical pressure cancels out, and a player who keeps grinding at a balanced wing is shadow boxing. Reading which part of the board still contains a game is the skill this test isolates.
options: White is much better, c6 is falling
The queenside is in perfect balance, weakness for weakness and square for square, so White's only winning try is on the kingside
Black is better, b3 is weaker than c6
White is strategically lost

ex.prompt: White to move. Play the critical try.
ex.why: Opening the g file gives White real attacking chances, and the book's analysis shows Black surviving only with the precise recapture with the e pawn. The game's Nc5 instead achieved nothing, the queenside stayed level, and Black slowly took over and won.

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 12, level 1400 to 1800
text: Philidor against a French amateur, 1749, the oldest position in the course, and the ask is simply to assess. The great man has just recaptured on e5, and the pawn structure has settled into its final shape.

The position is a tale of two majorities. White owns four against two on the kingside, Black owns four against two on the queenside, and each side's entire future consists of proving his majority matters more. Philidor's handling is the book's exhibit, create the majority, advance it, turn it into a passed pawn, promote the passed pawn, a plan he pursued with such single mindedness that he sacrificed an exchange mid-game just to stay on schedule for the f5 push.

Silman's band note says the problem is solved the moment you noticed both majorities. He adds a story, the ChessBase annotators became so invested in Philidor's plan that when f5 finally landed their note read YES YES, the kind of rapture worth bringing to your own games, even if the move was objectively a blunder in the exact position it arrived.

ex.prompt: Assess the position.
ex.why: Everything either player should do for the next twenty moves is written in the pawn count. Philidor read it perfectly, and his opponent, playing moves one at a time, never realised a race was on.
options: White is better, he has more central space
A race of majorities, four on two for White on the kingside against four on two for Black on the queenside, and each side must push his own
Black is better, White's e5 pawn is weak
Equal and lifeless

ex.prompt: Click the square White's whole plan marches through.
ex.why: The f4 and f5 advance is the kingside majority's first gear, and Philidor steered every piece and pawn toward it for thirty moves, sacrificing material rather than lose the thread. Silman crowns him the pawn whisperer for it.

ex.prompt: What does Philidor's play teach about majorities?
ex.why: At one point the same pawns switched from passer production to king hunting and back, and the game was won by connected passers in the end. One imbalance, read early and served relentlessly, organised every decision of the game.
options: Majorities only matter in endgames
A majority is a plan generator, advance it to create a passer or to smash the king, and let nothing distract you from its needs
Always trade majorities off
Queenside majorities beat kingside ones

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 13, level 1400 to 1800
text: Swiderski against Lee, Ostend 1907, a Caro-Kann that has congealed into a blocked centre. The book asks for an assessment and a move that fits it.

White has space, a protected passed d pawn, and an opponent with no counterplay. Two features decide the plan, Black intends to blockade the passer by routing a knight to d6, and a bishop against knight battle is brewing. So White should trade one pair of knights and post the survivor on the f5 support point, where it fights the d6 blockade and wins the minor piece war outright, since Black's dark squared bishop is condemned to tall pawn duty in front of its own pawns.

Silman's band note takes for granted that a 1400 sees the passer and the coming d6 blockade, awards real credit for the plan of swapping one pair of knights via f5, and extra credit for noticing that the trade leaves White's remaining knight against a tall pawn. The game followed the recipe exactly and the knight outplayed the bishop to the end.

ex.prompt: Assess, and name the plan that fits.
ex.why: A protected passer is only as good as the fight against its blockade. Every element of the plan serves that one fight, and the bishop against knight ledger falls out of it for free.
options: White is better on space alone, advance the kingside pawns
White is better, and the plan is to trade one pair of knights and plant the other on f5, spoiling the d6 blockade and winning the minor piece battle
Equal, the blockade on d6 will hold everything
White should open the f file and double rooks

ex.prompt: White to move. Start the manoeuvre.
ex.why: The knight heads for the hole that black's kingside pawns can never cover. From f5 it pressures g7, meets the d6 blockade head on, and when the knights eventually traded there, White's remaining knight against the tall pawn bishop decided the game.

ex.prompt: Why does trading one pair of knights favour White here?
ex.why: Black's knights are his only pieces that can fight for d6 and f5. Subtract one and the remaining contest is a healthy knight against a wall ornament, which is not a contest at all.
options: It simplifies toward a pawn endgame
It removes Black's only good minor piece, leaving knight against a bishop buried behind its own pawns
It wins the h6 pawn
It prevents castling

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 14, level 1600 to 2000
text: A King's Indian position that has appeared in a few games, and White has just played his knight to the rim with Nh4. The book asks why anyone would play such a move.

The answer lives in the pawn structure. The centre is locked, so both sides need pawn breaks to open files and gain space, and Black's whole position is built around one break above all, f5. Seen through that lens the rim knight makes perfect sense, it clamps down on f5 and cancels Black's main plan, and the sample line shows the break failing tactically the moment Black insists on it anyway.

Silman's band note says the problem is entirely about closed structures and their breaks, and that once you know f5 is Black's idea, Nh4 explains itself, whether or not it is objectively best. The postscript matters too, Black should not panic, moves like c6, Na4 and Bd7 switch the game to the queenside, where the stranded h4 knight cannot follow.

ex.prompt: Why would White put his knight on the rim with Nh4?
ex.why: In locked centres the pieces arrange themselves around the breaks. Rim or not, the knight sits on the one square that vetoes Black's main plan, and understanding that is worth more than any development rule.
options: It heads for the g6 fork
It clamps down on f5, the pawn break Black's whole position depends on
It prepares Nf5 next move
It was a mouse slip that later got fashionable

ex.prompt: How should Black respond to having his main break cancelled?
ex.why: Forcing the break loses material in the book's line, since after the g file opens the g7 bishop and king walk into the fire. A cancelled plan is not a crisis, it is a signal to open a second front, and h4 is a long way from the queenside.
options: Force f5 through anyway
Switch wings without panic, c6, Na4 or Bd7, playing where the stranded knight cannot help
Trade the dark squared bishops
Sacrifice on g4

ex.prompt: Click the square the knight move is really about.
ex.why: Neither player may ever put a piece there, and yet the whole middlegame bends around it. Break squares are worth watching even when they are empty, especially when they are empty.

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 15, level 1600 to 2000
text: A queenside space grabbing line against the Semi Slav, from Bologan against Grischuk, Poikovsky 2004. The question sounds like a trick, does Bb2 make any sense, given that the bishop would sit behind its own d4 pawn looking exactly like a tall pawn?

Answering no shows real understanding and is still wrong. The key is Black's main pawn break, e5, the only way he ever frees his cramped game. The moment that break comes, White captures on e5 and the tall pawn wakes up on the long diagonal as a very fine piece. So Bb2 is not a developing shrug, it is a move aimed at the opponent's only plan, and it is in fact White's most popular choice in the position.

Silman's band note gives an honest half credit to the tall pawn objection from anyone under 1900, because the instinct is sound and only the last step is missing, knowing the ideas for both sides. The game continuation shows the mechanism, e5 arrives, White trades on e5, and the b2 bishop's diagonal opens just as the knight lands on b6.

ex.prompt: Does Bb2 make any sense?
ex.why: A piece is judged against the coming pawn structure, not the current one. Knowing the opponent's only break tells you the diagonal will open, and placing the bishop there in advance is the deep version of development.
options: No, the bishop is a tall pawn behind d4
Yes, Black's freeing break is e5, and when it comes, dxe5 opens the long diagonal and the tall pawn becomes a fine piece
No, the bishop belongs on f4
Yes, but only to defend d4 once

ex.prompt: White to move. Play the move with the future in it.
ex.why: Watch the then moves, Black eventually has to play e5 or suffocate, White captures, and the sleepy bishop suddenly stares through the centre while the a4 knight heads for b6. Grischuk got the break in and still ended up in the less pleasant position.

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 16, level 1600 to 2000
text: A Nimzo Indian that has produced an isolated d pawn for Black, and the question mirrors the earlier King's Indian test, does Nh4 make any sense?

It does, and the isolated pawn recipe explains why. Against an isolani you want to control the square in front of it, swap minor pieces, and steer for queen and rook against queen and rook, where the pawn is a pure weakness with no active pieces to compensate. Nh4 forces the trade of the light squared bishops, one full step of the recipe, and after the follow up the other knight lands on f5 with a small but lasting edge.

Silman's band note frames it as a knowledge test on the isolated d pawn, and adds his standing caution, a rule is a guideline that must be weighed against the position in front of you. Here the rule and the position agree, and even the sideline where Black keeps the bishops hands White the pair and a better game.

ex.prompt: Recite the recipe against an isolated d pawn.
ex.why: Minor pieces are the isolani owner's payment for the weakness, so every trade devalues his position, and the heavy piece ending stamps the pawn as a permanent invalid. The recipe tells you what Nh4 is for before you play it.
options: Blockade it, attack it three times, win it
Control the square in front, swap minor pieces, and aim for queen and rook against queen and rook
Trade queens as fast as possible
Attack on the wing where you have more pawns

ex.prompt: White to move. Apply the recipe.
ex.why: The rim visit lasts one move, the light squared bishops come off, and the second knight arrives on f5 with threats like Nh6 hanging in the air. White kept a small, riskless pull, which is all an isolani position ever promises the better side.

ex.prompt: What if Black avoids the trade with Bg6?
ex.why: Dodging one trade walks into another, and the book's analysis shows the two bishops grinding Black down after the d5 pawn advances and perishes. The recipe wins material or wins concessions, whichever the defender prefers.
options: Black equalises, the bishop is safe
White takes on g6 and keeps two bishops plus pressure on d5, and the endgame lines favour him clearly
White loses time and stands worse
It transposes to the game

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 17, level 1800 to 2200
text: Svidler against Jakovenko, Foros 2007. Black's pieces look active and his plan of Be7 and castling is one move from completion. The question is whether the ugly looking g4 makes any sense for White.

It does, and only for a dynamic reason. Black's king is still in the centre, and the b6 and c4 squares are soft, so the knight leap to c4 begs to be played, threatening the fork on b6. Played at once it fails, since Black takes on f3 and centralises the queen with a fine game, so the g pawn advance is the necessary preparation, blunting that resource and buying the knight its tempo. From there White's pieces gained ground move after move while Black's plans of castling kept being postponed at gunpoint.

Silman's band note approves of feeling spooked by moves like g4, and says the move only makes sense once you have decided the position demands dynamics. When your advantages are temporary, a central king above all, you must play with all the energy you can muster, and weakening squares is simply the entry fee.

ex.prompt: Does g4 make sense here?
ex.why: The immediate knight jump allows the trade on f3 followed by the queen sliding to f5 with comfort. One preparatory pawn lunge turns the same idea into a rolling initiative, and the hole it leaves on f4 never gets a black visitor.
options: No, it wrecks White's king for nothing
Yes, it prepares the Nc4 leap by ruling out the capture on f3, and dynamics are mandatory while the black king sits in the centre
Only after castling queenside
No, simple development keeps an edge

ex.prompt: White to move. Pay the entry fee.
ex.why: Threats now come every move, the b6 fork first, and Black's hoped for Be7 and castling never happens. A few moves later every white piece stood actively, the black king was still in the middle, and the game ended in a rout.

ex.prompt: What general rule does this test rehearse?
ex.why: Temporary advantages spoil like fruit. The central king is the biggest temporary advantage there is, and a player who spends those moves tidying his position instead of cashing them will face a castled opponent and a weakened kingside with nothing to show for either.
options: Never move pawns in front of your king
Decide whether the position is static or dynamic first, and if dynamic, play with maximum energy even at the cost of weaknesses
Develop all pieces before starting play
Always trade queens against a central king

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 18, level 1600 to 2000
text: Timman against Hector, Malmo 2006. Black has just played Be6, and in the game there followed the queen retreat to c2, the knight lunge to c4, and the bishop's retreat all the way to c1. The book asks what you think of those two white moves, and how you assess the position after the second retreat.

Timman's own verdict is the model answer, White has had to withdraw his pieces for the moment, but he keeps holding all the strategic trumps, and the black initiative is short lived. The trumps are worth listing. A hole on b5 beckons the c3 knight. A hole on d5 may come in handy later. Black's queenside majority is devalued, because the single a4 pawn holds back both a5 and b7. And White's central majority becomes a real force after f4, or in some lines the immediate e5.

Silman's band note says the problem sounds hard and dissolves once you spot the holes and the central majority. The rest of the game is the trumps cashing themselves in seemingly effortless fashion, the knight reached b5, the c5 pawn fell, the e pawn marched, and Black was ground down without a single violent move.

ex.prompt: White's pieces just backed up two moves in a row. What is the verdict?
ex.why: Retreats and advantages are independent facts. Every long term feature of the position, both holes, the crippled majority, the central pawns, still belongs to White after the pieces step back, which is exactly what Timman wrote about the moment.
options: White is drifting and Black has taken over
The retreats are fine, White keeps every strategic trump and the black initiative is short lived
White is lost positionally
The retreats blundered the c4 knight... the c4 pawn

ex.prompt: Click the hole that beckons White's queenside knight.
ex.why: The a5 pawn fixed it forever, and once the knight arrives there it eyes d6 and c7 while nothing can ever chase it. The d5 hole is its quieter twin, and owning both is what made the game look effortless.

ex.prompt: Why is Black's queenside pawn majority not a real asset?
ex.why: A majority is only worth the passed pawn it can produce, and this one cannot produce anything. Meanwhile White's central majority needed only f4 or e5 to start rolling, and in the game it rolled straight through the centre to e6.
options: It is too far from the kings
One white pawn on a4 holds back both a5 and b7, so the majority can never advance as a unit
The c5 pawn is passed but weak
Majorities need rooks behind them

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 19, level 1600 to 2100
text: Rabren against girl-brain, an internet game from 2008, and a companion piece to the earlier test from the same player. Black is a piece down but saw that Ng3 regains it, extricating the cornered f1 knight while forking the two bishops. The book asks you to assess the position after that move.

The assessment is that Ng3 loses on the spot, and in the game nobody noticed, White recaptured on g6 and only drew. The refutation is the quiet Bg4, after which every branch fails, taking the f8 bishop lets the g6 capture and the bishop snap on d7 win a piece, taking on f5 runs into the capture on d6, and the pawn grab on f5 meets the same bishop retreat hitting the g3 knight. Three forks promised, none delivered.

Silman's band note calls this an I must problem in mirror image, his own framing said Black would regain the piece and your job was to refuse to buy the smokescreen. Opponents feed you their version of reality all game long, and seeking your own truth in each position is the habit that separates the sceptics from the swindled.

ex.prompt: Black plans Ng3, saving the knight and forking two bishops. Assess the position after it.
ex.why: The fork is real and the escape is not, because one calm move defends everything and keeps the extra piece. In the game both players believed the story, White recaptured on g6 instead and had to settle for an eventual draw from a winning position.
options: Black regains the piece with a fine game
The move loses, White has a quiet bishop retreat to g4 after which no capture works and the knight never escapes
It leads to a forced draw
It wins the exchange at least

ex.prompt: Black has played the knight to g3. Refute the whole idea.
ex.why: The bishop steps out of one fork and breaks the other, and every black try loses material, including this one, where the capture on d6 hits the g3 knight a second time. The cornered knight turns out to have been lost all along, it just needed White to say so.

ex.prompt: What is the habit this pair of tests trains?
ex.why: The problem statement itself asserted that Black regains the piece, and full credit went to readers who refused to accept it. An opponent's confident move order is a claim, not a fact, and I must have a way to punish this is the productive form of doubt.
options: Calculating three moves deep on every turn
Never buying anyone's delusion, including the author's, and demanding your own truth from each position
Avoiding internet blitz
Trading pieces when ahead

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 20, level 1400 to 2000
text: Bacrot against Bologan, Poikovsky 2005, a queenless middlegame with White's king comfortable on e2. Here White played the odd looking retreat Bb1, and the book asks for the point of the move.

The answer is pure target consciousness. Black's isolated d5 pawn is the long term target, and White wants his light squared bishop joining the siege from a2. The direct route fails, since going to b3 allows the knight trade that solves Black's problems, and pushing b4 first weakens the whole c file. So the bishop tucks into the corner, a3 comes to keep b4 covered, and the bishop emerges on a2 with the d5 pawn under permanent watch.

Silman's band note is blunt, if you did not notice that d5 was the target you had no chance on this problem. The game rewarded the plan handsomely, Black loosened his kingside trying for activity, the pieces traded at the right moments, and the two bishops finished the endgame in style.

ex.prompt: What is the point of the retreat Bb1?
ex.why: Every alternative route drops something, b4 hands Black the c file squares and Bb3 invites the trade that frees him. The corner is the only path that arrives with everything intact, and pieces that serve a named target rarely sit badly for long.
options: It avoids the knight trade after Bb3 and prepares a3 and Ba2, adding a whole bishop to the pressure on d5
It clears c2 for the king
It prepares b4 gaining space
It was necessary against the threat of Nd3

ex.prompt: White to move. Start the regrouping.
ex.why: Three quiet moves later the bishop stares at d5 from a2 and every white piece leans on the same point. Black cracked trying to generate play, and the resulting two bishop endgame was a clean win, the whole harvest of one modest retreat.

ex.prompt: Why not simply Bb3 at once?
ex.why: A target is only pressured by pieces that stay on the board. The c5 knight was waiting for exactly that trade, and the little triangle through b1 and a2 reaches the same diagonal while denying it forever.
options: It loses a tempo to a5 and a4
Black trades knight for bishop on b3, removing the attacker and solving his problems
It blocks the b pawn's advance
It allows d4 with equality

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 21, level 1600 to 1800
text: Zakharstov against Sidorov, Russian Championship 2007. White's advantage is built out of small things, the weak d5 and f5 squares, the offside knight on h5, and above all the targets on b6 and d6. The book asks whether the centralising Nd5 is a good idea.

It looks natural and it would be a serious mistake. After the trade and the recapture with the c pawn, the c file opens and the c6 square looks pretty, but the new pawn on d5 permanently covers the d6 weakness, converting White's best target into a protected bystander. The rule is short, when you see an enemy weakness, do not go out of your way to make it inaccessible. The right move was the other leap, to f5, going straight at d6.
Silman's band note passes anyone who saw both halves, that d6 is the prize and that the d5 jump seals it away. In the game the f5 knight won the d6 pawn within eight moves and the game with it.

ex.prompt: Is the centralising Nd5 a good idea?
ex.why: The evaluation still favours White afterward, which is what makes the move so tempting and so instructive. Advantages are cashed through targets, and a move that renders your main target unreachable is a strategic own goal whatever the engine says.
options: Yes, it opens the c file and wins c6 for a piece
No, after the recapture the new d5 pawn shields the d6 weakness forever, sealing away White's best target
Yes, knights belong on d5
No, because the knight is needed on defence

ex.prompt: White to move. Go at the target instead.
ex.why: From f5 the knight attacks d6 directly, the queen and rook join in behind it, and the pawn fell within a few moves, taking the game with it. Same knight, two destinations, and only one of them serves the position's stated purpose.

ex.prompt: State the rule this test exists to teach.
ex.why: Weak squares and weak pawns only matter while your pieces can reach them. It is a rule about restraint, the discipline of leaving a good looking move unplayed because it heals the opponent's worst problem.
options: Centralise knights whenever possible
When you see an enemy weakness, never go out of your way to make it inaccessible
Open files for rooks at any cost
Trade into endgames when you have targets

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 22, level 1400 to 1800
text: Rublevsky against Volkov, Smolensk 1991. The book says that if the hole on e5 hit you in the face and made you long for complete domination of that square, you possess a keen positional eye, and that is the entire test.

Domination of e5 comes first, pressure against the backward e6 pawn follows, and the move flows from the goal. Black's c6 knight is the main defender of e5, so the bishop pins and trades it off, which also relieves the pressure on d4 in the same stroke. Once a white knight lives on e5, its superiority over Black's remaining bishop is beyond dispute.

Silman's band note is a single sentence, you could only solve this if you noticed the hole and wanted it for yourself. The game is a lesson in how fast such positions win themselves, within a dozen moves the knight had hopped through g5 to e6, the queen invaded, and the black king was hunted across the board.

ex.prompt: Click the square that should hit you in the face.
ex.why: A central hole in front of a backward pawn is the strongest kind, because the piece that lands there can never be evicted by a pawn and the e6 pawn behind it needs permanent defence. Everything White plays for the rest of the game flows from this one square.

ex.prompt: White to move. Increase your claim on the square.
ex.why: The knight on c6 is e5's main defender, so it gets traded off, and as a bonus the pressure against d4 disappears. The queen's sidestep already eyes f8, and Black's game collapsed in a handful of moves once the invasion began.

ex.prompt: Why is the coming knight against bishop battle already decided?
ex.why: Superior minor piece is an imbalance you manufacture, not one you are given. Trade the defender, occupy the hole, and the label writes itself, which is why the game reads like a demonstration rather than a fight.
options: Bishops are always worse than knights
The knight will sit on e5 attacking everything while the bishop has no equivalent square and e6 needs babysitting forever
Black's bishop is on the wrong colour
White wins the d5 pawn by force

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 23, level 1800 to 2200
text: Svidler against Bareev, Wijk aan Zee 2004, a French where the pieces came off early. White has a queenside majority, a lead in development and the more active pieces, Black has a central majority and two bishops, and one problem, his king is still in the centre and castling is one move away.

The breakdown decides the move. If Black castles at no cost, his position is simply playable, so White must either prevent castling or make Black pay a price for it, and the knight lunge to c6 does exactly that, exploiting the loose e7 bishop and the b7 fork ideas. Bareev lashed out with e5 to trap the knight and lost by force, and even the best defence, castling into the trade on e7, leaves an endgame where White presses for free.

Silman's band note says you should have demanded something lasting from the position before the king escaped, and that the problem counts as solved if your verbal breakdown matched, castling must be prevented or taxed. The game's finish is the famous part, one more natural looking pawn move and the bishop capture on b7 forced resignation on the spot.

ex.prompt: Give the breakdown that finds White's move.
ex.why: Every static count favours a long game, but the one dynamic fact, the king on e8, has a one move shelf life. Moves that ignore an expiring advantage waste it, which narrows the candidate list to forcing ideas immediately.
options: Trade into the queenside majority endgame
Black is fine the moment he castles for free, so White must prevent castling or make it cost something, right now
Double rooks on the d file
Push the majority with c4 and b4

ex.prompt: White to move. Tax the king.
ex.why: The knight hits e7 and cannot be tolerated, and every reply pays a toll, castling walks into the queen trade and a joyless endgame, while the game's e5 tried to trap the knight and lost the two bishops on the spot. The pawn on f4 then pried at e5 with threats everywhere.

ex.prompt: In the game Black captured on f4. What happened?
ex.why: The centre opened with the king still on e8, which is the whole story of the test told one move deeper. Svidler's finishing shot is the picture to remember whenever an opponent spends tempi on anything but castling.
options: White recaptured with an edge
The bishop took on b7, and the double attack on the rook and the e file pins forced immediate resignation
White gave perpetual check
A long endgame followed

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 24, level 1400 to 2000
text: Gupta against Bhat, Spain 2007, a Botvinnik Semi Slav that has burned down to a strange ruin, White has tripled e pawns and a bishop locked on f7. The book offers mercy, instead of drowning in complications, find a single shred of clarity, the most important square on the board.

The tripled pawns are almost a distraction, because the front one on e6 is passed, and the passed pawn lesson from earlier in the course answers the question, the most important square is the one directly in front of a passer. The answer is e7. White's bishop already contains the h7 rook and guards the promotion square, so the whole game is about claiming e7 so the pawn can step forward.

Silman's band note says that if you understood the e6 pawn was passed, the square in front of it should have named itself. The game's finish is worth the price of admission, the proud e6 pawn sacrificed itself on e7 knowing it would be reincarnated at once by its twin from e5, and the third brother stood behind ready to do it all again.

ex.prompt: Find the single shred of clarity. Click the most important square on the board.
ex.why: The e6 pawn is passed, and a passer's fate is decided on the square directly in front of it. Every white piece already serves the promotion path, so the fight for this one square is the fight for the game.

ex.prompt: Why are the tripled pawns a distraction rather than a weakness here?
ex.why: Structure rules serve the position, never the reverse. Pawns that ugly would be a liability in a quiet middlegame, and here they are a production line, each one ready to replace the last on the sixth rank.
options: Because they can all promote
Because the front one is a protected passer two steps from queening, and the spares behind it are reinforcements, not weaknesses
Because Black cannot attack them
Because the endgame is drawn anyway

ex.prompt: White to move. Fight for the square.
ex.why: The knight protects e6 and prepares the jump to f5, the second claimant of e7. In the game the pawn then gave itself on e7 to drag the bishop onto a doomed square, the e5 pawn was reincarnated on e6 with check, and the knight won the piece back with interest. Black resigned within five moves.

lessons.title: Mixing imbalances test 25, level 1400 to 1800
text: Taimanov against Shishov, Moscow 1959, the final test of the course. Pawn structure tends to dictate the ideas and plans for both sides, and the book's closing question is simply, what is the structure saying in this position?

It is saying three things. White's central wedge points at e5, the advance that gains more space and hands the e1 rook a file. Black's chain points at the queenside, where b5 is his natural break, already prevented by a4, leaving only the e6 lever, and in emergencies f5, which loosens his own king and opens the e file for White. Read that way the position is already uncomfortable for Black, all of his levers are stopped or costly while White's works fine.

Silman's band note says moves are not important here, knowing what the structure expects of you is, and anyone aware of all three breaks has passed with flying colours. Taimanov's next move prepared e5, the entire game revolved around White's ever growing central space, and the rook lift down the h file finished it, a fitting last word for a course about listening to the board.

ex.prompt: What is the structure saying?
ex.why: Chains point at their breaks, and counting whose levers actually function is the fastest honest assessment there is. Three breaks, one working, and it belongs to White, which is the whole game in one sentence.
options: White attacks the king, Black attacks the centre
White's break is e5, Black's are b5, already stopped by a4, and the double edged e6 or f5, so White's plan works and Black's levers are jammed
The position is closed and both sides must wait
Black should trade dark squared bishops and stand equal

ex.prompt: White to move. Serve the structure.
ex.why: The pawn supports the coming e5 advance, and once it lands the centre grows every few moves, e5, then f5 ideas, then the e6 wedge. The whole game revolved around that swelling space until the rook lift ended matters on the h file.

ex.prompt: The course ends here. What is the discipline these twenty five mixing tests drilled?
ex.why: Silman's farewell point is that real games mix imbalances that argue with each other, and the player who names them all, his own and the opponent's, gets high caliber moves almost free of charge. That habit, not any single answer, is what the book was for.
options: Memorising the answers to common positions
Reading every imbalance for both sides first, then letting the moves fall out of the position's own needs
Calculating deeper than the opponent
Choosing openings that avoid imbalances
